title: The Passion of the Christ
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's analysis and Ebert's review document a film built around the unity of Calvary and the Mass, with Mary at its centre. The material objection, the 2003 ad hoc scholars' report on the portrayal of Caiaphas, the priests and the crowd, is now stated with the subtitle change, and the Roman Catechism's teaching on who bears the guilt of the Passion is given. The recommendation is for the 2004 theatrical cut (adults only); the 2005 Recut is noted.
summary: Mel Gibson's Passion, spoken in reconstructed Aramaic and Latin, follows Christ's last twelve hours with relentless physical realism and cuts from Calvary back to the Last Supper.
synopsis: At night in Gethsemane, Jesus (Jim Caviezel) prays while a pale, androgynous Satan tempts him. The Temple guard arrests him and beats him on the way to the high priest. Before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin he is condemned for blasphemy, then handed to Pilate. Pilate sends him to Herod, offers the crowd Barabbas, and orders a scourging in the hope that it will be enough. It is long and savage. Jesus carries the cross to Golgotha, helped by Simon of Cyrene, as Mary (Maia Morgenstern), John and Mary Magdalene follow. Flashbacks to the Sermon on the Mount, the woman taken in adultery and the Last Supper break up the march. Judas, harried by children who turn into demons, hangs himself. After the crucifixion an earthquake shakes the Temple, and a brief final shot shows the Resurrection.
inclusion: Gibson's subject is sacrifice, and the editing argues it. As Christ is nailed and the cross raised, the film cuts back to the Last Supper, so the bread and cup are shown as the same offering as Calvary. Steven Greydanus ties this to the Catholic teaching that the Mass and the Cross are one sacrifice. Mary is the other centre. Morgenstern plays her with almost no dialogue, and her run to her fallen Son, intercut with a memory of catching him as a child, is the film's most affecting scene. Caleb Deschanel's dark, candle-lit photography and the dead languages strip away Hollywood-biblical diction. Roger Ebert, who admired it, still called it the most violent film he had ever seen. The violence is the point and also the limit: it can numb as easily as it moves, and the Resurrection is a few seconds long.
themes: The Eucharistic frame carries the theology: the Mass is shown as a sharing in Calvary, not a memorial meal. Mary is shown as co-sufferer, and the two Marys wiping up the blood of the scourging with linen is a devotion to the Precious Blood. Satan moves through the crowds and at one point carries a deformed infant, a parody of Madonna and Child that Greydanus links to Genesis 3:15. The Catechism of the Council of Trent teaches that sinners are the authors of Christ's sufferings, and that the guilt is greater in Christians who sin knowingly than in the Jews who took part. The film's dramatic weight falls heavily on Caiaphas and the Temple crowd, and that teaching is the corrective.
history: The Gospels record the arrest, the hearing before the high priest, Pilate's sentence, the scourging and the crucifixion briefly. Caiaphas held office at the pleasure of the Roman prefect, and only Pilate could order a crucifixion. Before release, a group of four Catholic and three Jewish scholars, convened by staff of the US bishops' interreligious office and the Anti-Defamation League, reviewed a draft script. Their May 2003 report was informal, not an official statement of the bishops' conference. It argued that the script made Caiaphas the driving force and Pilate a reluctant bystander, and that it cast the Temple and the crowd as bloodthirsty. The group later said the finished film was largely the same as the script.
liberties: Much extra-biblical material comes from Anne Catherine Emmerich's Dolorous Passion: Jesus thrown in chains from a bridge, Pilate's wife bringing linens to Mary, Satan's presence throughout, and the demonic children who drive Judas to despair. Mary Magdalene is identified with the woman taken in adultery. Pilate is more troubled and sympathetic than Philo and Josephus describe him. The Romans speak Latin, where Greek is more likely. Caiaphas's 'His blood be on us and on our children' (Matthew 27:25) is still spoken, but it was left unsubtitled before release.
advisories:
Extremely graphic violence for long stretches: the beating, scourging, carrying of the cross and nailing are shown in detail with heavy bloodshed. The original cut was rated 18 in the UK.

Demonic imagery; a crow pecks out a crucified thief's eye; Judas hangs himself.

Not for children. Many adults find it overwhelming. The Recut (2005) removes about five minutes of the worst violence but is still very violent.

The portrayal of Caiaphas, the priests and the crowd has been criticised as reviving the charge that the Jews as a people killed Christ. Trent's Catechism places that guilt on sinners, Christians first.

title: The Song of Bernadette
decision: PUBLISH: AFI's production history, Steven Greydanus and John Clark document a reverent treatment of the Lourdes apparitions and of Bernadette's suffering at Nevers. The Werfel inventions (the Antoine romance, Peyramale at the deathbed, the villainous Dutour, Sister Vauzous's backstory) are now listed and do not change the religious meaning.
summary: Henry King's Oscar-winning Lourdes epic, with Jennifer Jones as a slow, guileless Bernadette, is long and studio-bound but takes her hidden suffering as seriously as the visions.
synopsis: Lourdes, 1858. Bernadette Soubirous, the sickly eldest child of a ruined miller living in a disused jail, sees a lady in white in the grotto of Massabielle. She keeps returning as she was asked; crowds follow, and a spring rises where she digs. The imperial prosecutor Vital Dutour and the police commissioner try to stop the visits and have her declared insane. Dean Peyramale is suspicious until the Lady gives her name, 'I am the Immaculate Conception'. The diocese opens an inquiry and cures are reported. To shield her from the curious, Bernadette enters the Sisters of Charity at Nevers. There her old schoolteacher, now novice mistress Sister Marie Thérèse Vauzous, resents the favour shown to a dull peasant girl. A painful disease of the bone in her leg is kept hidden until it is far advanced, and she dies young.
inclusion: Jennifer Jones won the Academy Award for a performance built on stillness: her Bernadette is not clever and is not trying to persuade anyone. Arthur Miller's black-and-white photography and Alfred Newman's score also won Oscars, and Gladys Cooper is formidable as Vauzous. Steven Greydanus notes that the third act turns from marvels to the meaning of suffering, and that is the film's best stretch. The film has weaknesses. At about two and a half hours it is slow. Lourdes is a Fox backlot. Vincent Price's sneering prosecutor belongs in a melodrama. Franz Werfel, the Jewish novelist who wrote the source novel to keep a vow made while hiding in Lourdes in 1940, adds romance and villainy the real story does not need. Still, it remains the best-known Lourdes film for good reason.
themes: The apparitions are treated as real but tested. Clergy, family and state all doubt Bernadette, and the film lets the doubt land. The Lady's name, 'I am the Immaculate Conception', comes four years after the dogma's definition and is the turning point for Peyramale. Greydanus notes that the film never explains why that phrase convinced him. Penance, prayer for sinners and the spring are presented plainly. In the Nevers section, holiness is ordinary work, humiliation and pain accepted without complaint. Linda Darnell plays the Lady, unbilled and briefly glimpsed, which keeps the image modest.
history: Bernadette Soubirous (1844–1879) reported eighteen apparitions between February and July 1858. The Bishop of Tarbes recognised them in 1862. She entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers in 1866, died there of tuberculosis of the bone in 1879, and was canonised in 1933. The film premiered in Los Angeles on 25 December 1943 and opened in New York in January 1944. After long roadshow engagements, it went into general release in 1945.
liberties: Antoine Nicolau, a real acquaintance, is turned into a devoted suitor who vows never to marry; no such romance is documented. Peyramale died in 1877, so he was not at Bernadette's deathbed. Vital Dutour, said to have been a practising Catholic who thought her deluded, is played as an anticlerical villain and given an invented end, dying of throat cancer at the grotto; he is also merged with another of Werfel's officials. There is no evidence that Sister Vauzous taught Bernadette in Lourdes, and her final repentance is invented.
advisories:
Suitable for older children and up; long.

Illness, a painful leg disease and a deathbed scene.

Some priests and nuns behave harshly or unjustly before relenting.

title: Bernadette
decision: PUBLISH: LUMIERE and Allociné settle identity (CH/FR/LU co-production, French release 17 February 1988). Steven Greydanus's detailed review documents a restrained, historically careful treatment that never shows the Lady. The conflicting accounts of the French and English versions are recorded. Independent secular criticism is thin; Le Monde's 1988 review is paywalled.
summary: Jean Delannoy's plain, careful account of the Lourdes apparitions never shows the Lady, and relies instead on Sydney Penny's spirited, unsentimental Bernadette.
synopsis: Lourdes, 1858. Fourteen-year-old Bernadette Soubirous, from a family sunk in poverty, goes to gather wood by the grotto of Massabielle and sees a small young lady in white in a niche of the rock. She returns again and again. Neighbours, the police commissioner, the imperial prosecutor and the formidable Dean Peyramale question her. Some want her to recant; others want her shut away. She will not add to or subtract from what she has said, even when officials try to trip her up. The crowds grow, a spring appears, cures are claimed, and the Lady at last names herself the Immaculate Conception. The film ends as the apparitions give way to the question of what to do with a girl whom everyone now wants to see. Her life as a nun is left to the sequel.
inclusion: Delannoy, a veteran of postwar French cinema, makes a sober chronicle rather than a Hollywood pageant. Shooting near Lourdes lends weight that Fox's backlot lacked. The visions are staged by sound and face, not effects: the noise of the river drops away, a simple Francis Lai theme plays, and we watch Bernadette. Greydanus credits fifteen-year-old Sydney Penny with 'spirit, even tartness'. Her Bernadette answers doctors and clerics with disconcerting directness, which is closer to the documented girl than Jennifer Jones's dreamy saint. The weaknesses are practical. The look is televisual. The English dub is awkward. And it was little seen outside France and the shrine, where it was screened for pilgrims for years.
themes: The film is about testimony. Bernadette is asked again and again to repeat exactly what she saw and heard, and her refusal to embellish becomes the evidence. The Church appears as cautious rather than credulous: Dean Peyramale wants the Lady's name before he will believe anything. The name, 'I am the Immaculate Conception', comes four years after the dogma was defined, from a girl who did not know the term. The Lady's calls for penance and prayer for sinners are given plainly. Because she is never shown, the viewer's attention stays on the witness, which is an honest way to film a private revelation.
history: Bernadette reported eighteen apparitions between 11 February and 16 July 1858. Her interrogations by Commissioner Jacomet and Prosecutor Dutour were documented, and René Laurentin later published the records. The Bishop of Tarbes recognised the apparitions in 1862. Delannoy shot each scene in both French and English in 1987, and the film opened in France on 17 February 1988.
liberties: Dialogue is reconstructed and the eighteen apparitions are selected and compressed. No detailed scholarly comparison with the documents has been found; Greydanus judges it unembellished. Accounts of the English version conflict: the distributor says each language was performed directly, while Greydanus says the English track was redubbed.
advisories:
Family viewing; Greydanus reports nothing objectionable.

A poor, sick child is interrogated and bullied by adults in authority.

title: The Passion of Bernadette
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review documents an earnest, reverent account of Bernadette's convent years, with a specific medical-image advisory. Year corrected to 1990: AlloCiné gives production year 1990 and French release 9 May 1990; the 1989 date used by Decent Films and MUBI has no release behind it that we could find.
summary: Delannoy's sequel follows Bernadette's thirteen years at Nevers, where obscurity, a suspicious novice mistress and bone tuberculosis replace the drama of Lourdes; quieter and less shapely than the first film.
synopsis: In 1866, eight years after the apparitions, Bernadette (Sydney Penny again) enters the Sisters of Charity at Saint-Gildard in Nevers, hoping to disappear. Her superiors decide that the famous visionary must not be allowed to think herself special. The novice mistress watches for pride. Bernadette is corrected for slipping away to pray at the convent's grotto during recreation. She also learns to work in the infirmary, where she nurses a blind old nun with a festering sore and rounds sharply on a postulant who recoils from it. A wounded soldier is brought in. Visitors still ask to see her; she wants none of it. Her own illness, tuberculosis of the bone, worsens year by year, and the film follows her to her death in 1879 at thirty-five.
inclusion: Few films about saints try to dramatise the long middle of a religious life: obedience, routine, bad health and other people. This one does, and that is its value. Penny is again strong. The Catholic News Service reviewer praised her 'down-to-earth sanctity', and Delannoy's period detail is careful. Steven Greydanus, who rates it lower than the first film, is right that it does not really tell a story; it is a sequence of convent episodes. The supporting cast includes Emmanuelle Riva and Georges Wilson. The US release defaults to an English dub, which flattens the performances; the original French with subtitles is the better choice.
themes: The hidden life is the subject: a visionary who has to be ordinary. Obedience to superiors, including unjust ones, is shown as costly but not foolish. Charity to the sick is concrete and unglamorous: she cleans a wound others will not touch. Her suffering is offered rather than explained, and the film does not turn illness into a spectacle of holiness. The superiors' suspicion of a famous young nun has some historical basis. The film presents it as a real trial without making the community villains.
history: Bernadette entered Saint-Gildard in July 1866 and made her profession in 1867. She worked as an infirmarian and sacristan and spent long periods ill. She died on 16 April 1879. Her body was exhumed in 1909 during the beatification process, and she was canonised in 1933. The film was produced in 1990 and released in France on 9 May 1990; US sources often date it 1989.
liberties: Convent episodes are selected and dialogue invented; the long periods of illness are compressed. Greydanus raises in passing the question of whether Penny's mannerisms suggest a developmental condition. That is the reviewer's speculation, not a documented trait of the saint.
advisories:
A brief, graphic glimpse of an ulcerated female breast during a medical procedure; a bloodied soldier; an ugly bedsore.

Illness, pain and a deathbed.

Greydanus thinks it suitable for children. Preview the medical scene for younger viewers.

title: The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima
originalTitle: The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima
decision: PUBLISH: with a historical caution. AFI's detailed production history and Greydanus's review document both the reverent apparition narrative and the specific inventions: the agnostic peddler Hugo, a Cold War 'socialist People's Republic' in place of Portugal's anticlerical liberal republic, and the detention moved and enlarged. All are now disclosed, and none touches the apparitions themselves. This is consistent with La Señora de Fátima (1951) staying on HOLD: that film is held for lack of any treatment evidence, not for having the same problems.
summary: Warner Bros.' colour Fatima drama is reverent toward the children and the Lady but recasts 1917 Portugal as a Cold War police state and adds a lovable fictional rogue.
synopsis: An opening narration tells of a 'socialist minority' that has seized Portugal and built a police state to crush the Church. In May 1917 Lúcia (Susan Whitney) and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta see a Lady above a holm oak at the Cova da Iria. Lúcia's mother calls her a liar, and the parish priest, Father Ferreira, is sceptical. Only Hugo (Gilbert Roland), an agnostic wandering peddler, humours the children, advising them to keep quiet. The local administrator Arturo closes the church, arrests the priest and finally has the children abducted. They are jailed with criminals and Hugo and threatened, but they refuse to recant. On 13 October an enormous crowd waits in the rain. The sun spins and plunges, the sick are healed, the ground dries, and Hugo believes.
inclusion: This is a well-made studio picture, shot in Warnercolor with location footage from the 1951 anniversary at Fatima. Max Steiner's score was Oscar-nominated, and the miracle of the sun is staged with real ambition. The three children are believable, and the film takes their prayer, fear and stubbornness seriously. The weaknesses are typical of 1952 Hollywood. Characters are types, and Greydanus finds Susan Whitney's Lúcia mostly anxious tearfulness. Gilbert Roland's charming rogue takes over too much of the story, and the politics are a Cold War sermon. Greydanus judges it short of The Song of Bernadette, and later called it more embellished than The 13th Day. As an introduction for families it still works, provided the history is corrected.
themes: The Lady's requests (the daily Rosary, prayer and sacrifice for sinners, the promise of a sign) are given clearly, and the children's endurance under threat is the film's moral spine. Hugo's arc turns the miracle into a story of conversion. The Cova da Iria is presented as a place of public prayer that the state cannot suppress. Fatima is a private revelation, recognised by the Bishop of Leiria in 1930. The film's dramatisation of the Lady's words is an interpretation, not a record.
history: Portugal's First Republic, set up in 1910, was liberal and fiercely anticlerical. It separated Church and State in 1911 and harassed clergy, but it was not a socialist people's republic. Lúcia dos Santos and Francisco and Jacinta Marto reported six apparitions from 13 May to 13 October 1917, preceded in 1916 by visits of an angel. In August 1917 the Ourém administrator, Artur de Oliveira Santos, took the children away and held and threatened them for about two days. Tens of thousands witnessed the solar phenomenon on 13 October.
liberties: Hugo is invented, and Father Ferreira and the administrator are fictionalised. The narration's 'socialist' police state recasts the 1910 republic in Cold War terms; Greydanus calls the villains 'militant Marxists'. The angel apparitions of 1916 are omitted. The children's detention is moved to October and enlarged into a jail term among criminals. The narration gives 15 May for the first apparition (it was Sunday 13 May), and the sun falls once instead of twice.
advisories:
Children are abducted, jailed and threatened; family anger and mockery.

Otherwise mild; suitable for families with some explanation.

title: Our Lady of Fatima
decision: PUBLISH: a contemporary Spanish review (Alfonso Sánchez, Hoja del Lunes, Madrid, 22 October 1951) and María Aimaretti's scene-level study (Accadere 7, 2024) establish a devout pre-conciliar telling of the apparitions, faithful in substance to Lucía's account (rosary, reparation, the warning about Russia, the miracle of the sun), with disclosed political anachronism (a Marxist villain) and an invented convert. Aimaretti is critical of the film's national-Catholic politics but reports no doctrinal problem. The subject is the apparitions approved in 1930, not Francisco and Jacinta (canonised 2017), so rule 1 does not apply. Editor may prefer GREY 'reservations' for the political transposition.
summary: Rafael Gil's Spanish account of the 1917 Fátima apparitions, told through Lucía's trials at home and at the hands of anticlerical officials, ending with the miracle of the sun.
synopsis: Portugal, 1917: the country is at war and its republican government is hostile to the Church. Near Fátima, Lucía, a devout shepherd girl, and her young cousins Francisco and Jacinta see a Lady above a holm oak who asks them to pray the rosary. Lucía's home is falling apart: her father drinks and sells off land, her brother leaves for the front, and her disbelieving mother has the village women try to make her retract; her father beats her. The district chief Oliveira, an atheist revolutionary, and the lawyer Duarte try to stop the cult. Oliveira holds the children and threatens Lucía with a furnace. On 13 October a vast crowd gathers in the rain, the sun spins, the Lady names herself Our Lady of the Rosary, the sick are healed and Duarte is converted.
inclusion: This is the Spanish Fátima film, made by Vicente Escrivá's Aspa Films, the most consistent of the 1950s Spanish Catholic production companies, and released in October 1951 as the Holy Year closed at Fátima. It was a major success. Aimaretti records 56 weeks in a Madrid cinema, national prizes and papal approval at its Rome premiere, and Alfonso Sánchez in Hoja del Lunes praised its simple, fervent telling. Gil shows the Virgin in fragments, the hem of a mantle, bare feet, light and a voice, rather than in full, and Michel Kelber's photography sets Lucía's moonlit room against a home full of shadows. Inés Orsini, the Maria Goretti of Heaven Over the Marshes, plays Lucía. Its weaknesses are a cardboard Marxist villain and politics that belong to Franco's Spain more than to 1917 Portugal.
themes: The faith on screen is the Fátima message as Lucía recorded it: the rosary, suffering offered in reparation for sin, the warning that Russia would spread her errors, and conversion as the fruit of a child's obedience. Lucía bears beatings, mockery and threats without complaint, and the healings and the lawyer's conversion are shown as the Virgin's answer. Aimaretti reads the film as a hagiography of a Marian daughter. One study notes that the priests, like the politicians, must be won over through Lucía. The anti-communism is explicit, and the ending joins the fictional pilgrims to documentary footage of the sanctuary's later crowds.
history: Between May and October 1917 Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto reported apparitions of the Virgin at the Cova da Iria near Fátima. In August the local administrator, Artur Santos, detained and threatened the children. On 13 October a crowd of tens of thousands reported that, after rain, the sun appeared to spin. The Bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in 1930, and Pius XII's legate crowned the image in 1946.
liberties: The administrator who detains the children is turned into Oliveira, a Marxist plotting to impose communism, an anachronism Aimaretti reads as aimed at Spain's Second Republic. The lawyer Duarte and his conversion are invented. The threat against Lucía is staged in a cellar furnace room, and the women's attempt to make her recant is presented as a kind of exorcism. The closing documentary montage of later pilgrimages is the film's own addition.
advisories:
A girl is beaten by her father and threatened with burning by an official; the furnace-room scene is intense.

A drunken father and family poverty.

Suitable for older children with an adult; younger ones may find the interrogation frightening.

The politics are crudely anti-communist and project the Spanish Civil War onto 1917 Portugal.

title: Apparitions at Fatima
decision: GREY: Greydanus documents a faithful telling of the apparitions from Lúcia's memoirs, but the film closes on premiere footage of John Paul II greeting the cast, which frames it as a tribute to the post-conciliar papacy. Reservation rather than rejection because the drama itself is the 1917 apparitions.
summary: Daniel Costelle's sober docudrama of the 1917 Fátima apparitions, shot at the Cova da Iria with a largely amateur cast and dialogue taken from Lúcia's memoirs.
synopsis: In 1917, in the hill country around Fátima, the shepherd children Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto report that a Lady from heaven has appeared to them at the Cova da Iria. The film follows the apparitions from May to October in a mixture of drama and documentary, with the dialogue drawn from the memoirs Lúcia later wrote. It gives full weight to the vision of hell that terrifies Jacinta, and to the penances the children take on for sinners: going without water in the summer heat and wearing a rope tied tightly round their waists, which the Lady tells them not to wear at night. The film closes with a postscript of premiere footage in which Pope John Paul II and Sister Lúcia greet the three young actors.
inclusion: Steven Greydanus judges this the most faithful screen account of Fátima, more accurate and spiritually serious than Hollywood's The Miracle of Our Lady of Fatima. In a later piece he calls it the film to beat for fidelity, though not compelling art. Costelle, a French documentary-maker, worked with the shrine's cooperation and built the script on Lúcia's memoirs. The mostly amateur cast is good, and the real locations, the Cova da Iria above all, give it an authenticity no studio could. Its limits are plain: a small budget, very simple effects for the visions, and narration and music that sometimes intrude. It suits families and anyone who wants the events without dramatic invention. The 13th Day (2009) is the more artful film; this is the more literal one.
themes: The message of 1917 is given straight: prayer, sacrifice for sinners and the reality of hell, which Greydanus notes the film does not soften as the Hollywood version did. The children's penances are shown as the heart of their response, with the Lady moderating them, a detail taken from Lúcia's account. Because the dialogue comes from her memoirs, the film presents her testimony rather than a screenwriter's reworking of it. Fátima is a private revelation, approved by the Bishop of Leiria in 1930; the film's images of the Lady are a reconstruction of that testimony.
history: Lúcia dos Santos (1907–2005) and her cousins Francisco (1908–1919) and Jacinta Marto (1910–1920) reported six apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria between May and October 1917, preceded by apparitions of an angel in 1916. Both Marto children died in the influenza epidemic. Lúcia became a religious and wrote her memoirs between 1935 and 1941. The Bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in 1930.
liberties: Greydanus notes no significant inventions; the dialogue is drawn from Lúcia's memoirs. A documentary-style voice-over links the episodes, which Greydanus finds sometimes intrusive. The apparitions are necessarily a reconstruction, staged with very simple effects.
advisories:
The vision of hell is shown directly and may frighten young children.

The children's self-imposed penances, including going without water and wearing a tight rope.

Greydanus finds nothing objectionable and rates it for children and up.

The postscript presents John Paul II's welcome as the film's endorsement; it is a coda, separate from the drama.

title: The 13th Day
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's detailed review documents a reverent, artful film that stays close to Lúcia's memoirs, and lists its liberties. The Fátima sanctuary's 2009 announcement and Companies House confirm the British production company, credits and world premiere. A reader's documented objection about frightening scenes is reflected in the advisory.
summary: Two illustrator brothers made this low-budget, mostly black-and-white Fatima film as Sister Lúcia's memory, with painterly images and a closer fidelity to her memoirs than Hollywood managed.
synopsis: In a convent in Spain, Sister Lúcia, now an adult, writes one of her memoirs, and the film unfolds as her recollection. In 1917 Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta are shepherd children near Fátima when a Lady appears to them at the Cova da Iria and asks them to return on the thirteenth of each month. They pray the Rosary, make sacrifices, and are shown a vision of hell. Lúcia's family disbelieves her; the town administrator abducts the children and threatens them. Crowds grow despite mockery from the press. On 13 October, in pouring rain, tens of thousands see the sun dance. The film closes back with the aging memory of the nun at her desk.
inclusion: Ian and Dominic Higgins were illustrators before directing, and it shows. Shot cheaply on digital video, the film is mostly black and white with spots of colour, soft-focused and composed like paintings. Steven Greydanus compares its frames to Vermeer and the austerity of Bresson. It moves in vignettes rather than scenes, almost like a silent film with dialogue, which some viewers will find static. The digital effects in the miracle of the sun are more effective than the budget suggests. Greydanus called it the best Fatima film, closer to the historical record than the 1952 Warner film and more artful than the 1992 Portuguese Aparição. The acting is modest and the English dialogue a little stiff.
themes: The content of the 1917 message is front and centre: daily Rosary, penance and sacrifice for sinners, the vision of hell, and the call for the consecration of Russia. The children's willingness to suffer for others is treated as the heart of the story rather than as an afterthought to the miracle. Lúcia's memory frame reminds the viewer that we know these events through her written testimony. That testimony is a private revelation, approved by the Bishop of Leiria in 1930, and the film's images of the Lady and of hell are an artist's rendering of it.
history: Lúcia dos Santos (1907–2005) and her cousins Francisco (d. 1919) and Jacinta Marto (d. 1920) reported six apparitions from May to October 1917. Lúcia wrote her memoirs between 1935 and 1941 as a Dorothean sister in Spain; she entered the Carmel of Coimbra only in 1948. The film was produced by 13th Day Films Ltd and shot in Portugal and England. It had its world premiere at the Fátima sanctuary on 13 October 2009.
liberties: Greydanus notes that the 1916 angel apparitions are omitted and that the six apparitions are condensed to four on screen. Lúcia's father is drawn differently from the account in Fr. John de Marchi's history. Lúcia is played as reserved, where the historical girl was outgoing.
advisories:
A vision of hell and other fleeting infernal imagery; children are imprisoned and threatened.

Greydanus watched it with his young family without trouble, but a reader reported that his children found it frightening. Preview for under-tens.

title: The Miracle of Marcelino
decision: PUBLISH: Two independent Spanish analyses (Instituto Cervantes; Vida Nueva) describe the treatment of the crucifix scenes and the ending in detail, and the Danish Film Institute and festival record settle identity. The film is a literary fable, not a claimed miracle, and the child's death is clearly advised.
summary: Ladislao Vajda's Spanish classic about a foundling raised by friars who feeds bread and wine to the crucifix in the attic: tender, beautifully lit, and unashamedly a tearjerker.
synopsis: At a village feast, a friar (Fernando Rey) visits a sick girl and tells her family how the feast began. After the war against Napoleon, a few Franciscans rebuild a ruined building as their friary and find a baby abandoned at the door. They fail to find him a family, so twelve friars raise Marcelino among them, each with a nickname and a trade. At five he is mischievous, lonely and longs for the mother he never knew. He is forbidden the attic, goes up anyway, and finds a large crucifix. Thinking the man looks hungry, he steals bread and wine from the kitchen for him. The figure comes down from the cross, eats, and talks with him. Asked what he wants most, Marcelino asks to see his mother. Fray Papilla, spying through the door, sees the miracle.
inclusion: Six-year-old Pablito Calvo gives one of cinema's most natural child performances, and the friars, each a gentle comic type, are warmly drawn. Enrique Guerner's lighting makes the attic scenes glow. The Cervantes essay notes that Christ is shown almost only through his hands, and that the miracle is signalled by changes of light rather than spectacle. That discretion keeps the film on the right side of kitsch. It won a Silver Bear at Berlin and a special mention for Calvo at Cannes in 1955, and it was a huge international success. It is also deliberately heartbreaking. The critic José Luis Guarner called it 'un cuento para niños que parece un cilicio' (a children's tale that feels like a hair shirt). The English dub on some US discs is poor; choose the Spanish track.
themes: The crucifix in the attic becomes a real person to a lonely child, and his instinct is charity: the hungry should be fed. Bread and wine carried to Christ recall the Eucharist without staging a Mass, and the title, 'Marcelino, bread and wine', makes the link explicit. Christ's answer to the boy's longing is heaven: he takes Marcelino to his mother, and the boy dies in his sleep. The friars' household shows religious life as a family. Fray Papilla's witness turns the story into the origin of a local devotion. The film treats the miracle as a pious tale, which is what Sánchez-Silva's story is.
history: José María Sánchez-Silva published Marcelino Pan y Vino (Cuento de padres a hijos) in 1953 and co-wrote the screenplay with Vajda. Vajda was a Hungarian-born Jewish director who had settled in Spain in 1942. The film was shot in 1954 and premiered in Spain on 24 February 1955. It is unrelated to any recorded miracle.
liberties: It is fiction based on a literary fable. Vida Nueva notes that the film heightens the light-and-dark contrasts of the death scene well beyond the book. Later remakes, Luigi Comencini's Marcellino (1991) and a Mexican Marcelino pan y vino (2010), as well as an animated series (2000), are different works.
advisories:
The death of a small child (shown as falling asleep in Christ's arms), and his longing for his dead mother.

Very sad; younger children need an adult to talk it through.

No violence or sexual content.

title: Mary of Nazareth
decision: GREY: A 2012 Lux Vide production. The only reviews are from post-conciliar Catholic outlets (Aleteia, DeCine21, iObserve, and Catholic World Report, which is published by the US distributor), so they establish what the film contains but cannot serve as approving evidence under the Founder's position. No independent assessment of its theology exists.
summary: Lux Vide's life of the Virgin Mary from her girlhood in the Temple to Easter morning, carried by Alissa Jung's grave, quiet performance.
synopsis: Joachim and Anna give their young daughter Mary to be raised at the Temple. Her childhood friend Mary of Magdala drifts instead into the court of Herod Antipas and Herodias. Betrothed to the carpenter Joseph, Mary receives the angel's message, visits Elizabeth and returns pregnant to a village that scorns her; Joseph, after a dream, takes her as his wife and accepts that their marriage will be unlike others. The Nativity, the Presentation and the flight into Egypt follow. Years later Joseph dies, Jesus begins to preach, and Magdalene, rescued from stoning, becomes His follower. Mary follows her Son to Calvary, and on the third day the risen Christ appears to Magdalene and then to His mother.
inclusion: Most screen lives of Christ treat Mary as a face in the crowd. This one puts her at the centre, and Alissa Jung, a German actress, makes her quiet, firm and believable as a young woman whose 'yes' costs her something. Luca Marinelli's Joseph is the supporting performance every reviewer praises. Campiotti grounds the Gospel in daily work, with Mary salting bread as Jesus speaks of the salt of the earth. This is conventional television filmmaking: David Ives finds it only a little better than most TV fare, and DeCine21 faults the poor ageing of the cast and a melodramatic Herodias. The Magdalene subplot is pure invention, and in the shortened version, as Cooney and Ford both note, the cuts leave the two Marys' friendship confusing.
themes: The film presents Mary as the obedient handmaid whose fiat is the hinge of the story, with the Magnificat, Simeon's prophecy of the sword and her presence at the Cross all given weight. Her virginal conception is stated plainly, and Joseph's acceptance of a virginal marriage is handled with tact. Christ's divinity, miracles, Passion and Resurrection are affirmed, and Mary sees the risen Christ after Magdalene. Ives credits it with keeping its theology straight, though he dislikes one line suggesting dogs can smell sin. DeCine21 notes a real effort not to contradict the Gospels, and Cooney likens its additions to the medieval pious legends.
history: The Gospels say little of Mary's life outside the infancy narratives and the Passion. The film draws on the tradition of her presentation in the Temple and of Joachim and Anna, found in the Protoevangelium of James. It was shot in English in Tunisia and broadcast in two parts on Rai 1 at Easter 2012.
liberties: Mary and Mary Magdalene are made childhood friends, and Magdalene is given a past at Herod's court and identified with the woman saved from stoning and the woman who anointed Jesus' feet, a Western tradition the film follows freely. Herodias is drawn from medieval legend as something of a sorceress. Mary's wedding, Joseph's death and episodes from Jesus' childhood are invented. The 153-minute version drops an early meeting between the two Marys.
advisories:
The massacre of the innocents is violent, and the scourging and crucifixion are shown with some graphic detail, though far less than in The Passion of the Christ.

An attempted stoning.

Magdalene falls into prostitution at Herod's court; implied, not shown explicitly.

Suitable for families with older children, not the very young. An English song over the end credits jars.

title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's detailed review, Criterion's edition notes and the film's well-documented history establish Dreyer's use of the trial record, the sacramental climax (confession and Communion before the burning) and the unhistorical riot. The judges' cruelty is presented as that of particular men, while Joan seeks Christ through the Church's sacraments.
summary: Dreyer compresses Joan's months of trial into one day of faces in close-up, and Renée Falconetti gives what may be the greatest performance in silent film.
synopsis: Rouen, 1431. Joan (Renée Falconetti), nineteen and in chains, is led before a tribunal of churchmen and university doctors, with English soldiers at the door. They question her about her voices, her male dress and her mission, and try to trap her: will she say the Our Father? Is she in a state of grace? A forged letter from the king is used to deceive her, and she is shown the instruments of torture. Exhausted and ill, she is bled. Facing the fire, she signs a recantation and her head is shaved. Then she retracts, saying she betrayed God to save her life. A sympathetic young priest hears her confession and gives her Communion. She is burned in the market square, and the watching crowd rises against the soldiers and is beaten back.
inclusion: Dreyer built the film almost entirely from close-ups of unpowdered faces against bare white walls. There are hardly any establishing shots, so the viewer is trapped in the interrogation with Joan. Falconetti, a stage actress who never made another major film, plays Joan as frightened, peasant-plain and immovable. Her face is the film. The dialogue intertitles are drawn from the trial record, compressed so that months feel like one day. Greydanus finds some religious films more theologically profound and some of the trial dialogue confusing, but few films convey so physically what it costs to stay faithful. Watch the Gaumont restoration; Richard Einhorn's oratorio Voices of Light is the most admired accompaniment.
themes: Joan's anguish turns on the sacraments. Her judges withhold confession and Communion to break her, and the climax is not the burning but her reception of the Eucharist from a compassionate priest. Greydanus notes that her refusal to say the Our Father, which the judges treated as a test for possession, was historically a request to say it in confession. Dreyer links her mocking by soldiers to the mocking of Christ. The judges are clerics acting for English political interests, and the film shows them as men abusing an office, not as the voice of the Church, which later annulled the verdict and canonised her in 1920.
history: Joan of Arc was captured at Compiègne in 1430, sold to the English, and tried for heresy at Rouen under Bishop Pierre Cauchon from January to May 1431. She was burned on 30 May 1431. A papally authorised retrial annulled the sentence in 1456, and she was canonised in 1920. Dreyer drew on Pierre Champion's 1921 edition of the trial records.
liberties: Many sessions spread over months are compressed into what feels like a single day. The closing riot in the square is Dreyer's invention, inspired by Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin. Characters among the judges are composites. The Archbishop of Paris and the censors cut scenes before the Paris premiere; the restored Oslo print is Dreyer's uncut version.
advisories:
Burning at the stake shown graphically; the instruments of torture; medicinal bloodletting; the crowd is clubbed by soldiers.

Sustained distress rather than gore. Greydanus thinks older children can watch it; it is silent, slow-paced and intense.

title: Joan of Arc
alternateTitles: The Life of Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH (restored 145-minute version): the AFI Catalog's cutting-continuity synopsis and history, Felicia Feaster's TCM production essay and the Fordham Medieval Hollywood entry establish a pious, canonisation-framed portrait: voices of Sts Michael, Catherine and Margaret, confession for the army, a politically driven trial under Cauchon. The trial's hostility matches the Catholic Encyclopedia's account and the Church's own annulment; the film's political compressions are disclosed.
summary: Ingrid Bergman plays Joan in Victor Fleming's lavish Technicolor biography, from Domrémy to the stake, with the trial at Rouen as its strongest stretch.
synopsis: A peasant girl in Lorraine hears the voices of saints telling her to save France. She persuades the governor at Vaucouleurs to send her to the Dauphin at Chinon, convinces the weak and evasive Charles, and is given command at Orleans. She makes the soldiers confess, stop swearing and send away camp followers, then leads them to victory and sees Charles crowned at Reims. When the court makes peace with Burgundy she is pushed aside, her voices fall silent, and she is captured at Compiègne. Sold to the English, she is tried for heresy at Rouen by Bishop Cauchon. Worn down, she signs an abjuration, recants it when she understands she has been tricked, and is burned in the market square.
inclusion: This is the big Hollywood version: Technicolor, armour made with help from the Metropolitan Museum's armourer, thousands of extras, Oscars for Winton Hoch's colour photography and Barbara Karinska's costumes. Bergman had played Joan on Broadway and wanted the part for years; her performance is earnest and physical, and José Ferrer, in his first film, makes a memorably slippery Dauphin. The first half is stiff pageantry, a long run of processions and speeches; critics from Bosley Crowther onward found it short on spiritual fire. The trial is better: Joan argues with her judges, insists she is a prisoner of the English rather than of the Church, and breaks and recovers. The film opens on her canonisation and never doubts her mission.
themes: Joan's voices are presented as real messages from St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret, not as a psychological symptom. Her campaign is framed as a religious reform as much as a military one: she sends the soldiers to confession and calls them God's army. The trial is a corrupt proceeding run by a partisan bishop for English masters, which is how the Catholic Encyclopedia describes it, and the film shows a sympathetic priest at her side to the end. It does not suggest the Church's faith was on trial; the prologue showing her canonisation makes the point that the Church reversed the verdict.
history: Joan was captured at Compiègne in May 1430 by Burgundian forces and sold to the English. Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais and a Burgundian partisan, conducted the trial at Rouen. She abjured at Saint-Ouen, resumed male dress, was declared relapsed and burned on 30 May 1431. A papally appointed court annulled the sentence in 1456; she was beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920.
liberties: Charles VII is made into a villain who effectively sells Joan out for Burgundian money; historically his counsellors arranged a truce and then made no effort to ransom her. The capture is simplified. The Inquisitor of Rouen's arc, from lone defender to accuser, is dramatised. Joan's appeal to the Pope, central to the real trial, does not feature in published synopses of the film. The 1950 general-release cut removed about 45 minutes, rearranged scenes and added narration; the restored version is the one to watch.
advisories:
Medieval battle scenes with arrows, falls and burning; Joan is wounded by an arrow.

The burning at the stake is shown, though without graphic detail.

References to camp followers and an English captain calls Joan a strumpet. Suitable for older children and up.

Choose the restored 145-minute version; the 100-minute cut is confusing.

title: The Trial of Joan of Arc
decision: PUBLISH: DVDClassik's analysis and Florence Delay's account establish a film built from the condemnation trial record, with rehabilitation testimony for the final hours. The critical dissent (Time Out's 'voyeurism' reading) is recorded. It won the OCIC prize at Cannes. Its severe material is advised.
summary: Bresson's sixty-five-minute Joan uses only the words of the trial record, delivered flatly by non-actors, and becomes a film of doors, chains, glances and a calm, unbreakable voice.
synopsis: Joan's mother asks for her daughter's rehabilitation, and then the film goes back to Rouen in 1431. Joan (Florence Delay, then a student) is already a prisoner in the castle. The interrogations follow one after another: her voices, her male clothing, her submission to the Church. Between them she is chained in her cell, spied on through a hole in the wall by English soldiers and churchmen, examined to establish her virginity, and threatened. She abjures under the threat of fire, resumes her men's clothes after an attempted assault in her cell, and is condemned as a relapsed heretic. She walks quickly, barefoot, to the stake. The film ends on the empty post and the chain.
inclusion: Bresson rejected Dreyer's expressive acting, and this is his opposite version: brief, cold and exact. Every word comes from the documents, spoken without emphasis, and the drama lies in what the camera chooses to watch: hands, feet, doors opening and closing. DVDClassik singles out the single backward tracking shot as Joan hurries to the stake, as if toward the sky. Delay, twenty and untrained, is remarkable for her stillness. The film won the Special Jury Prize and the OCIC (Catholic film office) prize at Cannes in 1962. It is not easy. Time Out called it Bresson's essay in 'sado-masochistic voyeurism', and many viewers find it too austere to feel. Its brevity and fidelity make it the best companion to Dreyer.
themes: Joan's words carry the theology: she submits to God first and to the Church militant as far as she can without denying her voices. She asks to be judged by the Pope. Her abjuration and relapse are not hidden, and her return to fidelity is the turning point. Bresson presents grace as something that works through constraint rather than feeling. The ecclesiastical judges act in concert with English interests, and the film's restraint lets the injustice speak without caricature.
history: Joan was tried at Rouen from January to May 1431 by a court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon and burned on 30 May 1431. The verdict was annulled in 1456 after a retrial in which witnesses described her last days. Bresson shot the film in the summer of 1961 at the Meudon observatory near Paris, and it premiered at Cannes in May 1962.
liberties: Hearings spread over months are reduced to a handful of exchanges. The scenes of her last hours, including the assault that led her to resume male dress, come from later rehabilitation testimony rather than the condemnation record. Bresson's selection of what to keep is itself an interpretation.
advisories:
Older teens and adults: imprisonment in chains, coercive interrogation, an implied attempted rape, a virginity examination observed by men, and execution by burning (shown with restraint).

UK rating 12. Very austere; younger viewers may find it impenetrable.

title: The Flowers of St. Francis
decision: PUBLISH: Peter Brunette's Criterion essay, Greydanus's review and Chris Shields's Screen Slate piece independently document a film drawn from the Fioretti and the Life of Brother Juniper, centred on poverty, obedience and joy, and played by real friars. Recommended in the original Italian cut; the 1952 US version cut episodes and added a prologue.
summary: Rossellini and Fellini turn the Little Flowers into nine comic, tender episodes of the first friars, played by real Franciscans: the most joyful film about religious life ever made.
synopsis: In the rain, Francis and his brothers come back to the Portiuncula after visiting the Pope, and find their hut taken over by a peasant and his donkey. They build a new home. Brother Juniper gives away his habit to a beggar and comes back naked. To make soup for a sick brother, he cuts the foot off a living pig, to its owner's fury. Clare visits and the brothers prepare a humble meal. Francis meets and embraces a leper at night. Juniper, sent out to preach, wanders into the camp of the tyrant Nicolaio, is beaten and nearly hanged, and his meekness disarms the warlord. Francis and Brother Leo learn what perfect joy is by being turned away in the snow. At the end, Francis has the brothers spin round until they fall, and each sets off to preach in the direction he faces.
inclusion: Made between Stromboli and Europe '51, this is Rossellini's lightest film and one of his best. He cast friars from the Franciscan house at Nocera Inferiore: Brother Nazario Gerardi plays Francis and Brother Severino Pisacane plays Juniper. Their unaffected faces carry more conviction than actors could. Aldo Fabrizi, the only star, plays Nicolaio as a buffoon trapped in absurd armour, and Brunette reads that scene as the clash between the noisy world and the friars' simplicity. Steven Greydanus notes that Francis is the straight man and the brothers are the holy fools. The episodes do not add up to a plot, and the comedy is slapstick at times, but the film's simplicity is the point.
themes: Poverty here is freedom, not grim deprivation: the friars possess nothing and are happy. Obedience is literal. Francis commands under holy obedience, and the final spinning game turns obedience into a children's game that sends them out to preach. Charity reaches the leper, the beggar and the tyrant. Juniper's foolishness, as with the pig, shows that zeal without prudence wounds others, and Francis corrects him. Clare's visit gives a glimpse of the Poor Clares' share in the same life. Prayer is constant and unforced. The film makes no claim to biography. It is a film of the Fioretti spirit, faithful to how the Franciscan tradition remembered its beginning.
history: The episodes come from the Fioretti (Little Flowers of St. Francis), compiled in the fourteenth century, and the Life of Brother Juniper. Both are collections of edifying stories written down well after Francis's death in 1226, not documentary history. Rossellini and Fellini wrote the screenplay. The film premiered at the Venice festival in August 1950 and opened in Italy in December 1950.
liberties: It is selective and legendary by design: there is no conversion, stigmata or death of Francis. The American release of 1952 cut episodes, including the leper scene, removed the chapter titles and added a prologue of paintings and frescoes. Criterion's restoration is the Italian version, with the prologue as an extra.
advisories:
Juniper is beaten and threatened with hanging in the tyrant's camp; a pig's foot is cut off (offscreen) and its owner is enraged; Juniper returns naked after giving away his habit (not shown explicitly).

Suitable for all ages; Italian with subtitles.

title: Francis of Assisi
decision: PUBLISH: the AFI Catalog establishes the production (Fox/Perseus, shot at Assisi and Rome with Franciscan and Benedictine cooperation) and a full plot; independent contemporary reviews (New York Times, Variety, Harrison's Reports, LA Times, Washington Post, Monthly Film Bulletin, quoted via Wikipedia) and a later British review agree that it is reverent and static, with nothing doctrinally objectionable reported. The invented Paolo plot is disclosed. No Legion of Decency rating located; OSV's A-I is cited only as a fact. Primary 1961 review texts were not opened.
summary: Michael Curtiz's reverent, static CinemaScope life of St Francis, from rich man's son to stigmatic, with Bradford Dillman as Francis and Dolores Hart as Clare.
synopsis: Francis Bernardone, the pleasure-loving son of an Assisi cloth merchant, rides out with his friend Paolo, an impoverished nobleman, to fight for the Pope. In battle he hears a voice telling him to go home; he obeys and is jailed as a coward. Freed, he is told to rebuild a ruined church, gives up his inheritance, gathers followers, and Innocent III approves his order. Clare, his childhood friend, whom Paolo loves, is moved by his preaching and becomes a nun; the embittered Paolo joins the Crusade. Francis goes to the Holy Land, offers to walk through fire before the Sultan, and is appalled by the Crusaders' plundering. Back in Italy he finds friars abandoning poverty, withdraws, loses his sight, receives the stigmata and dies, visited by a repentant Paolo.
inclusion: It is the only Hollywood studio life of St Francis, shot at Assisi and in Rome with the cooperation of the Franciscans and the Benedictines of Assisi, and it covers more of his life than most Francis films: conversion, the rule, Clare, the Sultan, the troubles of the order and the stigmata. Mario Nascimbene's score makes use of Gregorian chant. Contemporary critics found it respectful and inert. A. H. Weiler in the New York Times compared it to tapestries hanging limp on castle walls, Variety missed any sustained dramatic friction, and Harrison's Reports judged it too talky. Bradford Dillman, usually cast as a villain, plays Francis straight. Dolores Hart, who plays Clare, entered the Benedictine abbey of Regina Laudis two years later. It is a pageant rather than a drama, suitable for the whole family.
themes: The film takes Francis's spirituality chiefly as poverty and obedience. He hears a voice and obeys, strips himself of his inheritance, rebuilds a church with his own hands, submits his rule to the Pope and fights to keep his friars poor. The Church is shown approving him through Innocent III and Cardinal Hugolino, and the stigmata are presented as a real miracle. Prayer and the sacraments are less prominent than renunciation, and one British reviewer complained that the spiritual is smothered by the religiose. The invented rivalry with Paolo supplies most of the conflict.
history: Francis was born at Assisi in 1181 or 1182, son of the cloth merchant Pietro Bernardone. Around 1205 he set out for Apulia to join Walter of Brienne's campaign but turned back at Spoleto after a dream. He renounced his inheritance before the bishop, restored San Damiano, and won Innocent III's verbal approval for his rule. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. In 1219 he went to Damietta and was received by the Sultan. He received the stigmata on La Verna in 1224, died on 3 October 1226 and was canonised in 1228.
liberties: Paolo, Francis's friend and Clare's suitor, has no counterpart in the early lives of Francis and carries much of the plot, including a pardon he grants Francis at Clare's request. Francis's aborted military venture becomes a papal campaign for Sicily; in fact he set out for Apulia. Clare is given the surname Scefi. Francis's offer to walk through fire before the Sultan is staged as a set-piece. The troubles of the order are compressed into a single crisis.
advisories:
Battle scenes and sword fights; nothing graphic.

Blindness, the stigmata and a deathbed.

Suitable for all ages; the slow pace may tire children.

title: Monsieur Vincent
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review and Steve Vineberg's essay independently document an unsentimental portrait of priestly charity, with specific episodes (the plague village, the Ladies and Daughters of Charity, the foundlings) and a brief war-time assault image advised. AlloCiné settles identity.
summary: Pierre Fresnay's austere Vincent de Paul turns the organisation of charity into high drama in Maurice Cloche's understated, Oscar-honoured 1947 biography.
synopsis: Vincent, a young priest who has been comfortable as chaplain to a great family, takes the poor parish of Châtillon-les-Dombes. Plague has struck it, and the villagers stone him from their windows. He shames a lord who has barred his doors, finds an orphaned girl beside her dead mother, and persuades an overburdened neighbour to take her in. His first confraternity of charity grows from this. In Paris he enlists aristocratic Ladies of Charity, who soon send their maids instead of coming themselves. With Louise de Marillac he forms the Daughters of Charity from country girls. He serves as chaplain to the galley convicts, argues with Richelieu, and struggles over abandoned infants whom even the sisters at first refuse to touch. War ravages the provinces. Old and nearly blind, he charges a young sister with the hardest lesson of service to the poor.
inclusion: Fresnay won the Best Actor prize at Venice, and his Vincent is no plaster saint. He is dry, ironic, sometimes harsh, and always working. Jean Anouilh co-wrote the screenplay, and the dialogue has an edge; Claude Renoir's black-and-white images are sober and handsome. Steven Greydanus calls it a towering achievement. He praises its refusal to romanticise the poor or excuse the rich, and its sense of Vincent as an organiser who turned almsgiving into institutions. Steve Vineberg singles out the foundling sequence. The film is episodic, and some threads, the galleys and the foundlings, are left hanging; Greydanus calls it a fragment of a larger story. It received a special Academy Award as best foreign-language film in 1949.
themes: Charity here is a duty laid on the Christian, and it is uncomfortable. The poor are often ungrateful, dirty and rude, and Vincent insists they are owed help anyway. The rich are criticised not for having money but for wanting the satisfaction of giving without the labour. Vincent's priesthood is the source of his work: he prays, preaches and hears confessions, and the film never presents him as a social reformer who happens to wear a cassock. The Daughters of Charity appear as a new form of consecrated life lived in the streets. The final lesson, that the poor must be served humbly enough to forgive us our bread, is the film's moral centre.
history: Vincent de Paul (1581–1660) was parish priest at Châtillon-les-Dombes in 1617, where he founded the first Confraternity of Charity. He founded the Congregation of the Mission in 1625 and, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity in 1633. He was royal chaplain of the galleys and organised care for foundlings and relief for war-ravaged Lorraine. He was canonised in 1737.
liberties: The film omits Vincent's early life, including the disputed story of his capture by pirates. It compresses forty years into a series of episodes and leaves several outcomes unclear. One German plot summary says he takes a galley convict's place at the oar, a hagiographic legend historians reject; this is unconfirmed for the film.
advisories:
Brief violence (stoning); a fleeting war montage with a glimpse of rape, nothing explicit.

Plague, death, misery and abandoned babies.

Best for teenagers and adults.

title: The Reluctant Saint
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a detailed plot and production record, TCM's article documents the US–Italian co-production and its reception, and Greydanus's review recommends it for families. It is gentle, accurate in spirit, and has no content concerns beyond a brief exorcism scene.
summary: Maximilian Schell plays Joseph of Cupertino, the slow-witted friar who flew, in Edward Dmytryk's gentle, funny and finally moving Italian-shot comedy.
synopsis: In seventeenth-century Apulia, Giuseppe Desa is a clumsy, dim young man whom nobody in his village wants. His mother Francesca, tired of him, gets her brother to have the Franciscan friary take him. Giuseppe is put to work in the stables, where he is happy with the animals and humble before everyone. The kindly bishop sees something in him and lets him try for ordination, and against all expectation he passes the examination when he is asked the one text he knows. Father Raspi (Ricardo Montalban), a strict and learned friar, distrusts him and suspects the devil when strange things start to happen, even attempting an exorcism. Then Giuseppe, praying before a statue of the Madonna, rises into the air, and the whole friary has to reckon with a holiness it did not see coming.
inclusion: This is a modest film, and it knows it. Schell, fresh from his Oscar for Judgment at Nuremberg, plays Joseph without condescension: slow, sweet and stubborn. He later counted it among his best performances. Montalban's Raspi is a good foil, a clever man humbled by a simple one. Shot in Rome and Lazio with Nino Rota's score, it looks and sounds Italian. Steven Greydanus calls it fine family viewing and admires the way the film holds back the miracles for over an hour, so that we know Joseph as a person before we see him fly. The comedy is broad and the special effects are dated, and it failed at the box office; Dmytryk called it his biggest flop. It deserves better.
themes: The film is about humility and how God chooses the weak to confound the strong. Joseph is not clever, and the friars, especially Raspi, assume that holiness must look like learning. His obedience is total: he does whatever task he is given. Raspi's suspicion of the devil reflects the Church's real caution about extraordinary phenomena, and the film treats it fairly before showing the truth. Joseph's love of animals and his joy in prayer echo St. Francis. The ordination scene, where he passes by being asked the one thing he knows, is told as Providence. The levitations are a fruit of his love for Our Lady, not a show.
history: Giuseppe Desa (1603–1663) was born at Cupertino in Apulia, was accepted by the Conventual Franciscans after several rejections, and was ordained in 1628. His ecstasies and levitations, witnessed by many, led the Inquisition to examine him and move him from friary to friary; he died at Osimo. He was canonised in 1767 and is the patron of students taking examinations.
liberties: The film compresses his life to the years up to his first levitations and omits the Inquisition's investigations and his later confinement. Father Raspi is largely an invented composite. The exam story is told as a single scene. The plot puts much of the early action at the friary at Grottella, where the historical Joseph lived.

title: Heaven over the Marshes
decision: PUBLISH: Identity is established by the Museo Nazionale del Cinema and contemporary Italian criticism, and the treatment by the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico synopsis, Aristarco (1949) and Morandini. The record gives no running time, so the unresolved 111 v. 98 minute discrepancy between festival records and the 2010 Fox DVD does not affect anything published; it is noted for viewers.
summary: Augusto Genina's neorealist-style life of Maria Goretti, filmed in the Pontine marshes with peasant non-actors: the story of a twelve-year-old who resisted, died and forgave.
synopsis: Luigi Goretti, a farm labourer, brings his wife and six children to the malarial marshes near Nettuno, where the landowners lodge them in a farmhouse with the Serenellis, a father and son who resent them. Luigi works tirelessly, but malaria kills him, and the fatherless family is left at the Serenellis' mercy. The drunken old man pursues the widow, who rebuffs him. His son Alessandro becomes obsessed with Maria, the eldest daughter and still almost a child. He tries small gifts, then force; she escapes him, and he threatens her. On a July afternoon, with everyone in the fields, he drags her into the house and, enraged by her refusal, stabs her again and again. Taken to hospital, she suffers for a day, holds firm in her faith, and forgives her murderer before she dies.
inclusion: Genina shot on location in the marshes with non-professional actors, and Ines Orsini, a peasant girl, plays Maria with plain conviction. G. R. Aldo's photography of the flat, fevered landscape won admiration, and Genina won the Nastro d'Argento for direction. A 1955 survey of Italian cinema found it lacking in religious depth but called it sincerely moving and a faithful chronicle of events. Guido Aristarco, writing in Cinema in December 1949, faulted its pictorial calligraphy and sentimental touches with the children, yet judged it the best film Genina had made in Italy. Morandini called it neorealism in a Catholic key. It is a serious, restrained treatment of a martyrdom that could easily have been exploited.
themes: Maria's purity is presented as a choice of the will, not innocence alone: she knows what Alessandro wants and refuses it, even at the cost of her life. Her forgiveness of her murderer on her deathbed is the film's spiritual climax and the heart of her holiness. The poverty of the family, the fever of the marsh and the absence of the father show the conditions in which sin grows, without excusing it. The title sets heaven against the stagnant swamp. The film ends with Maria's death, before Alessandro's conversion, and so leaves the fruit of her forgiveness to the viewer's knowledge.
history: Maria Goretti was stabbed on 5 July 1902 at Le Ferriere di Conca, in the Pontine marshes, by Alessandro Serenelli, and died the next day at Nettuno after forgiving him. Serenelli later repented in prison and was reconciled with her mother. Pius XII beatified Maria in 1947 and canonised her on 24 June 1950, seven months after the film opened on 24 November 1949.
liberties: Genina compressed and shaped events, and his screenplay was more explicit in its symbolism than the finished film, according to the Torino retrospective essay. The film stops at Maria's death and omits Alessandro's later conversion. Andreotti recalled that Pius XII, at a screening, was troubled by one scene that showed more of the girl than he thought fitting.
advisories:
Attempted sexual assault of a child, implied and not explicit; a fatal stabbing; a long death scene.

Death of a father from malaria; drunkenness and threats.

For older teenagers and adults; discuss with younger viewers before watching.

The 2010 Italian DVD is listed at 98 minutes against the 111 minutes in festival records; it may be cut. No English-subtitled edition was found.

title: Thérèse: The Story of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
originalTitle: Thérèse: The Story of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
decision: PUBLISH as a modest family film, with its weaknesses stated: the Austin Chronicle review confirms credits, PG rating and 2004 release; Greydanus's review (Decent Films/National Catholic Register) documents a reverent, faithful outline of Story of a Soul with an engaging lead, while noting thin treatment of the Little Way. Secular reviews (Austin Chronicle, Film Threat) and the Catholic News Service reviewer's 'hagiographic tableaus' confirm the craft is weak. No doctrinal or reverence concerns are recorded by any source.
summary: A sincere, low-budget American biopic of the Little Flower, reverent and family-safe, that walks through Story of a Soul without quite catching its depth.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin grows up the youngest of five sisters in a pious, loving household in Alençon and Lisieux. Her mother dies when she is four, and she becomes her father Louis's 'little queen'. One by one her sisters enter the Carmel, and Thérèse, still a girl, resolves to follow. Refused because of her age, she appeals to the bishop and then, on pilgrimage to Rome, to Pope Leo XIII himself. Admitted at fifteen, she learns to serve awkward, elderly sisters with patience and to make small sacrifices out of love. Her father declines into illness. Thérèse falls ill with tuberculosis and dies in the infirmary at twenty-four.
inclusion: This is a film to watch with children rather than one to admire for craft. It was made on a small budget, and it shows: the staging is stiff, much of the supporting cast is weak, and the script tells rather than shows. What it has is sincerity and an attractive lead. Lindsay Younce plays Thérèse as a normal, likeable young woman rather than a plaster figure, and Steven Greydanus finds her deathbed scenes genuinely affecting. Defilippis himself is good as Louis Martin. Passages from Thérèse's own writing are read in voiceover, which is the best thing about it.
themes: The film follows the main events of Story of a Soul: the devout family, the call to Carmel, the appeal to Leo XIII, the patient charity of convent life, the trial of illness. Prayer, the sacraments and religious life are shown with uncomplicated reverence. Its weakness is the teaching. Greydanus and Marjorie Baumgarten both note that the film gives little sense of the 'little way' of spiritual childhood that made Thérèse a Doctor of the Church, and her dark night of faith is reduced to a voiceover line.
history: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897) entered the Lisieux Carmel at fifteen and died of tuberculosis in 1897. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, spread her Little Way worldwide, and Pius XI beatified her in 1923 and canonised her in 1925, naming her patroness of the missions in 1927.
liberties: The film omits Thérèse's scrupulosity and emotional struggles, the troubles of her sister Léonie, her work with the novices and much of her spiritual trial at the end. The Martin family is presented as almost flawless. Greydanus notes at least one small factual slip in the Christmas conversion scene.
advisories:
The death of a parent and a brief frightening image.

Thérèse's final illness and death are shown plainly.

Rated PG. Suitable for children with parents.

title: Fray Escoba
decision: PUBLISH: José María Aresté's DeCine21 critique describes specific episodes (the food basket, clashes with the porter, the farewell to his mother) that place Martín's charity and humility at the centre; the ICAA record confirms identity, a Dominican religious adviser and an all-ages video rating. The film's whimsy and anecdotal structure are noted as weaknesses, not doctrinal problems.
summary: A modest Spanish biopic of Martín de Porres, the mixed-race Dominican lay brother of Lima whose broom became the emblem of his holiness.
synopsis: Martín, son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman, grows up in Lima between his father's world and his mother's poverty. He gives up the advantages his father could offer and asks to serve the Dominicans. Set to sweeping and menial work, he earns the nickname "Fray Escoba" (Brother Broom). Episodes follow his care for the sick and the poor, his friction with the convent porter, Padre Barragán, and a growing reputation for wonders he does not seek: in one scene a basket keeps yielding food for the hungry. The film closes its family story with Martín's emotional parting from his mother.
inclusion: Ramón Torrado made a plain, warm film for a broad audience, and its best quality is that it keeps Martín at floor level. Holiness here is measured by the broom, the infirmary and the begging round rather than by spectacle. René Muñoz gives Martín a gentle, unpushy presence, and the Círculo de Escritores Cinematográficos gave him a special prize for it in 1961. José María Aresté calls the farewell with his mother the film's strongest moment. The weaknesses are those of Spanish devotional cinema of the period: episodic construction, some sentimental comedy and miracle scenes staged with a fairy-tale touch that Aresté compares to Mary Poppins. As an introduction to the saint for a family, it does its job.
themes: The film's Catholic subject is humility made concrete. Martín chooses the lowest work in a religious house and treats it as service to Christ in the poor and the sick. Miracles are present, but they arise from works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, rather than replacing them. Martín's patience with a sharp-tongued superior shows obedience as a daily discipline, not a pious attitude. A Dominican priest, Fr. Antonio Sánchez, served as religious adviser on the production.
history: Martín de Porres (1579–1639) was born in Lima to the Spaniard Juan de Porres and Ana Velázquez, a freed woman of African descent. Barred by colonial rules from entering as a full religious at first, he joined the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary as a donado (lay helper) and later professed as a lay brother. He was known for nursing the sick, caring for the poor and animals, and for reported miracles. He was beatified in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962, the year after this film was made.
liberties: The screenplay by Jaime G. Herranz is credited as "inspired by" the life of the then Blessed Martín, and it arranges traditional anecdotes into a loose sequence. Conversations, the porter's characterisation and the staging of individual miracles are dramatic inventions.
advisories:
Rated suitable for all audiences on its Spanish video releases (1988 and 2008).

Illness, poverty and an emotional parting between mother and son.

Suitable for children; younger viewers may need help with the period setting.

title: Un mulato llamado Martín
