decision: GREY: Identity, credits and the main episodes are established (Sentido Fílmico, Spanish Wikipedia, a Lima devotional blog), but no critic has assessed how the film treats the saint, and its synopses frame his life as a 'fight against slavery' in a 1970s Peruvian production made under the Velasco-era film law. That framing is unexamined. Martín was canonised in 1962, so the post-1965 rule does not apply. Settled by a review or recorded viewing that addresses the miracles, the convent life and the slavery theme. Year: the SIC and INAH listings give 1974 (probably production); IMDb and Sentido Fílmico give the Lima premiere, 25 September 1975.

grey.question: The film is securely identified: Tito Davison directed it for Mexican and Peruvian producers, with René Muñoz as Martín, and it opened in Lima in 1975. What is missing is any critical review of how it treats the saint. Its published synopses present his life as a struggle against slavery and against the barriers between slaves, priests and nobles, and it was made under Peru's state film law of the early 1970s. A review or a recorded viewing showing whether this is the charity of the traditional lives or a social reading of the saint would settle it.

summary: Tito Davison's Mexican–Peruvian life of St Martin de Porres, with René Muñoz returning to the role he first played in Fray Escoba.
synopsis: Martín is the illegitimate son of a Spanish nobleman, Don Juan de Porres, and a woman of African descent. The film follows him from a devout childhood in colonial Lima to the Dominican convent of Santo Domingo, where his birth allows him only the place of a donado, a lay helper, and he takes the lowest work. Episodes described in published accounts include a trader at the port of Callao trying to sell him as a slave until a friar intervenes; his care for Balu, an enslaved man who has turned to violence and later gains his freedom; a temptation by the devil on the convent stairs; and his gift of his father's shirt to Tupac, an Indigenous man whose son is sick. Fray Barragán, the porter, is his companion and a comic foil.
inclusion: Few films about the Lima saint were made in Peru itself, and this one was shot partly in the real convent of Santo Domingo, where Martín lived and died, with a largely Peruvian supporting cast drawn from television. René Muñoz, the Cuban actor who first played Martín in the Spanish Fray Escoba (1961), took the part again here and in Mexican television serials. A Lima devotional writer says this film gives more room to Martín's works of mercy than the earlier Spanish one, which he calls sugary. No critic has described how well it is made or how it stages the saint's miracles. On present evidence it is of most interest to viewers who know Fray Escoba and want a Latin American treatment of the same saint.
themes: In the accounts available, Martín's holiness is shown through humility and charity: a donado who sweeps, serves and gives away what he has. The convent of Santo Domingo frames his religious life, and his temptation by the devil, a traditional element of his legend, is staged on its stairs. The film's synopses also present his life as a struggle against slavery and against the barriers between slaves, priests and nobility. That may be no more than the charity of the old lives of the saint, or it may be a 1970s social reading; no source yet says which. The same devotional writer notes that some episodes are not historically proven.
history: Martín de Porres (1579–1639) was born in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porres, and Ana Velázquez, a freed woman of African descent. He entered the Dominican convent of the Holy Rosary (Santo Domingo) as a lay helper, later professed as a lay brother, and became known for his care of the sick and poor, his penances and reported miracles. He was beatified in 1837 and canonised by John XXIII on 6 May 1962.
liberties: The devotional account notes that not every episode in the film is historically proven. The enslaved man Balu and the Indigenous father Tupac are not figures of the standard biographies, and the attempted sale of Martín at Callao is not part of the usual record. The friendship with Fray Barragán is played partly for comedy.
advisories:
A violent enslaved character; an attempt to sell the young Martín as a slave.

A scene of diabolical temptation.

No source records sexual content or strong violence, but no detailed content review exists.

Its treatment of slavery and social class has not been assessed.

What has not been assessed is how it treats the saint and his institute. The reviews found judge its craft, not its faith or its history, and the fullest descriptions of its content come from the De La Salle Brothers, who sponsored its DVD release. summary: Luis César Amadori's Spanish biopic, with Mel Ferrer as the Reims canon who gave up rank and fortune to found the Brothers of the Christian Schools.
synopsis: Set in the France of Louis XIV, the film follows Jean-Baptiste de La Salle, a canon from a well-off family, as he turns to the education of poor children. Catalogue summaries and the Lasallian Brothers' own notice describe its arc: his first involvement with schools, the founding of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, and the hardship and obstacles he meets in trying to offer free schooling to all children. Mel Ferrer plays La Salle, with Fernando Rey, Mabel Karr, Manuel Alexandre and Antonio Ferrandis among the Spanish cast. No detailed scene-by-scene account of the film has been found.
inclusion: La Salle is one of the great figures of Catholic education, yet he has rarely been filmed, and this is the only feature about him. Spain put real resources into it: Amadori, a veteran of Argentine cinema then working in Spain, Mel Ferrer in the lead, and a strong supporting cast that includes Fernando Rey. The one detailed review found, by Paco Casado for Cine y Max, calls Amadori's direction diligent, the colour photography acceptable, Gregorio García Segura's score good and Ferrer well suited to the part. But he blames a weak script and a polished, Hollywood-style surface that leaves the saint himself thinly drawn. DeCine21 rates it 5/10. It reached the United States in 1976 as Who Are My Own and returned on DVD in 2010.
themes: The film's subject is the founding of a teaching institute: La Salle's renunciation of comfort and status, and his dedication of his life to free Christian schooling for poor children. DeCine21 presents him as a holy man whose service of others follows Christian teaching. No source describes how the film treats the Brothers' community life and prayer, the sacraments, or La Salle's conflicts with church authorities and the Paris schoolmasters. Its picture of Catholic reform in seventeenth-century France has not yet been assessed.
history: Jean-Baptiste de La Salle (1651–1719), a priest and canon of Reims, founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools in the early 1680s. He pioneered free elementary schools, teaching in French rather than Latin, and the training of teachers. He resigned his canonry and gave away his inheritance for the work, and faced lawsuits from the guilds of schoolmasters. He was canonised by Leo XIII in 1900, and Pius XII named him patron of teachers in 1950.
advisories:
No violence or sexual content is recorded; DeCine21 lists it as suitable for young people.

Cine y Max records an adults-only (over 18) Spanish classification for the original release, without explanation.

decision: GREY: identity is secure (ACMI, Box Office Mojo, Wikipedia credits) and one independent, scene-level review exists (Avellina Balestri, Catholic Insight, 2016), which is enthusiastic. grey.question: The film's identity is secure, and one independent review, Avellina Balestri's in Catholic Insight, finds it devout and balanced. That is not yet enough. It was co-produced by the Salesians' own publishing house, it adds an invented subplot about a girl and a brothel, and nobody has examined how it presents Bosco's quarrel with Archbishop Gastaldi. A second independent review, or a documented viewing that checks the Lina subplot, the dreams and the Gastaldi conflict against the historical record, would settle it.

summary: Leandro Castellani's centenary-year biopic, co-produced by the Salesians' publishing house, with Ben Gazzara as the Turin priest who battles poverty, the state and his archbishop for his boys.
synopsis: In nineteenth-century Turin Don Giovanni Bosco, guided by a dream he has had since boyhood, gathers poor and abandoned boys into his oratory. Officials complain that he is harbouring misfits. During political unrest he is offered money to stop, and there are attempts on his life, among them poisoned wine; a large grey dog that he believes heaven sent turns away an assassin. A subplot follows Lina, a girl whose mother wants her to work in a brothel beside the oratory, and Giuseppe, one of Bosco's boys, who takes her side and is later arrested for robbery. A hostile bishop suspends Bosco's faculty to hear confessions. He goes to Rome, wins the support of Pius IX and founds the Salesians. The film ends with his last days.
inclusion: Ben Gazzara's Bosco is the film's main asset. Avellina Balestri, reviewing it for the Canadian magazine Catholic Insight, calls it his finest performance and praises its mixture of earthy realism and mysticism. She finds the production uneven, thinks Patsy Kensit miscast as Lina, and is irked by the English dubbing of some Italian actors. Released in the centenary year of Bosco's death, it was written by Ennio De Concini and scored by Stelvio Cipriani, with Laurent Terzieff as Archbishop Gastaldi, Raymond Pellegrin as Pius IX and Philippe Leroy as Leo XIII. Unusually for a saint's film, it puts on screen the opposition Bosco met from his own archbishop as well as from the state. It runs about 108 minutes.
themes: The Catholic content is Bosco's pastoral method and his supernatural life: the oratory as a place of work, prayer and play for boys nobody else wanted; his dreams, treated as genuine guidance, including visions of the Christ Child and Our Lady that he recounts before the Pope; and the grey dog that protects him. Balestri finds it balanced, showing good and bad churchmen without attacking the Church. How the conflict with Archbishop Gastaldi is weighted, and whether the invented Lina story serves the portrait of Bosco or distracts from it, has not been examined by any other reviewer.
history: John Bosco was born near Castelnuovo in Piedmont in 1815. As a young priest in Turin he began his oratory for poor boys on 8 December 1841; by 1868 the Salesian Society he founded had fifty priests and teachers. He met complaints from the authorities and even an attempt to have him confined in an asylum. He died in Turin on 31 January 1888 and was canonised by Pius XI in 1934. The film's account of his quarrel with Archbishop Gastaldi has not been checked against the record.
liberties: Lina, her mother and the brothel, and Giuseppe's romance and arrest, form a subplot that no source identifies as historical; it appears to be invented. Balestri does not discuss historical liberties. The order of events in the film, with the bishop's sanctions coming before the Roman journey and the founding of the Salesians, has not been checked against the record.
advisories:
A subplot involves a brothel and a mother pressing her daughter to work there; sources do not describe explicit content.

Assassination attempts, a poisoning and an arrest.

ACMI classifies it PG.

The English version dubs some Italian actors.

title: Molokai: The Story of Father Damien
originalTitle: Molokai: The Story of Father Damien
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Damien of Molokai, beatified 1995, canonised 2009).
summary: David Wenham plays the Belgian priest who went to the Hawaiian leper settlement of Kalawao in 1873, stayed sixteen years, caught the disease and died there.
synopsis: In 1873 Father Damien, a young Belgian priest of the Sacred Hearts Fathers, volunteers to go to Molokai, where the Hawaiian kingdom exiles people with leprosy. He finds a lawless, filthy settlement where the sick are left to die. He dresses sores, builds houses, digs graves, says Mass and badgers the Board of Health and his own superiors in Honolulu for money, medicine, nuns and a confessor. Officials find him tactless; a cynical Anglican patient enjoys resisting his offer of the sacraments; a shrewd rancher becomes an ally. Years later he learns he has leprosy himself, and he keeps working while new helpers, among them Mother Marianne Cope, arrive to carry on.
inclusion: Cox, a Melbourne director known for small, personal films, plays the material straight and lets the place do the work: the cliffs, the sea, the faces of the sick. Wenham is the reason to watch. His Damien is stubborn, irritable, funny and plainly holy, a man whose charity is practical and whose priesthood is not decoration: he wants souls as well as bandages. David Stratton found the leper scenes and Wenham's performance the heart of a flawed film, and Time Out called it engrossing and often moving. The supporting cast is starry but uneven, the structure episodic, and the music sometimes pushes too hard.
themes: Damien's charity is inseparable from his priesthood. He celebrates Mass, hears confessions, baptises and tries, openly, to bring the dying into the Church. The film shows him, unable to land a confessor, shouting his sins in French to a priest on a ship offshore. His struggles with obedience are treated honestly: he is often in conflict with his superiors, but the film also shows good bishops and sympathetic clergy. He faces sexual temptation and resists it. Greydanus doubts two brief moments, a line about Hawaii's 'old gods' and a wedding Damien performs that would have been invalid.
history: Joseph de Veuster (1840–1889) took the name Damien in the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts and went to Molokai at Easter 1873. Superiors found his zeal indiscreet and his bishop called him tempestuous. Leprosy was confirmed in 1885 and he died on 15 April 1889. Robert Louis Stevenson defended him against a Protestant minister's slanders. He was beatified in 1995 and canonised in 2009.
liberties: Based on Hilde Eynikel's biography, the film compresses sixteen years into episodes and invents or composites some patients and officials. Greydanus could find nothing in the biographies to support the 'old gods' remark or the wedding scene. The producers' 1999 Belgian release was disowned by Cox; the version he later restored runs about two hours.
advisories:
Disfigurement from leprosy, death and burial are shown frequently.

A brief, shadowy massacre; minor profanity; a restrained scene of resisted sexual temptation and a reference to impure thoughts.

Rated PG. Better for teenagers and adults than young children.

title: A Man for All Seasons
decision: PUBLISH: The 'autonomous conscience' objection (Duffy; echoed by Weigel) is aimed chiefly at Bolt's preface and at the historical More's omitted record, while the film itself has More defend papal primacy at his trial, refuse a heretic son-in-law and die 'God's first' (Wilson, Weigel, plot record). The omission of More's actions against heretics is disclosed as a historical liberty rather than treated as a doctrinal defect.
summary: Zinnemann's film of Robert Bolt's play follows Thomas More from royal favour to the scaffold as he refuses to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church.
synopsis: Sir Thomas More, a lawyer and devout family man, is admired across England when Henry VIII wants his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled. Cardinal Wolsey asks for More's help; More will not give it. After Wolsey's fall More becomes Lord Chancellor, then resigns when the clergy submit to the King. He keeps silent on the marriage and the new oath, trusting that the law protects a man who says nothing. Thomas Cromwell works patiently to break that silence. More is imprisoned in the Tower, separated from his wife Alice and daughter Meg, and finally convicted on the perjured evidence of Richard Rich, a young man he once refused to promote. Only after the verdict does he say plainly what he believes.
inclusion: This is a film made almost entirely of conversations, and it is gripping. Bolt's dialogue is sharp and often funny, and Paul Scofield plays More as a man of wit and warmth who would much rather live than die. The supporting cast is excellent: Orson Welles as a bloated, worldly Wolsey, Leo McKern as Cromwell, Robert Shaw as a boisterous and dangerous Henry, Wendy Hiller as Alice, John Hurt as the weak, ambitious Rich. Ted Moore's photography and Georges Delerue's score keep it handsome without fuss. The Catholic case is clear: More's quarrel is not over a divorce as such but over whether a king can make himself head of the Church. The film lets his conviction emerge slowly, under pressure, through legal caution, family love and finally open witness.
themes: The film turns on papal primacy and the indissolubility of marriage. More refuses to take an oath that would deny the Pope's authority, and at his trial he argues that no temporal ruler may claim the government of the Church, citing Christ's commission to St Peter. He forbids his daughter to marry Will Roper while Roper holds Lutheran views, and his last words are that he dies the King's good servant, but God's first. Critics such as Eamon Duffy argue that Bolt made More a modern hero of personal integrity; Bolt's own preface encourages that reading. Joe Wilson and George Weigel reply that on screen More rarely talks about conscience at all and grounds himself in God. The more convincing reading is theirs, though the film's emphasis on keeping one's 'self' is real and worth noticing.
history: More resigned as Lord Chancellor in 1532, refused the oath attached to the Act of Succession in 1534, and was tried for treason on 1 July 1535. Accounts of the trial record that, at its close, he declared the Act on which he was indicted contrary to the laws of God and his holy Church. He was beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535 and canonised in 1935.
liberties: The film leaves out More's writings against Protestants and his part, as Chancellor, in prosecuting heretics; the biographer Richard Marius thought this produced a More who would barely be recognised in his own time. Rich's long acquaintance with More is expanded for dramatic shape. Several private conversations, including those with Norfolk and Cromwell, are invented, though the main events follow the record.
advisories:
More is beheaded at the end; the blow is not lingered on.

No sexual content or strong language. Long dialogue scenes and legal argument suit teenagers and adults more than young children.

The film omits More's role in the prosecution of heretics, so it should not be taken as a complete biography.

title: Becket
decision: PUBLISH (teens and up): AFI Catalog identity and synopsis; Greydanus's Decent Films review (+3) judges it reverent, with sincere faith and carefully staged liturgy. The serious historical liberties, above all the invented libertine past and mistress, which the Catholic Encyclopedia flatly contradicts, and the unfair portrait of Alexander III, are stated plainly; they shape the drama but do not turn the martyrdom against the faith.
summary: Richard Burton's Becket and Peter O'Toole's Henry II, drinking companions turned archbishop and king, in a lavish film of Anouilh's play about friendship broken by the honour of God.
synopsis: Henry II spends his days hunting and carousing with his clever friend Thomas Becket and makes him Chancellor, where Becket bleeds the Church for the Crown. When Henry demands Becket's mistress for himself, Becket gives her up and she kills herself. On the death of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Henry forces Becket into the see, expecting a compliant ally. Becket warns him he cannot serve both God and the king, resigns the chancellorship and defends the Church's rights. Henry turns on him with false charges; Becket flees to France and the Pope. A last meeting on horseback produces a hollow peace. Becket returns to Canterbury, Henry cries out to be rid of him, and four barons kill him at the altar.
inclusion: The two performances carry it. O'Toole's Henry is needy, funny, petulant and frightening, and Burton plays Becket with a cool reserve that slowly becomes something like holiness. Greydanus calls the film a reverent masterpiece, though less incisive than A Man for All Seasons, and finds Burton harder to warm to than Scofield's More, which is fair. Geoffrey Unsworth's colour photography and the huge Canterbury set are handsome, and the ceremonies, the consecration, an excommunication, the chant, are staged with real care. It is long and theatrical, and Anouilh's dialogue is more epigrammatic than devout. But the moment when Becket, having found a cause worthy of his honour, chooses God over his friend is genuinely stirring.
themes: The question is the freedom of the Church from the Crown. Once consecrated, Becket gives his goods to the poor, takes up prayer and penance, and refuses to let the king control ecclesiastical courts or appointments. Greydanus judges that he genuinely loves God, though Anouilh frames his conversion as the discovery of an honour worth serving, the honour of God. Liturgy and the sacramental office of a bishop are treated with dignity. The papacy fares worse: Alexander III and his court are shown as calculating politicians, which Greydanus thinks unfair. The ending, Henry submitting to a flogging by monks and proclaiming Becket a saint, honours the martyr.
history: Thomas Becket was born in London of Norman parents, served Henry II as Chancellor, and was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury in 1162. He resisted the Constitutions of Clarendon, spent six years in exile, returned in 1170 and was killed in his cathedral by four knights on 29 December. Alexander III canonised him in 1173, and Henry did public penance at his tomb in 1174.
liberties: Anouilh made Becket a Saxon to set him against the Norman king; he was Norman. The film gives him a mistress and a life of drinking and womanising with Henry; the Catholic Encyclopedia records that no word was ever said against his purity. Gwendolen is invented. The Pope is made a cynic. Gilbert Foliot's role is simplified, and Becket's exile is compressed.
advisories:
Implied sexual immorality and womanising in the early scenes; Henry takes Becket's mistress, who then kills herself.

The murder in the cathedral is violent but brief. Some coarse language and demeaning treatment of women.

Greydanus rates it for teens and up.

The saint's pre-ordination life is invented and should not be taken as history.

title: The Carmelites
decision: PUBLISH: Identity confirmed by AlloCiné and the Gaumont catalogue; James Travers's detailed review and the Aleteia appreciation establish a faithful adaptation of Bernanos centred on fear, grace and martyrdom, and the film won the OCIC Grand Prix hors-festival in 1960. The fictional Blanche and the dramatised convent are disclosed; Time Out's dissent concerns style, not doctrine.
summary: A Dominican priest and Bresson's former cameraman film Bernanos's play about the Carmelites of Compiègne and a frightened novice who finds her courage at the scaffold.
synopsis: In 1789 two young women enter the Carmel of Compiègne. Sister Constance is cheerful and ready for the life; Blanche de la Force is crippled by fear of death and doubts her vocation. The dying prioress asks that Blanche be watched over. As the Revolution turns against religious houses, the community shelters Blanche's brother, attends a clandestine Mass said by a hunted priest, and is ordered to disperse. The sisters keep their common life in secret, are arrested and condemned. Blanche has already fled. On the day of the execution she watches her sisters climb to the guillotine, and joins them.
inclusion: Most of Bernanos's dialogue survives, and it is the reason to see the film: hard, plain exchanges about fear, pride and what it costs to give one's life. The cast is remarkable for a religious picture of its day. Jeanne Moreau plays Mother Marie de l'Incarnation, the nun most eager for martyrdom; Madeleine Renaud is the old prioress; Alida Valli the new one; Pascale Audret is Blanche. The style is more conventional and more lavish than Bresson's, and Time Out found it static and pallid. James Travers thought the opposite, judging that it does justice to the play and that the final scaffold sequence is overwhelming. The real strength is the subject: a community of contemplatives who choose to die together rather than abandon their vows.
themes: The film is about fear and grace. Blanche does not overcome her terror by willpower; the story suggests she is carried by the prayer and sacrifice of others, and Bernanos's line that fear is a fantasy of the devil sums up its view. Religious vows, the cloister, the Mass and the Divine Office are treated as realities worth dying for, not as picturesque background. The revolutionary officials are shown as persecutors of the Church, but the film's interest is less in politics than in the different temperaments of the nuns: Constance's simplicity, Marie's zeal, the prioresses' humility. Bernanos was a Catholic novelist and Bruckberger a Dominican, and the treatment of martyrdom is orthodox.
history: Sixteen Discalced Carmelites of Compiègne were guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794 after offering their lives for peace and for the Church in France. They sang the Salve Regina and the Veni Creator on the way to the scaffold. Pius X beatified them in 1906.
liberties: Blanche de la Force is fictional, invented by Gertrud von Le Fort for her 1931 novella and kept by Bernanos. Conversations inside the convent, Blanche's family and her flight are imagined. Jean-Louis Barrault has an odd cameo as a mime. The martyrs' real vow and community life are compressed into a few scenes.
advisories:
The final sequence shows the nuns going one by one to the guillotine; it is grim rather than graphic.

Revolutionary menace and the execution sequence may disturb younger viewers. No sexual content is reported. Suitable for older children with an adult, and for teenagers and adults.

title: Vaincre ou mourir
decision: GREY: Independent treatment exists, so the film is not 'unverified'. Press critics (Le Monde, Télérama, L'Obs, François Huzar) judge the craft poor; historians (Jean-Clément Martin, Paul Chopelin and François Huzar, Guillaume Lancereau, as reported by French Wikipedia and Euronews) find few factual errors but a narrow, partisan frame and little attention to the religious crisis. The question is that historical frame and a thin religious dimension: the film is Catholic-centred only through the Vendéens' cause, Charette's chaplain and the final absolution. Removed from 'martyrs'. The editor may prefer HOLD as not Catholic-centred.

grey.question: The reservation is historical. The film was made by the Puy du Fou, and its opening interviews include Reynald Secher, whose description of the 1794 repression as genocide is widely disputed. Historians who examined it, Jean-Clément Martin among them, found few factual errors but a narrow and partisan frame. The Republic's massacres are shown, the Vendéen killings at Machecoul are not, and the religious causes of the rising get little explanation. Viewers sympathetic to the Vendéens should weigh that one-sidedness against the history.

summary: The Puy du Fou's first feature tells the Vendée war through Charette, the reluctant former naval officer who led the rising and was shot at Nantes in 1796.
synopsis: In 1793 François-Athanase Charette de La Contrie, a former naval officer living quietly at Fonteclose, is pressed by angry peasants to lead their rising against the Republic. He proves a skilful and charismatic guerrilla leader, fighting with an army of peasants, women and young men, among them the fighter Céleste Bulkeley and his companion Hervouët de La Robrie, with the abbé Remaud at his side. Victories give way to losses and to the reprisals of the Republic's infernal columns. In 1795 he makes peace at La Jaunaye, but the peace breaks down. Betrayed and hunted, he is captured by General Travot and shot at Nantes in March 1796, after receiving absolution. Short interviews with historians open the film, and Charette's voice-over carries it.
inclusion: It is the only recent French feature on the Vendée war, a subject French cinema has largely avoided, and it drew nearly 300,000 spectators in France despite a hostile press. Hugo Becker's Charette is the performance reviewers single out. Most notices are poor: Le Monde called it a historical dud, Télérama said it was bad enough to put off royalists, L'Obs found it inert and preachy, and François Huzar, judging it purely as cinema, found the dialogue false, the voice-over constant and the battles illegible. DeCine21 is kinder, praising the costumes and photography and noting the small budget. Jean-Clément Martin found its women fighters, émigré links and infernal columns broadly credible while faulting the narrow focus on Charette. It is worth seeing as a sincere but clumsy attempt at a neglected chapter of Catholic France.
themes: The Vendéens fight for God and the king, and the film keeps a priest, the abbé Remaud, at Charette's side; Charette receives absolution before he is shot, and Aleteia's critic reads the execution as a deliberate echo of Calvary. L'Obs complained of a heavy Christian message. Yet Paul Chopelin and François Huzar note that the film pays little attention to the religious crisis behind the rising: the clerical oath and the persecution of priests who refused it. The faith appears more as loyalty and as consolation in defeat than as a cause the film explains. It does not make Charette a saint; Aleteia quotes his line that he is no saint but will not go to hell.
history: The Vendée rising began in March 1793, provoked by conscription and by the persecution of priests who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Charette led the insurgents of the Marais and the Pays de Retz. After the Catholic and Royal Army was crushed at Savenay in December 1793 he fought on as a guerrilla leader, made peace at La Jaunaye in February 1795, took up arms again, and was captured and shot at Nantes on 29 March 1796. The Republic's repression of 1794, including Turreau's infernal columns, killed many civilians; historians still dispute the totals and the word genocide.
liberties: Jean-Clément Martin points to one clear error: the film shows Charette signing the 1795 peace of La Jaunaye, which, he says, only the Republican side signed. He adds that the Republicans were more numerous and better armed than the film suggests, and Vendéen society more varied and organised. The massacre of Republicans at Machecoul in March 1793 is left out, and rival leaders such as Stofflet are pushed aside by the focus on Charette.

Battle scenes, executions, and reprisals against civilians by Republican troops.

Charette is shot by a firing squad.

title: The War of the Vendée
decision: GREY: identity, outline, cast and the director's own account of his liberties are documented by several sources, so it is not HOLD; but no independent critic has assessed its history. The only full review by an outsider, Joseph Pearce's (2013), is appreciative, sets historical accuracy aside and has an indirect tie to the DVD's distributor (Ignatius Press). Settles with an independent review, or a scene log checked against academic histories of 1793-94 (Huchet 1988; Jean-Clément Martin), covering Robespierre, the devil figure, Fr Bernier and the morality of the rising.

grey.question: No independent critic has assessed how this film handles its history. What has been written comes from the director, from Catholic outlets that promoted it and from family-viewing guides. Joseph Pearce's appreciative essay concedes that it gives up historical nuance and shows Robespierre as demonically possessed. Morlino drew mainly on Reynald Secher's disputed genocide thesis and combined people and events. A review or documented viewing that checks the Revolutionaries, the devil figure, the priest Fr Bernier and the rising itself against academic histories of 1793–94 would settle it.

summary: Jim Morlino's low-budget drama of the 1793 Catholic rising in western France, played entirely by a cast of some 250 children and teenagers.
synopsis: In 1793 the Revolutionary government has outlawed priests who refuse the constitutional oath and orders a mass levy of conscripts. In a village of the Vendée, peasants and local nobles decide to take up arms for their priests and their king. The film follows the villagers and their families through secret meetings, a Latin Mass celebrated before battle, early victories, losses and reprisals. A boy, Remy, is turned away from the men's council and longs to fight; the village women push the hesitant men to act. In Paris, Robespierre appears as the sinister face of the Revolution. A priest, Fr Bernier, ministers to the rising, and the devil appears as a hooded figure. Every role, the adults included, is played by young performers, more than 250 of them.
inclusion: It is one of very few English-language films about the Vendée, and it keeps the religious cause of the rising at the centre: the persecution of priests who refused the oath, and Mass said in Latin before battle. Morlino made it through his Navis Pictures as a children's cinema project, with a cast all under 21 and a tiny budget. Fr John Zuhlsdorf, writing from a DVD supplied for review, found the acting uneven but praised Kevin Kaska's score. Joseph Pearce, an editor for Ignatius Press, which distributes the DVD, expected a bad film and was charmed, while admitting that it trades historical nuance for plain good against plain evil. Catholic festivals gave it prizes for young audiences. It is made for families and older children.
themes: The film's Catholic content is the defence of the sacraments and of faithful priests. The rising is presented as a response to the persecution of clergy who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and the Mass before battle is its central religious image. The devil appears as a hooded figure, and Pearce reads Robespierre as shown possessed. What has not been established is how the film handles the morality of armed rebellion, the Republican atrocities it chose to omit, and its priest character, Fr Bernier.
history: The Vendée rising began in March 1793, when conscription for the levy of 300,000 men set off armed revolt across parts of Maine-et-Loire, Vendée, Deux-Sèvres and Loire-Inférieure. Françoise Huchet's study traces its first days in Maine-et-Loire between 2 and 22 March 1793. Hostility to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the persecution of priests who refused the oath were central grievances. The Catholic and Royal Army won early victories before defeat at Cholet and Savenay in late 1793, followed by severe Republican repression in 1794. Historians still argue over death tolls and over Secher's description of the repression as genocide.
liberties: Morlino says he combined characters and events and put historical figures together in one village "for convenience", though several never met. He also says he left out many atrocities because the film was made for young people. His main research source was Reynald Secher's A French Genocide, whose central term he acknowledges is hotly contested by historians. Pearce notes that the film removes the nuance that historical accuracy demands.
advisories:
Battle scenes with swords, muskets and cannon; parent reviews report no blood.

Persecution of priests, deaths and bereavement.

The devil appears as a hooded figure.

All adult roles are played by children and teenagers; the acting is uneven.

The film presents the conflict as plain good against plain evil and follows Secher's disputed genocide framing.

title: A Forbidden God
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (the Claretian martyrs of Barbastro, beatified 1992).
summary: A sincere, cheaply made account of the 51 Claretian seminarians, brothers and priests held and shot at Barbastro in August 1936, notable for its stress on forgiveness.
synopsis: In July 1936, after the military rising, a revolutionary committee takes control of Barbastro in Aragon. The Claretian community is arrested. The superiors are separated and shot first; the young students and brothers are crowded into the assembly hall of the Piarist school. A local CNT leader, Eugenio Sopena, tries at first to protect them, but the arrival of harder men from Barcelona sweeps him aside. The prisoners are pressed to renounce their vocation, mocked and tempted, including by a young militiawoman, Trini, who is drawn to the student Esteban Casadevall. They smuggle the consecrated Host into their breakfast bread, write farewell notes, and go to their deaths in groups in August 1936. Two Argentine students are released.
inclusion: Pablo Moreno, working from Ciudad Rodrigo with a small company and a young cast, took the more difficult route: a martyrdom film about the victims' faith rather than their killers' cruelty. Jerónimo José Martín (Aceprensa) calls it "more religious than denunciatory". Esther Rodríguez (Contraste) credits it with conveying the faith that let the men accept death while forgiving, and with giving human dimensions to characters on both sides. There are real weaknesses. Several performances are amateurish, sound and lighting are poor, some exteriors are obviously faked, and the 39 students blur into a single group. Beatriz Martínez (SensaCine) found it slow, naive and full of stock villains. For viewers interested in the Spanish martyrs, its sincerity and historical grounding outweigh its limits.
themes: The Eucharist is the film's spiritual centre. The prisoners receive Communion secretly for as long as they can, and one priest slips up to the chapel to rescue the consecrated Hosts. The second strand is fidelity to religious vows under pressure, including sexual temptation; the young Claretian courted by a militiawoman answers that he is "married to God". The third is forgiveness. The farewell notes the men left, preserved by the order, forgive their executioners and offer their deaths for the Church and the Congregation. The film shows the anticlerical view of the Church as an ally of the rich without endorsing it, and it does not make the militiamen uniformly monstrous.
history: In July 1936 the Claretian community at Barbastro numbered nine priests, 39 students and 12 lay brothers. A revolutionary committee of anarchists and communists held them from 20 July. Over August 1936, 51 were shot, the superiors first. The two Argentine students who were freed carried testimony and keepsakes to Rome. The same repression killed the Bishop of Barbastro, Florentino Asensio, and the Romani layman Ceferino Giménez Malla ("El Pelé"). John Paul II beatified the 51 Claretians in 1992 and Asensio and Giménez Malla in 1997.
liberties: Moreno says about 90 percent of the screenplay rests on the martyrs' writings and contemporary testimony. Trini's infatuation with Casadevall and Sopena's attempt to protect the prisoners are documented episodes, according to La Vanguardia. Dialogue, the treatment of the student group as a near-collective character and the compression of events across several weeks are dramatic choices. Some comic moments, such as seminarians drilled with wooden rifles, are invented.
advisories:
Imprisonment, humiliation, beatings, torture and mass executions by firing squad.

Sexual temptation of the prisoners, including a militiawoman's advances to a seminarian (rejected).

Best for teenagers and adults.

It shows one local episode of anticlerical violence, not the whole Civil War.

title: For Greater Glory
originalTitle: For Greater Glory: The True Story of Cristiada
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (José Sánchez del Río, beatified 2005, canonised 2016).
summary: A big, earnest English-language epic of Mexico's Cristero War, built around an unbelieving general and a boy martyr, stronger on conviction than on history or subtlety.
synopsis: In 1926 President Calles enforces the anticlerical articles of the Mexican constitution: foreign priests are expelled, churches closed and public worship suspended. Peaceful protest fails and armed rebels rise under the cry 'Viva Cristo Rey'. The National League for the Defence of Religious Liberty hires Enrique Gorostieta, a retired general and sceptic, to turn the scattered bands into an army. Among them are the rancher Victoriano 'El Catorce' Ramírez and Fr José Reyes Vega, a priest who carries a rifle. A boy, José Sánchez del Río, sees the old priest who taught him shot by federal troops and joins the rebels. Women smuggle ammunition. As Gorostieta's campaign succeeds, the American ambassador Dwight Morrow brokers a settlement between the government and the Church, and José is captured.
inclusion: This is the only large-scale film about the Cristiada in English, and its Catholic stakes are explicit: Mass said in secret, priests killed at the altar, a boy who will not say 'Death to Christ the King'. The martyrdom of José Sánchez del Río, now a canonised saint, is the emotional centre, and it is staged with obvious debts to the Passion. Andy Garcia gives Gorostieta's slow movement towards faith a dry, watchful dignity, and Bruce Greenwood is sharp as Morrow. Location shooting and James Horner's score give it scale. The weaknesses are typical of the faith-based epic: heavy exposition, insistent music, flat villains, too many characters introduced and dropped. Steven Greydanus rates it a flawed but worthwhile film.
themes: The film's subject is religious persecution and martyrdom, and it handles both with conviction: the Mass, the priesthood and the Kingship of Christ are what the Cristeros fight for. It argues that the faithful may defend their liberty by force once peaceful means fail, which is broadly the reasoning Pius XI set out in Firmissimam constantiam (1937): lawful, proportionate means, never an end in themselves. Pius XI also said armed defence is no part of the clergy's task, and the film admires Fr Vega's fighting without much question. The 1929 settlement between the bishops and the government, brokered with Rome's involvement, is presented as a bitter compromise that left the rebels exposed.
history: Calles's enforcement of the 1917 constitution provoked the Cristero rising of 1926–29. Jean Meyer, the war's principal historian, interviewed hundreds of veterans for La Cristiada. Fr José Reyes Vega led the attack on the Guadalajara train near La Barca in April 1927 and, having lost a brother in the fight, set it on fire; Meyer counts 52 soldiers and about 30 civilians dead. José Sánchez del Río was killed in 1928 and canonised in 2016.
liberties: Fr Vega is turned into a pious warrior who burns the train in a moment of confusion and spends the rest of the film seeking forgiveness; the historical Vega had a much worse reputation and burned the train in anger. Gorostieta's arc from unbelief to faith is disputed: Greydanus calls the real man an anticlerical Freemason, while Herodote reports letters to his wife, known to Meyer, showing a convinced Catholic. Anacleto González Flores is reduced to a cameo. Several relationships between characters are invented.
advisories:
Rated R for war violence and executions. Priests are shot and hanged, a boy is hanged, civilians are killed in a church, and José is tortured, including having the soles of his feet cut, before being killed. Screams are heard from a burning train.

Desecration of churches and sacred objects.

Little bad language and no sexual content beyond a married couple in bed. Older teenagers and adults.

A priest takes part in combat and the film largely admires him for it; the Church did not.

title: The Scarlet and the Black
decision: PUBLISH: Television Academy records confirm the 1983 CBS film; Greydanus's Decent Films review gives a scene-aware positive assessment (priestly charity, accurate closing coda) and flags the invented Pius XII Concordat scene; CNA/Catholic World Report confirms the history of O'Flaherty's escape line and Kappler's 1959 baptism. Dramatic liberties are ordinary for the genre and do not distort the religious meaning.
summary: Gregory Peck plays Mgr Hugh O'Flaherty, the Irish Vatican priest who hid thousands of escaped prisoners and Jews under the nose of the SS in occupied Rome.
synopsis: Rome, 1943. German troops occupy the city, and SS chief Herbert Kappler paints a white line across the edge of St Peter's Square: if Monsignor O'Flaherty steps over it, he will be shot. O'Flaherty, an Irish official of the Holy Office, has already started hiding escaped Allied prisoners and Jews in flats, convents and monasteries, with help from priests, diplomats and Roman families. He slips past the line in disguises, outwits raids and survives an attempt on his life inside the Vatican. As the Allies approach, Kappler, fearing for his own family, asks his enemy for help. A closing coda follows the two men after the war.
inclusion: This is a well-made, old-fashioned television thriller with a priest as its hero, and it never lets you forget he is a priest. Peck plays O'Flaherty as blunt, funny and fearless, a man who boxes and plays golf but treats every life he hides as a charge from God. Christopher Plummer's Kappler is cold and intelligent rather than a cartoon villain, and their duel gives the film its spine. The best scenes turn on mercy: O'Flaherty's choice when Kappler pleads for his wife and children, and the true postscript about what the priest did for Kappler in prison. Steven Greydanus calls it riveting and edifying. Rome locations and an Ennio Morricone score help; the pacing sags in the middle.
themes: The film's Catholic heart is the priest's refusal to divide people into those who deserve help and those who do not. O'Flaherty hides Jews, Communists and Allied soldiers alike, and finally extends the same charity to the man who tried to have him killed. The Vatican appears as a place of real moral tension: O'Flaherty's superiors worry that his work threatens the Holy See's neutrality, and John Gielgud's Pius XII is sympathetic. Greydanus notes one scene in which the Pope has second thoughts about the Concordat with Germany, which is a filmmakers' invention.
history: Hugh O'Flaherty, from Kerry, served in the Holy Office and ran what became known as the Rome Escape Line during the nine-month German occupation; a 2016 Vatican plaque credits him with saving over 6,000 lives. Kappler was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1948. O'Flaherty visited him every month and baptised him in 1959. O'Flaherty died in Ireland in 1963.
liberties: The film is based on J. P. Gallagher's book The Scarlet Pimpernel of the Vatican and compresses events into a cat-and-mouse plot. The SS general Max Helm is a fictionalised stand-in for Karl Wolff, who was still alive. The scene of Pius XII doubting the Concordat is invented. Kappler's appeal to O'Flaherty over his family is dramatised for the climax.
advisories:
Wartime violence, including executions, a raid and the murder of a priest; no graphic gore by modern standards.

No sexual content of note. Suitable for teenagers and up; younger children may find the menace and killings upsetting.

The Vatican scenes are dramatised and should not be taken as a record of Pius XII's words.

title: The Ninth Day
decision: PUBLISH: the Film Fund Luxembourg catalogue confirms identity; Greydanus's detailed review and Thomas Wolter's essay in forum (Luxembourg, 2004) establish both the film's moral seriousness and exactly what is invented. The interrogation is openly a dramatisation of nine days Bernard's diary barely describes. The Pius XII material is a character's doubt answered by his bishop's account of reprisals, not the film's verdict; its one chronological slip (the Dutch reprisals of summer 1942) is noted. A Luxembourg critic's complaint that the film is pro-Church propaganda is recorded.
summary: A starved priest is let out of Dachau for nine days and given a choice by a Gestapo officer: win over his bishop for the Reich, or go back to the camp.
synopsis: Dachau, early 1942. Abbé Henri Kremer, a Luxembourg priest, survives in the priests' block amid hunger, beatings and executions. Suddenly he is released and sent home, apparently for his mother's funeral. In Luxembourg he must report each day to Untersturmführer Gebhardt, a young Gestapo officer who once studied for the priesthood. Gebhardt wants Kremer to persuade the Bishop of Luxembourg, who has shut himself away in protest, to accept the occupation; then a signed declaration will do. If Kremer refuses or runs, the priests in Dachau will pay. Over nine days the two men argue about faith, obedience and the Church's silence while Kremer's family urges him to save himself.
inclusion: Schlöndorff turns a small episode into a tight moral drama, and the film's achievement is that the arguments are real arguments. Ulrich Matthes, gaunt and hollow-eyed, plays Kremer as a man with no heroism left, only conscience. August Diehl's Gebhardt is clever, polite and a theologian of sorts, which makes him more dangerous than a thug. The Dachau scenes are brief and restrained but unforgettable. Steven Greydanus gives it his top grade, noting that it shows several kinds of resistance and their costs rather than offering a simple defence or accusation. It is short, grey and austere.
themes: Kremer's choice is the classic one between apostasy dressed as prudence and fidelity that may cost his life. The film is sharp on how temptation works: Gebhardt does not ask him to deny Christ, only to compromise a little for the good of others. The priests in Dachau pray, say Mass in secret and share bread; some of them are shown collaborating or bitter. The Church's public silence is debated openly. Kremer says he never doubts the Church but sometimes doubts the Holy Father, and his bishop answers that protests have brought reprisals on the very people they were meant to help.
history: Jean Bernard (1907–1994), a Luxembourg priest, was arrested in 1941 and sent to Dachau, where he was among the many priests held in the clergy block. In February 1942 he was released for nine days, apparently to win over Luxembourg's clergy, refused, and returned. He was freed in August 1942, later edited the Luxemburger Wort and led the international Catholic film office (OCIC). His memoir is Pfarrerblock 25487.
liberties: The hero is renamed Kremer. Bernard's diary says almost nothing about the nine days, so the daily interrogations and Gebhardt are invented; Thomas Wolter notes none of the conversations happened as staged. A detail from Primo Levi's memoirs is borrowed. The bishop's reference to reprisals after the Dutch bishops' protest is anachronistic: that protest and the arrests that followed, including Edith Stein's, came in July and August 1942, after the story's February setting.
advisories:
Concentration-camp brutality: beatings, starvation and deaths, shown briefly and without lingering.

Some crude language. No sexual content.

Suitable for older teenagers and adults.

The film raises the question of Pius XII's public silence through its characters; it is a drama, not a historical verdict.

title: A Hidden Life
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Franz Jägerstätter, beatified 2007).
summary: Malick's long, lyrical film about Franz Jägerstätter, the Austrian farmer who refused to swear loyalty to Hitler and was executed in 1943, and the wife who stood by him.
synopsis: In the mountain village of St Radegund, Franz and Fani Jägerstätter farm, raise three small daughters and go to Mass. After the Anschluss Franz becomes the only man in the village to vote against it, and when he is called up he cannot bring himself to swear the oath to Hitler. Neighbours turn on the family. The parish priest and then the Bishop of Linz urge him to think of his wife and children. Franz reports for duty, refuses the oath and is imprisoned, first in Linz and then in Berlin. Lawyers and officers offer him easy ways out. Fani keeps the farm going alone while letters pass between them. He is tried and condemned.
inclusion: This is Malick's most direct film about faith, and the one where his methods most suit the subject. Long passages of farm work, mountains and weather build a world worth losing. August Diehl's Franz says little; Valerie Pachner's Fani is the film's emotional anchor, and Combs singles out Bruno Ganz, in his last role, as a judge crushed by his inability to save him. Voiceover drawn from the couple's letters carries much of the meaning. At nearly three hours it demands patience, and CNS warns that much of it is domestic routine. For viewers who give it the time, the last hour is overwhelming.
themes: Franz's refusal is grounded in his Catholic faith: he will not swear an oath to a regime he believes evil, whatever it costs. The film shows Mass, prayer and the sacristy as parts of ordinary village life, and its opening scene of a church painter who admits he paints a comfortable Christ sets out its subject: the difference between admiring Christ and following him. CNS's John Mulderig calls the treatment of the parish priest and bishop ambivalent at best; they counsel prudence and family duty. Pappas reads Fani's endurance as a hidden, Marian counterpart to Franz's martyrdom.
history: Franz Jägerstätter (1907–1943), a farmer and sacristan in St Radegund, refused military service in March 1943 on religious grounds. He had sought the counsel of Bishop Joseph Calasanz Fliesser of Linz, who by his own account explained a citizen's duties towards those in authority 'in vain'; Franz came out saying the clergy did not dare speak. He was condemned for undermining military morale and guillotined at Brandenburg on 9 August 1943. He was beatified in Linz on 26 October 2007. Franziska died in 2013, aged 100.
liberties: Dialogue is largely invented around the letters, and the clergy's scenes compress several conversations. The village's hostility is heightened. Combs notes that the film never lets Franz articulate his position as a formal conscientious objection, which leaves his reasoning more mysterious than his writings are.
advisories:
Prison beatings and humiliation, and the threat and fact of execution, handled without gore.

The family is shunned and harassed by neighbours.

Rated PG-13; CNS A-II (adults and adolescents). Running time 174 minutes.

Priests and a bishop are shown urging compromise; the portrayal reflects the historical record but is not flattering.

title: Triumph of the Heart
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Maximilian Kolbe, beatified 1971, canonised 1982).
summary: A harrowing chamber drama set almost entirely in the Auschwitz starvation bunker, where Maximilian Kolbe leads nine condemned men in prayer during their last days.
synopsis: After a prisoner escapes from Auschwitz in 1941, the SS deputy commandant Karl Fritzsch picks ten men from the block to starve to death. When one of them cries out for his wife and children, the Franciscan priest Maximilian Kolbe steps forward and asks to take his place. The rest of the film unfolds in the underground cell. The men bring fear, rage, guilt and old injuries with them. Kolbe hears their confessions, leads them in prayer and song, and holds the group together as hunger, thirst and hallucinations take hold. After two weeks only Kolbe and three others are alive, and the guards kill them by lethal injection.
inclusion: Writer-director Anthony D'Ambrosio confines a famous act of self-sacrifice to one dark room, and the confinement works. The story becomes less about the heroic gesture than about what a priest does with the days that follow. Marcin Kwaśny, a Polish actor performing in English, plays Kolbe as steady rather than saintly in a stained-glass way. OSV News's Joseph McAleer and the National Catholic Register's Joseph Pronechen both praise the script and the central performance; Pronechen notes how flashbacks and visions open up the men's inner lives. The film is hard to watch. McAleer rates it for adults only, and the starvation scenes, hallucinations and abuse by guards make that limit essential.
themes: The film is explicitly sacramental. Kolbe hears the condemned men's confessions and makes them a brotherhood of prayer. He asks Our Lady for the words he needs. The men sing a lullaby based on the Salve Regina, which enrages the guards and heartens prisoners who hear it. When despair sets in, Kolbe points to Christ's own cry of abandonment on the cross and urges the men to die with their eyes on God. The film reads his substitution through John 15:13, "greater love hath no man". It does not soften the cost: the men's anger at God is given real voice before it is answered.
history: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941), a Polish Conventual Franciscan, founded the Militia of the Immaculata and the friary-publishing centre at Niepokalanów. Arrested in February 1941, he became prisoner 16670 at Auschwitz. In late July 1941, after an escape, ten men were condemned to the starvation bunker. Kolbe volunteered in place of Franciszek Gajowniczek, a sergeant with a wife and sons. Gajowniczek survived the war and died in 1995. Kolbe, still alive after two weeks, was killed by injection of carbolic acid on 14 August 1941. He was beatified in 1971 and canonised as a martyr by John Paul II in 1982.
liberties: Nothing is known of what was said in the bunker beyond survivors' reports that prayers and hymns were heard from the cell. The other prisoners' identities, backstories, quarrels and conversations are invented or composite. The Salve Regina lullaby, the visions and the dialogue are dramatic constructions.

Graphic violence and executions by guards; humiliation of prisoners.

Starvation shown in detail, with hallucinations and violent mood swings; sickness, death, crematorium ashes.

Two crude oaths.

title: Rome, Open City
decision: REJECT: Editor ruling under the Founder's position (2026-10-11). The film's centre is the Resistance, not the faith, and it presents a priest's common cause with Communist partisans as exemplary, against Pius XI's Divini Redemptoris (1937). It is not Catholic-centred and its outlook on that point is contrary to pre-conciliar teaching.
summary: Rossellini's raw, half-documentary account of occupied Rome in 1944, in which a parish priest and a Communist resistance leader are hunted by the Gestapo and die together.
synopsis: Rome, winter 1944, under German occupation. Giorgio Manfredi, a Communist leader of the resistance, escapes a Gestapo raid and seeks shelter with Francesco, a fellow resister, whose fiancée Pina is a widow expecting his child. The local parish priest, Don Pietro, carries money and messages to the partisans outside the city and is to marry Pina and Francesco. In a German round-up of their tenement Francesco is arrested, and Pina is shot dead running after the truck. Francesco escapes, and he and Manfredi hide with Manfredi's girlfriend Marina, who depends on drugs supplied by Ingrid, a Gestapo agent. Marina betrays them. Manfredi and Don Pietro are taken to Gestapo headquarters, where Major Bergmann has Manfredi tortured to death while trying to break the priest. Neither talks. Don Pietro is shot by firing squad the next morning.
inclusion: Shot within months of the liberation, on the streets and with scavenged film stock, it made Rossellini and Anna Magnani international names and won the top prize at Cannes in 1946. Its rough, newsreel look is mixed with old-fashioned melodrama, as Alex Barrett notes for the BFI, and the mixture is what gives it force. Pina's death in the street is one of the great shocks of the decade. Aldo Fabrizi's Don Pietro starts as a comic figure, refereeing a boys' football match, and grows into a man who dies with complete resolve. Steven Greydanus grades it A+. The German villains are stereotypes, some scenes are contrived, and the politics are of its moment. It is a primary document of how Rome remembered the occupation, and of a priest's courage in it.
themes: Don Pietro is a recognisable parish priest: he uses his cassock to move after curfew, claims to be going to anoint a dying man to get past German soldiers, and holds firm under interrogation. Barrett notes how heavily the script draws on Catholic symbolism, and Greydanus points to Manfredi's body posed like the crucified Christ. The problem is the frame. The film celebrates a united front of Catholics and Communists, and when Bergmann calls Manfredi an atheist and an enemy, the priest answers that whoever fights for justice and liberty walks in the ways of the Lord. Pius XI had forbidden Catholics to collaborate with Communism in any undertaking, and in 1949 the Holy Office excommunicated Catholics who supported it. The film never raises that question.
history: The story was first planned as a documentary about Don Giuseppe Morosini, a Roman priest executed by the Germans in April 1944 for helping the resistance. Sergio Amidei, Federico Fellini and Alberto Consiglio worked on the script with Rossellini. It opened in Italy on 27 September 1945 and in New York, as Open City, on 25 February 1946, in a cut version.
liberties: Don Pietro is a composite fiction; Morosini was not executed alongside a Communist leader, and the film's events are dramatised rather than reconstructed. The German officers are drawn as decadent stereotypes.
advisories:
Torture: a prisoner is tortured to death largely off screen, and his beaten body is shown.

A pregnant woman is shot dead in the street; a priest is executed by firing squad.

Drug dependency: a Gestapo agent keeps a young woman supplied with drugs; the agent's interest in her is implied to be sexual.

A couple expecting a child before marriage; a nightclub milieu.

For older teenagers and adults.

The Legion of Decency classified the film as objectionable (B or C; sources differ).

title: Quo Vadis
decision: PUBLISH: Re-checked against the AFI Catalog's full synopsis. The joint suicide is real but belongs to the pagan Petronius and his slave Eunice, while the Christians die by martyrdom and Nero's own suicide is shown as cowardice; the coercive start of the romance is Nero's act, which Lygia escapes and refuses until Vinicius turns towards Christ. Neither is endorsed by the film. Liz Gloyn and the Dickinson College essay give substantive treatment. Both elements are flagged in advisories.
summary: MGM's Technicolor epic of Nero's Rome sets a Roman commander's pursuit of a Christian girl against the Great Fire, the first persecution and the deaths of St Peter and St Paul.
synopsis: In AD 64 the commander Marcus Vinicius returns to Rome and falls for Lygia, a Christian hostage raised by a retired general. When she rebuffs him, his uncle Petronius gets Nero to hand her to Marcus as a gift; her giant servant Ursus rescues her. Marcus tracks her to a secret gathering where St Peter tells of his time with Christ. Lygia will not marry him at the price of her faith. Nero burns Rome to inspire a poem and, to save himself, blames the Christians. On the Appian Way Peter meets his Lord and turns back to Rome. Christians are thrown to the lions, Peter is crucified, Petronius takes his own life, and Lygia is tied in the arena before a bull, with Ursus her only defender.
inclusion: This is the film that started the 1950s epic cycle, and it has the virtues and faults of the type. The sets, crowds and Robert Surtees's colour photography are lavish; the burning of Rome is spectacular. Peter Ustinov's Nero, vain, petulant and murderous, steals the picture, and Leo Genn's ironic Petronius runs him close. Robert Taylor and Deborah Kerr are stiff, and the romance is the weakest part. What surprises modern viewers, as the classicist Liz Gloyn found, is how central the Church is: Peter and Paul appear in person, the catacomb liturgy and Peter's preaching are given time, and the martyrs go to the lions singing. The Christian community is idealised but attractive.
themes: The film's subject is the Church's first persecution and the witness of the martyrs. Peter recounts the miraculous catch and the Resurrection, the Domine, quo vadis legend sends him back to Rome to die, and he is crucified head downward, as tradition reports. Paul preaches that Christ conquers by love. Lygia prays for Marcus's conversion and refuses to buy his love with her faith; Peter marries them in prison. Against this the film sets Roman decadence and Nero's claim to divinity. Petronius dies as a cultivated pagan; the contrast with the Christians who 'know how to die' is the point.
history: Rome burned in July 64, and Nero blamed the Christians, whom Tacitus records were killed in his gardens. Early tradition, reported by Origen through Eusebius, says Peter was crucified head downward at his own wish; the date of his death is uncertain within 64 to 68. The Quo vadis encounter on the Appian Way is an ancient legend, not a scriptural event. Petronius's forced suicide is recorded by Tacitus.
liberties: Lygia, Vinicius and Ursus are fictional, from Henryk Sienkiewicz's 1896 novel. The joint suicide with a slave is borrowed from Seneca and Paulina, who survived. There is no evidence that Poppaea proposed blaming the Christians. Nero's death and Galba's arrival are compressed into the aftermath of the persecution. The flowering staff is a pious legend.
advisories:
A long scene shows Petronius and his slave Eunice opening their veins and dying at table; it is calm and bloodless but sympathetic to them.

Christians are killed by lions and burned at the stake, mostly offscreen; Nero strangles Poppaea and is helped to stab himself; sword fights and a man's neck broken.

Nero orders Lygia given to Marcus as a slave at the start; scantily dressed dancers and Roman revels.

Younger children may find the arena scenes frightening.

title: Fabiola
decision: GREY: The reservation is documented by contemporary pre-conciliar Catholic evidence: Paola Palma's archival study (Schermi, 2017) shows the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified the Italian commercial version 'adulti con riserva', Morlion (OCIC review) called that rating deserved after his cuts to love scenes, a banquet dance and semi-nude courtesans were refused, and Vittorino Veronese of Catholic Action found the film 'molto discutibile' for its thesis and sensual material. Not REJECT: no hard rule applies and nothing suggests sacrilege; the subject is the early martyrs. Not PUBLISH: the reservation stands and the film departs widely from Wiseman. What would settle it: the CCC's published review (Segnalazioni cinematografiche, 1949) or a scene-level account of the complete Italian version.

grey.question: Fabiola was sold as a Catholic epic, but the Italian Catholic film office of its own day classified the release 'adults with reservations', and Catholic Action's Vittorino Veronese found it very questionable for its thesis and its gratuitous sensual scenes. It also uses Cardinal Wiseman's novel loosely, putting a gladiator romance and a murder plot in place of the catacomb saints. The question is whether its account of conversion and martyrdom survives the love story. The Catholic office's published review, or a viewing of the full Italian version against the novel, would settle it.

summary: Blasetti's huge postwar epic, very loosely from Cardinal Wiseman's novel, turns the Church of the catacombs into a gladiator romance and murder plot that ends in the arena.
synopsis: In Rome around 312, Fabiola, a senator's daughter, falls for Rhual, a Gaulish gladiator who is secretly an agent of Constantine. Her father, Senator Fabius, who favours tolerance and the freeing of slaves, is murdered, and the Christians are blamed and put on trial. Rhual is condemned with them to the arena. Fabiola at first suspects him, then takes her stand with the Christians in the arena. Rhual refuses to kill his opponents and the other gladiators follow him. Constantine's army reaches Rome, the city rises, and the film ends under the Christian standards of the new emperor.
inclusion: Fabiola opened the postwar wave of religious epics, as the Treccani film encyclopedia notes, and it was the biggest Italian spectacle since the war: Michèle Morgan, Henri Vidal and Michel Simon, enormous sets, and the top box office of its Italian season. French critics in 1949, as Paola Palma's archival study shows, admired Blasetti's handling of crowds while finding the film too long. Time Out's reviewer finds it dull until the violent climax in the arena; Manny Farber, seeing the shortened American version, called it a chaos of disconnected sequences. Its interest now is largely historical: an ambitious Catholic spectacle in postwar Italy, made by a company widely taken for a Vatican enterprise, whose Catholic credentials the Catholic film bodies then publicly disowned.
themes: Wiseman's 1854 novel is a Catholic apologetic for the Church of the catacombs: Agnes, Sebastian, Pancratius and the acolyte Tarcisius die for the faith, and the pagan Fabiola is finally baptised with her household. The film keeps the persecution, the arena and names such as Sebastiano, Cecilia, Sira and Fulvio, but builds its story on an invented gladiator who serves Constantine, a murder mystery and a love affair. A French critic in 1949 complained that Fabiola reaches Christianity by way of profane passion. Vittorino Veronese of Catholic Action judged the film's thesis very questionable and its sensual touches superfluous. Whether Fabiola's conversion is shown as faith or as loyalty to a lover is the point to watch.
history: Salvo D'Angelo's Universalia Film made Fabiola with French money and stars through Franco-London Films, though it was not an official co-production. It opened in Italy on 3 March 1949 and in France a few months later. The Centro Cattolico Cinematografico classified the Italian commercial version 'adults with reservations'. The Dominican Félix Morlion had praised it in the OCIC's new review, expecting cuts he had asked for; they were never made, and a correction in his name accepted the Catholic office's rating. Shortened dubbed versions reached Britain and America in 1951. A restoration was presented in Rome in 2001.
liberties: Rhual, the gladiator-agent of Constantine, the murder of Fabiola's father and the love story are invented. The novel's martyrdoms of Agnes, Pancratius and Tarcisius do not appear in the cast lists consulted. The film sets its action around 312, on the eve of Constantine's victory, rather than in the Diocletian persecution where Wiseman places most of the story, and it ends with Constantine's army entering Rome; the plot summaries consulted do not mention the baptism of Fabiola and her household that the novel narrates.
advisories:
Prolonged kisses and love scenes, a banquet dance and semi-nude courtesans: the material a 1949 Catholic critic asked to have cut.

Arena martyrdoms and mass violence at the climax.

Classified 'adults with reservations' by the Italian Catholic film office in 1949. Adults and older teenagers.

Versions vary widely, from the Italian release of about 164 minutes to an American dubbed cut of about 97, and the French release differed again. Check which version a copy is.

title: Diary of a Country Priest
alternateTitles: Le Journal d'un curé de campagne
decision: PUBLISH: Steven Greydanus's detailed review and the critical tradition around the film establish a portrait of priestly perseverance and grace in apparent failure, drawn faithfully from Bernanos. Adult material (an affair, a threatened suicide) is part of the moral drama and is disclosed.
summary: Bresson's spare adaptation of Bernanos follows a sickly young curé whose parish rejects him, and finds holiness in apparent failure.
synopsis: A young priest arrives in Ambricourt, a village in northern France. He is poor, ill, inexperienced and awkward, and his parishioners respond with indifference or mockery. He records everything in a diary. The older curé of Torcy gives him blunt advice about running a parish. At the château, the count is having an affair with the governess, and the count's daughter Chantal hates them both and threatens to kill herself. The priest confronts the countess, who has been bitter towards God since the death of her son. In a long exchange she yields and makes her peace, and she dies that night. Gossip about the encounter turns the village further against him. Diagnosed with stomach cancer, he travels to Lille and dies in the lodgings of a former seminary friend who has left the priesthood.
inclusion: This is one of the essential films about the priesthood. Bresson strips away everything decorative: Claude Laydu's still face, the diary voice-over, Léonce-Henry Burel's grey images of the Artois countryside. What remains is a man trying to do his duty with almost no visible success. The scene with the countess is the dramatic peak; Greydanus compares it to the great dialogues in The Brothers Karamazov. André Bazin's 1951 essay on the film helped make it a landmark of modern cinema. It won the Prix Louis Delluc and the International Award and OCIC (Catholic) prize at Venice. The pace is slow and the tone severe, and some viewers find it opaque. It rewards patience.
themes: The film's subject is the priesthood stripped of consolation. The curé suffers spiritual dryness, physical weakness and the contempt of his flock. He feels unable even to pray, yet keeps saying Mass, visiting and hearing confessions. Greydanus notes how he accepts failure, dryness and persecution and turns them into a kind of victory. The countess scene shows the cure of souls in action: he refuses to accept her despair and leads her to surrender her grief to God. The end gives Bernanos's last words to the priest: "All is grace." The film treats a priest's life as fruitful in ways he cannot see.
history: Georges Bernanos published his novel Journal d'un curé de campagne in 1936; it won the Grand Prix du roman of the Académie française. Bernanos died in 1948, before Bresson's adaptation. The curé is fictional, though Bernanos drew on the rural clergy of the Pas-de-Calais.
liberties: Bresson follows the novel closely but cuts heavily, especially the long reflective passages and several conversations with the curé of Torcy. He invents almost nothing; his changes are mainly omissions and a sharper focus on the priest's isolation.
advisories:
An adulterous affair (implied, not shown).

A girl threatens suicide; a death; terminal illness.

Slow and austere; best for older teenagers and adults.

title: I Confess
decision: PUBLISH: America's Catholic Movie Club essay, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish the seal of confession as the film's governing moral fact; the priest keeps it at the risk of his life. Mature material (murder, blackmail, a past romance) is disclosed.
summary: Hitchcock's most Catholic film: a Quebec priest hears a murderer's confession and then, bound by the seal, cannot clear himself when suspicion falls on him.
synopsis: In Quebec City, Otto Keller, a German refugee who works at the parish, confesses to Father Michael Logan that he has killed a lawyer named Villette during a robbery, wearing a cassock as a disguise. Witnesses saw a priest leaving the house. Inspector Larrue learns that Villette had been blackmailing Ruth Grandfort, a married woman who had loved Logan before his ordination, and Logan becomes the chief suspect. He will not say what he knows. Keller, increasingly afraid, plants evidence against him. Logan is tried, acquitted for want of proof and jeered by a hostile crowd outside the courthouse, before the truth comes out in a confrontation at the Château Frontenac.
inclusion: Hitchcock, raised a Catholic and taught by Jesuits, built a thriller around a rule most of his audience did not understand, and the film's power comes from treating that rule as absolute. Montgomery Clift plays Logan almost entirely through silence and posture. Robert Burks's location photography makes Quebec's steep streets and churches part of the drama. The flaws are real: Hitchcock himself thought it heavy-handed and humourless, and the Ruth flashbacks are stiff. But few Hollywood films show a priest paying so high a price for keeping the seal, and none does it with more conviction.
themes: The seal of confession is the hinge of the plot. Logan may not reveal what Keller told him, even to save himself from the gallows, and he never considers doing so. Hitchcock blamed the film's weak box office on audiences who did not grasp why a priest would stay silent. John Dougherty, writing in America, calls it a uniquely Catholic moral conundrum. The film also draws the contrast between the penitent's duty and the priest's: Keller confesses but does not make amends, and his fear drives him to frame the man bound to protect his secret.
history: The screenplay by George Tabori and William Archibald adapts Paul Anthelme's 1902 French play Nos deux consciences. Hitchcock had owned the rights for years. Warner Bros. vetoed the original ending, in which the priest is executed before his innocence is proved, and a pre-ordination illegitimate child, according to TCM "for fear of offending Catholics". The film was shot on location in Quebec City, with a priest, Father Paul LaCouline, credited as technical adviser.
liberties: This is fiction, not a reconstructed case. The investigation and trial are simplified for suspense. The play's darker ending, in which the innocent priest dies, was replaced at the studio's insistence, and the play's illegitimate child was cut.
advisories:
A murder, blackmail and a police shooting.

Flashbacks to the priest's pre-ordination romance with a woman who had married another man; restrained.

Suitable for teenagers and adults.
