title: Angels of Sin
decision: PUBLISH: Doug Cummings's detailed essay and the BFI record establish a drama of zeal, pride, humility and repentance inside a Dominican congregation that receives women from prison; the ending joins the religious and the legal acceptance of guilt. Murder and emotional cruelty are disclosed.
summary: Bresson's first feature: a novice in a convent for former prisoners sets out to save a hardened young woman, and has to be saved from her own pride first.
synopsis: Anne-Marie, a well-off young woman with a fervent vocation, enters the Dominican Sisters of Bethany, a congregation that welcomes women released from prison. Accompanying the sisters to collect a released inmate, she fixes on another prisoner, Thérèse, who insists she was framed by her former lover. On release, Thérèse shoots him, then takes refuge in the convent as a novice. Anne-Marie's possessive zeal to convert her irritates the community and leads to her own humiliation and expulsion. She keeps vigil by the grave of the congregation's founder and falls gravely ill. Readmitted and dying, she is nursed by Thérèse, who is finally moved by her. As Anne-Marie dies, the police arrive, and Thérèse holds out her wrists.
inclusion: Made under the Occupation by a director just back from a German prison camp, this is a remarkable debut. The style is not yet the bare Bresson of later films. There are professional actresses, a score and Jean Giraudoux's polished dialogue. But the concentration is already there in the white habits, the closed spaces and the faces of Renée Faure and Jany Holt. Doug Cummings shows how carefully the film weighs Anne-Marie's humility against her pride, and the convent's rivalries against its charity. It is not a sentimental convent picture. The community is petty at times, and the heroine is often wrong. That honesty makes the final act of grace convincing.
themes: The film is about the purification of zeal. Anne-Marie genuinely wants to save a soul, but her charity becomes possessive and proud, and the community's discipline, including penance and obedience, exposes this. Her suffering and death become the means of Thérèse's conversion. The film insists that repentance includes accepting earthly justice: Thérèse's surrender to the police completes her change of heart rather than contradicting it. The religious community is shown with its faults, but its vocation and rule are taken seriously.
history: The Dominican Sisters of Bethany were founded in 1866 by the Dominican Jean-Joseph Lataste, who had preached in women's prisons and wanted a community in which former prisoners and women without a criminal past lived as equals. The Dominican priest Raymond-Léopold Bruckberger proposed a film about them and worked on the script with Bresson and Jean Giraudoux. Producer Roland Tual took over the project after Pathé dropped it. It was released in 1943.
liberties: Anne-Marie, Thérèse and the crime are fictional. The congregation is real, but the film condenses its life into a few dramatic months, sharpens its internal rivalries, and gives Giraudoux's literary dialogue to its sisters. It is not a documentary of Bethany houses.
advisories:
A deliberate killing (shown in preparation, act brief).

Humiliation, emotional cruelty, illness and death.

Mature teenagers and adults.

title: I Was a Parish Priest
decision: PUBLISH: the Italian Catholic Cinematografo record gives a full narrative and a 1955 Segnalazioni cinematografiche notice; together they establish a priest who sides with exploited miners and is then sent back to them by his bishop. The 2019 diocesan capsule is retained only for production context; its synopsis echoes the DVD blurb and is not independent criticism.
summary: Rafael Gil's prize-winning drama of a young priest who takes the miners' side in a bitter strike and pays for it with his superiors and his own body.
synopsis: In 1930, Father Andrés Mendoza, just out of the seminary, is sent to Aldemoz, a poor mining village full of resentment. The mine owner, Don César, tries to win him over, while the miners, led by the embittered Martín, distrust him. When a worker is unjustly dismissed, the men strike and occupy the mine. Andrés tries to mediate, fails, and then openly backs the strikers. Don César has to give way but complains to the bishop. Later, the owner's son and Martín's small daughter wander into an abandoned, unstable gallery and have to be rescued. Then a cave-in traps several men, among them Martín, Don César and the priest, until their comrades dig them out. Martín will not reconcile with Don César even underground, but does so at his injured daughter's bedside. The bishop summons Andrés and lets him return to his miners.
inclusion: This is one of the more interesting Spanish religious films of the 1950s because it takes sides. Rafael Gil and the writers Vicente Escrivá and Ramón D. Faraldo give the young priest a real fight, on the side of the workers, against the man who owns the mine. Claude Laydu, two years after Diary of a Country Priest, plays another young curé, dubbed into Spanish. Francisco Rabal won best-actor prizes as Martín. The 1955 Italian Catholic notice found the opening slow and somewhat naive but called the mine sequence intense and convincing and praised the photography. It won the top prize at the first San Sebastián festival and was also shown at Venice.
themes: The film puts the Church's social teaching into the mouth of a parish priest. Andrés defends a just wage and fair treatment, which he sees as part of caring for souls, and he refuses to be the owner's chaplain. The script also checks him. His siding with the strike costs him the trust of his superiors, and the decisive reconciliation comes through suffering and charity in the mine rather than through victory. The bishop's decision to send him back makes the point that the priest's place is with his poor parishioners, under obedience. The approach fits Rerum novarum and Quadragesimo anno rather than any revolutionary programme.
history: Released on 30 September 1953, the film was declared "of national interest" by the Franco regime's film authorities, which brought official support. The Colegio de Médicos reportedly objected to its portrayal of a doctor and sought to have it banned. It won the Gran Premio at the first San Sebastián International Film Festival in 1953. Music is by Joaquín Rodrigo.
liberties: Aldemoz and its strike are fictional. The film should not be taken as a portrait of Spanish labour relations in 1930. The concentration of rescue and reconciliation into a few days is dramatic shorthand.
advisories:
Mining accidents, trapped men and children in danger; a child is injured.

Class hostility and threats.

Best for older children with an adult, teenagers and adults.

title: Balarrasa
decision: PUBLISH: Independent treatment is now substantial: DeCine21's review, Rubén Higueras Flores's close textual analysis (ZER, 2017), Matt Losada's article (Romance Notes, 2011) and Fernán Gómez's own recollection (via Joan Ripollès, Centro Virtual Cervantes). Higueras finds undercurrents linking religion with coercion and renunciation, but concludes they do not overturn the plain reading: a sinner's conversion, a priestly vocation and the restoration of a family to the faith. That reading is sound, and the adult material serves it. Year 1951 (Cannes competition 1951; scholars date the production 1950).
summary: Nieves Conde's postwar melodrama about a reckless Legion officer whose comrade dies in his place, and who becomes a priest and sets out to save his own family.
synopsis: A Spanish missionary is lost in an Alaskan blizzard, and as he faces death he remembers his life. During the Civil War, Lieutenant Javier Mendoza, known as Balarrasa, is a hard-drinking Legion officer. He gambles away his guard duty to a comrade, Joaquín, who is shot on the watch that should have been Javier's. Shaken, he leaves the army for the seminary in Salamanca. Back home as a seminarian, he finds his family in moral ruin: his widowed father gambles, his brother Fernando trades in black-market currency, his sister Lina is the mistress of the crook their father owes money to, and his youngest sister Mayte drifts between suitors. Javier sets about putting them right. Lina dies in a car crash while fleeing with her lover, and the shock brings the family back to the faith. Javier is ordained and leaves for the missions.
inclusion: Balarrasa was one of the most successful Spanish religious films of its time. It was chosen for the Cannes competition in 1951, and it made Fernando Fernán Gómez a leading man; he and Nieves Conde won the Spanish film writers' medals for actor and director. Vicente Escrivá's script is a moral fable, but Nieves Conde gives it a hard edge. The family scenes have the shadows and night-time look of film noir, and the picture of a prosperous postwar family rotting from within anticipates his social drama Surcos. DeCine21 praises the realism, the humour that leavens the drama and Fernán Gómez's performance, and notes that priests advised the production. Fernán Gómez himself later found the family's sins mild stand-ins for the real problems of the time.
themes: This is a vocation story built on guilt and reparation. Javier reads his comrade's death as a debt: the life left to him is not his own, so he gives it to God. The film shows seminary study, Latin and Thomist philosophy, ordination with the kissing of the new priest's hands, and the missions. At home his work is the cure of souls: grace at table, a Gospel warning about empty hands, steady pressure on each sinner. Lina's death, with her empty hands raised and Javier, not yet a priest, unable to absolve her, is a stark lesson about dying unprepared. Higueras Flores argues that the film quietly ties religion to renunciation and coercion, but he concludes that this does not overturn its plain religious meaning.
history: Balarrasa is fiction. Its writer, Vicente Escrivá, co-founded the production company Aspa Films with the director Rafael Gil in 1950 and became a leading maker of Catholic films in 1950s Spain. The story of a Legion officer who exchanges his uniform for a cassock reflects the early Franco years, when the regime increasingly presented itself through the Church rather than the army; Matt Losada and Higueras Flores both read the film in that light.
advisories:
A soldier is shot dead; a fatal car crash; a young woman's deathbed.

An officers' drinking party in a brothel (not explicit); an illicit affair, gambling and black-market dealing.

Javier urges a shy suitor to punch a rival, a scene played for comedy.

DeCine21 recommends it for adults; Spanish television rates it for all audiences.

title: The Fugitive
decision: PUBLISH: AFI and TCM establish the film and its changes to Greene; Greydanus (A-, +3) and the 1948 Venice International Award (reported as the first OCIC prize) support a reverent treatment of a hunted priest who baptises, seeks to say Mass and dies rather than apostatise. The reservation about the altered protagonist dissolves: the changes remove the novel's sacrilegious and sexual sins rather than add doctrinal error, at the cost of Greene's complexity. Legion of Decency rating not found; verify.
summary: John Ford's stark, stylised version of Greene's The Power and the Glory: Henry Fonda's hunted priest, the last in a state where religion is outlawed, walks back towards martyrdom.
synopsis: In an unnamed Latin American state the government has outlawed religion and hunts its priests. One nameless priest remains. He returns to his abandoned village church, where María Dolores, an unmarried mother whose child was fathered by the police lieutenant, finds him, and he baptises the village children in secret. The lieutenant takes hostages to force him into the open. The priest flees towards the port, shadowed by an informer and crossing paths with an American wanted for murder. Unable to say Mass without wine, he is arrested, unrecognised, with a bottle of brandy. Safe over the border, he goes back when a beggar brings a note, supposedly from the dying American, asking for confession. Captured, he refuses to renounce his faith and is shot. At the end another priest comes to the church to pray with the faithful.
inclusion: This is the most openly religious film John Ford made, and Steven Greydanus notes that Ford himself thought it his best. Gabriel Figueroa's black-and-white photography, shot on location in Taxco, Cholula and Cuernavaca, is its great strength. Henry Fonda plays the priest as a frightened man whose courage comes late, with Pedro Armendáriz as the lieutenant and J. Carrol Naish as the informer. Greydanus grades it A- and says that, though it softens Greene, it still packs spiritual punch; the debate between priest and lieutenant remains a high point. Its faults are real: Dennis Schwartz found it turgid and its religious symbols simplistic, and Bret Wood suggests the images are so striking that they distract from the priest's plight. It shared the International Award at Venice in 1948. As a parable of the persecuted Church and of a people's need for priests, it is direct rather than subtle.
themes: The film's subject is the sacramental priesthood under persecution. The priest baptises children who have had no priest for years. The plot turns on the Mass: without altar wine he cannot celebrate, and his search for it leads to his arrest. An informer betrays him, and he goes back across the border because a dying man may need a priest. Offered his life for apostasy, he refuses. His flaw in the film is pride in his office and fear, not the novel's drunkenness and fathered child. That makes him more conventionally edifying: Greydanus calls the result a softened, conventionalised Greene, and Schwartz thinks it loses the novel's moral urgency. The closing image of another priest arriving to pray states plainly that the Church outlasts its persecutors.
history: Graham Greene travelled in Mexico in 1938, when anti-clerical laws had closed churches and driven priests into hiding, and drew on that for his novel. Ford read it in 1940 but could not sell the project because of censorship problems. He and Merian C. Cooper made it for their company, Argosy Pictures, with RKO distributing. It was shot in Mexico with a largely Mexican crew and Emilio Fernández as associate producer, and released on 3 November 1947.
liberties: Greene's 'whisky priest' is an alcoholic who has fathered a child with María; the film makes the lieutenant the father and gives the priest only pride and fear. Greene's lieutenant is an idealist who wants to help the poor; Ford's is a harder tyrant. The setting is left unnamed rather than Mexico, and a spoken prologue presents the story as true.
advisories:
Hostages are taken and threatened; a gunfight in a cornfield; the priest is executed (not shown graphically).

An unmarried mother and the officer who fathered her child; she dances in a cantina to distract the police.

Drinking and a jail sequence.

Steady tension and menace; best for teenagers and adults.

title: Léon Morin, Priest
decision: GREY: Several independent reviews (Video Librarian, avcesar, the Criteria podcast at CatholicCulture.org) agree that Morin keeps his vows and turns Barny away, so the feared scandal does not occur. What remains is the film's sustained erotic focus, the mixed motives behind Barny's conversion, and a priest whose private meetings with a widow invite the question of prudence. No Legion of Decency or Centrale Catholique rating was found; one would settle the question for this site's purposes.
summary: Melville's quiet Occupation drama sets a Communist widow against a young priest who argues her back to the faith, and refuses what she then wants from him.
synopsis: A small Alpine town under the Occupation. Barny (Emmanuelle Riva), a widow whose Jewish husband has been killed, is a Communist and a lapsed Catholic bringing up her daughter alone and correcting work for a correspondence school. To mock the Church she goes to confession and baits the young priest, Léon Morin (Jean-Paul Belmondo), with the old line that religion is the opium of the people. He answers her, and she keeps coming back. Over months of private conversations she returns to the faith. Her feelings for him turn romantic, and other women of the town are drawn to him too; none succeeds in seducing him. When the Germans leave, the school returns to Paris and Morin is transferred to another parish. On his last night he sees her once more, tells her they will meet in another life, and she leaves in tears.
inclusion: Jean-Pierre Melville works here in a chamber register: most of the film is two people talking in small rooms, and it holds because the arguments are real. Belmondo plays a quick, blunt priest who questions authority and is not afraid of gossip; Dennis Schwartz found his case for God forceful and intelligent. Riva is the real centre, and even Eye for Film, otherwise cool on the film, praises her nuanced performance. Sean Axmaker in Video Librarian called it a solid chamber drama, respectful of the Church, with a priest who is chaste and devoted; the hosts of the Catholic film podcast Criteria call it one of the best priest films ever made and read it as a study in pastoral prudence. Not every critic agrees: Eye for Film found the theological exchanges grating and the story close to soap opera. It is talky and deliberately low-key.
themes: The core is a conversion worked out through argument: Morin meets Barny's Marxist jibes head-on, and her views shift as they talk. He is also a pastor in wartime, and Dennis Schwartz notes the film's insistence that Christians cannot look away from the persecution of the Jews. The difficulty is that Barny's desire for Morin grows with her faith, and the film never quite separates the two. Morin keeps his vows and sends her away, but he also lets the meetings run on in private for months. Whether that is patience or imprudence is left to the viewer.
history: Béatrix Beck's novel Léon Morin, prêtre won the Prix Goncourt in 1952 and was published in English as The Passionate Heart. Melville cut a first assembly of about three hours down to the 117-minute release; a longer director's cut of about 128 minutes was restored in 2019. The film drew 1.7 million admissions in France.
advisories:
Sustained romantic and sexual tension between a widow and a priest; no sex scene. The heroine is also shown as attracted to a female colleague.

Occupation setting, with the deportation of Jews in the background; reviews do not report graphic violence.

Adult in theme and slow in pace; for older teenagers and adults.

The heroine's conversion is entangled with her desire for the priest, and the film leaves the purity of her motives open.

grey.question: Morin keeps his vows and sends Barny away; on that every account agrees. The reservation is about what the film dwells on. Barny's return to the faith grows alongside her desire for the priest, the film keeps the erotic tension in the foreground for two hours, and Morin lets the private meetings go on long after he must see where they are heading. title: Going My Way
decision: PUBLISH: The AFI Catalog gives a full synopsis and production record; John Clark (NCRegister), Anthony Esolen and Joe Wilson give detailed Catholic readings of its portrait of parish priesthood. The Criteria critique and David E. White's scholarly chapter (the film nearly omits the supernatural and sacramental) are real limits and are stated in the record, but they describe an emphasis, not a teaching that contradicts the faith.
summary: Bing Crosby's easygoing young curate quietly takes over a debt-ridden New York parish from its stubborn old pastor, played to perfection by Barry Fitzgerald.
synopsis: St Dominic's, a poor New York parish, is about to lose its church to the mortgage holder. The bishop sends Father Chuck O'Malley, a former songwriter who wears a sweatshirt and plays golf, ostensibly as curate to the elderly Father Fitzgibbon, in fact to take charge without humiliating him. O'Malley turns a gang of street boys into a choir, helps a runaway girl, marries her to the landlord's son, and sells a song to pay the debt. Fitzgibbon learns the truth and runs away into the rain, then comes round. When the church burns, the parish starts again, and O'Malley moves on to the next troubled parish.
inclusion: McCarey made a comedy about two priests, and the comedy is real. Barry Fitzgerald's Fitzgibbon, crotchety, vain, devoted and finally touching, is one of the great character performances of the period, and his scenes with Crosby have an easy rhythm that holds the film together. Crosby underplays O'Malley's tact: he takes over without ever saying so. The film is long and loosely plotted, the opera interlude with Risë Stevens stops it dead, and the delinquents reform suspiciously fast. But its picture of a parish as a place where a priest knows the landlady, the policeman and the boys stealing turkeys has warmth and observation. The final scene, with Fitzgibbon's mother, is famous for good reason.
themes: The film's subject is the parish priest as a father to his people: patience with an older priest, care for the poor and the young, refusal to humiliate anyone. Esolen calls its governing virtue tact, a form of charity. John Clark draws out its respect for ordinary priestly service and a line affirming the indissolubility of a valid marriage. What it hardly shows is the supernatural centre of the priesthood. The scholar David E. White notes that it leaves out nearly all supernatural, sacramental and theological reference, and Thomas Mirus and James Majewski argue that O'Malley is admired for singing and charm rather than anything spiritual. That criticism is fair. Watch it as a portrait of priestly kindness, not of the priest at the altar.
liberties: Fiction; no historical persons. The parish is idealised and the plot runs on coincidence and a hit song.
advisories:
No violence beyond a church fire. A runaway girl lives in an apartment paid for by a young man before they marry; nothing is shown.

Suitable for all ages, though younger children may find it slow.

The priesthood is presented almost entirely through pastoral kindness; sacramental life is largely absent.

title: The Bells of St. Mary's
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog record plus Stephen B. Earley's 1945 America review, which judged it 'tremendously spiritual' and among the best screen portraits of a sister's life, and Joe Wilson's detailed reading. The 'personable priest' critique (Criteria; White) applies more weakly here than to Going My Way because the sisters' vocation and prayer are central; it is noted in the record.
summary: Father O'Malley meets his match in Ingrid Bergman's Sister Benedict as a parish school fights to survive, in McCarey's warmer, more prayerful sequel to Going My Way.
synopsis: Father O'Malley becomes pastor of St Mary's, whose sisters run a crumbling parish school. The superior, Sister Mary Benedict, disagrees with him about almost everything, from school holidays to whether a struggling girl should pass her exams. She prays that the businessman Horace Bogardus will give the school the new building he is putting up next door; Bogardus wants the school site for a car park. O'Malley helps a deserted mother and her daughter Patsy, and nudges Bogardus towards charity. Bogardus gives the building. Then Sister Benedict is found to have early tuberculosis, and the doctor wants her transferred without being told why. She believes O'Malley has had her removed.
inclusion: This is the better of McCarey's two priest pictures, and the reason is Ingrid Bergman. Her Sister Benedict is strict, competitive, funny and devout, and she plays the part without condescension: Earley, writing in America in 1945, said sisters at an advance screening recognised themselves in her. The rivalry with Crosby's O'Malley is gentle comedy between two people who respect each other. Some scenes are pure McCarey: the infants' Nativity play, the nun teaching a bullied boy to box. It is sentimental and long, and the Bogardus subplot is contrived. But the last scene, in which Sister Benedict goes to the chapel to pray for guidance before leaving, and O'Malley finally tells her the truth, is beautifully done.
themes: The film takes religious life seriously. Sister Benedict's vocation is the teaching of children, and she holds to standards because she believes they serve the child. She prays for the school and the prayer is answered, though through a cranky businessman rather than a wonder. Her final trial is obedience: she accepts a transfer she does not understand and takes it to prayer before she knows the reason. O'Malley is still more pastoral counsellor than sacramental minister, and critics such as Thomas Mirus find the faith shallow; but here the sisters' prayer and obedience give it more spiritual weight than Going My Way.
liberties: Fiction. McCarey based Sister Benedict on his aunt, a sister of the Immaculate Heart community in Hollywood; Bergman's habit is a composite of two orders.
advisories:
A deserted mother says she has relied on 'the generosity of men', and her daughter mistakes her father for one of her mother's clients; this is handled discreetly.

A nun is diagnosed with tuberculosis. A schoolyard fight and a boxing lesson.

Suitable for all ages.

title: Come to the Stable
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review, TCM and the AFI Catalog establish a gentle comedy in which two French nuns' trust in providence and works of mercy drive the plot, with a sympathetic bishop. The sentimentality noted by Greydanus is disclosed.
summary: Two French nuns arrive in a Connecticut village determined to build a children's hospital with no money, in a gentle Fox comedy loosely based on the founding of Regina Laudis.
synopsis: Sister Margaret and Sister Scholastica arrive in Bethlehem, New England, on a snowy night, with a promise to keep: a children's hospital. They take shelter with Amelia Potts, an eccentric painter of religious pictures. They set their hearts on a hilltop owned by a gambler, Luigi Rossi, and on land next to a songwriter, Robert Mason, who wants peace and quiet. With prayer, persistence and some cheerful bending of the rules, they work on the bishop, the gambler and their reluctant neighbour. Not every scheme works, and the bishop worries about their judgment, but the hospital begins to take shape.
inclusion: Henry Koster's film is a well-made studio comedy with real affection for religious life. Loretta Young and Celeste Holm play the nuns with conviction rather than winks, and Elsa Lanchester is a delight as their painter friend. All three were Oscar-nominated, and the film received seven nominations in total. Steven Greydanus calls it sweet and uplifting, and also more conventional and sentimental than Lilies of the Field. The sisters sometimes get their miracle and sometimes look credulous and silly. That is about right. It is a warm Christmas-season film for the whole family rather than a serious study of a vocation.
themes: The sisters' faith is simple and direct. They pray for what they need and expect an answer, and the film plays this both as comedy and as sincere trust in providence. Their hospital is a concrete work of mercy. The bishop is portrayed sympathetically: he supports their mission but doubts their practical sense. Greydanus suggests the film leaves open whether God is testing their faith or teaching them prudence, and perhaps both. The Bethlehem setting and the Nativity imagery tie the story to Christmas.
history: Clare Boothe Luce, a recent convert, wrote the original story. It was based on the arrival in 1946–47 of two Benedictine nuns from the Abbey of Jouarre in France, Mother Benedict Duss and Mother Mary Aline Trilles de Warren, in Bethlehem, Connecticut. The painter Lauren Ford gave them hospitality, and a Protestant industrialist, Robert Leather, gave land. They founded the Priory of Regina Laudis in a disused factory; it later became an abbey. Fox negotiated with the nuns and church authorities before making the film.
liberties: The real foundation was a contemplative Benedictine monastery. The film turns it into an active order building a children's hospital, invents the gambler, the songwriter and other neighbours, and adds the comic set pieces. TCM notes the plot was changed partly to avoid needing the real nuns' rights.
advisories:
Nothing objectionable; suitable for children.

title: Of Gods and Men
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church, presented as normal or exemplary: the Tibhirine community's interreligious witness, culminating in a testament that speaks of Islam in the language of post-conciliar dialogue.
summary: Beauvois's patient drama about the Trappists of Tibhirine, who chose to stay with their Algerian village through the civil war of the 1990s, knowing it could kill them.
synopsis: In the Atlas mountains of Algeria, a small community of French Cistercian monks keeps the Hours, farms, sells honey and runs a free clinic for the Muslim village below. When an armed Islamist group murders Croatian workers nearby, the army offers protection and the government urges the monks to leave. The abbot, Dom Christian, refuses the soldiers without first consulting his brothers, and the community is split. On Christmas Eve armed men come to the monastery demanding medicine; Christian faces down their leader. Over the following months each monk has to decide whether to go home to France or remain. They vote, pray, quarrel and eat a last meal together. One night in 1996 men take most of them away into the snow.
inclusion: Few films show the ordinary texture of monastic life this exactly: the chanted Office, manual work, chapter meetings, a hard-pressed infirmarian. Lambert Wilson's Christian is clever and sometimes high-handed; Michael Lonsdale's Brother Luc, the old doctor, is gruff, funny and unshakeable. The drama is a vocational one. Men who have already given their lives to God must decide whether that gift includes staying put when staying may mean death, and the film lets their fear, doubt and slow agreement play out without speeches. Caroline Champetier's photography and the long passages of plainchant give it a slow, steady rhythm. The wordless last supper, built on faces and a piece of recorded music, is one of the great ensemble scenes of recent cinema. Steven Greydanus calls its picture of lived Christian faith more appealing than any dramatic feature of the previous quarter-century.
themes: Steven Greydanus counts fewer than 2,000 words of substantive dialogue from the monks, and much of it is Scripture, psalmody and liturgy: the Good Shepherd who does not abandon his flock, the Incarnation preached at Christmas, a Communion scene, Compline, the Paschal mystery behind their choice. The monks do not try to convert their neighbours, and the film presents their relationship with Islam as friendship and service. It does not claim that Islam saves or that all religions are equal. The closing testament is the point of real tension: Christian hopes to see 'his children of Islam' as God sees them, calls Algeria and Islam 'a body and a soul', and ends 'Insh'allah'. Read with the pre-conciliar teaching against indifferentism (Mortalium animos), these lines are ambiguous rather than heretical, and a viewer may legitimately dissent from them.
history: The monks of Notre-Dame de l'Atlas at Tibhirine were kidnapped in the night of 26–27 March 1996; seven were killed and two, who were not found, survived. The Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed the killings; later testimony that the Algerian army was involved remains disputed. The seven were beatified at Oran on 8 December 2018 with twelve other religious killed in Algeria between 1993 and 1996.
liberties: The film draws closely on the monks' writings and was made with advisers who knew the community, but conversations, the Christmas Eve confrontation and the last supper are dramatised. Christian's testament is shortened: Greydanus notes that the film drops the phrase about Muslims 'shining with the glory of Christ' and other passages, and judges the cuts were made for length. The deaths themselves are not shown.
advisories:
Brief graphic violence, including the murder of foreign workers, and a few disturbing images.

One obscene expression. Rated R in the United States; 15 certificate in the UK. Best for older teenagers and adults.

French and Arabic dialogue with subtitles.

The abbot's testament speaks of Islam in terms traditional Catholics may find too irenic; the film does not endorse religious indifferentism, but it does not argue against it either.

title: The Little World of Don Camillo
alternateTitles: Le Petit Monde de don Camillo
Il piccolo mondo di don Camillo
decision: PUBLISH: Jacques Lourcelles (Cinema Ritrovato programme note), contemporary reviews (Valobra in Rassegna del Film, Crowther in The New York Times, Offord in the Socialist Standard) and Cathopedia's scene list together document a comedy built on a priest's rivalry with a Communist mayor, the crucified Christ's rebukes, the sacraments and reconciliation. Edition differences (French version longer, including the attempted suicide) are disclosed.
summary: Fernandel's hot-tempered parish priest and Gino Cervi's Communist mayor feud, brawl and make peace in a Po Valley village, while Christ on the altar crucifix keeps the priest in line.
synopsis: In a small town on the Po plain after the war, the Communists win the local elections and Peppone becomes mayor. His rival is the parish priest, Don Camillo, a big man with big fists, who takes his grievances to the crucifix above the altar, and Christ answers him, usually with a rebuke. The two men clash over a new Casa del Popolo, a strike, a football match, a procession and the baptism of Peppone's son, whom the mayor wants to name after Lenin. Between quarrels they cooperate when the village needs them. Two young lovers from feuding families try to drown themselves, which forces both men to help. After a final brawl the bishop transfers Don Camillo to a mountain parish. Peppone forbids the town to see him off, but waits for him at the next station.
inclusion: Julien Duvivier and René Barjavel turned Giovannino Guareschi's newspaper stories into one of the most popular European films of the 1950s. Fernandel's elastic face and Gino Cervi's slow-burning mayor make an ideal comic pair. Jacques Lourcelles called Fernandel's mix of serenity and mischief superb, and Bosley Crowther praised its vigorous and amiable conflict. The film is episodic. Fabrizio Valobra, reviewing in 1952, found it fragmentary and sketch-like, with only the procession and the closing walk to the station showing Duvivier's real style. That is fair, but the episodes are well built, and the conversations with the crucifix give the comedy a moral centre.
themes: The crucifix is the film's conscience. Christ, voiced by Ruggero Ruggeri in the Italian version and Jean Debucourt in the French, regularly checks the priest's temper and vanity; in one scene he tells him to throw away the stick he means to use. Don Camillo submits, grumbling. The sacraments are taken seriously beneath the jokes. He insists on a proper Christian name at the baptism, but he baptises the child. He also blesses the Communists' new building. The film's argument is that a priest may oppose Communism with all his strength and still owe its members love and pastoral care. Its anti-Communism is comic, not hateful.
history: Guareschi, editor of the satirical weekly Candido, began the stories in 1946 and collected them as Mondo piccolo: Don Camillo (1948). They grew out of the bitter 1948 election campaign between the Christian Democrats and the Communist–Socialist Popular Front. Guareschi presented the Christ of the stories as the voice of his own conscience. The film was shot in Brescello, Emilia, and released in Italy in March 1952 and in France in June 1952.
liberties: The screenplay selects and links separate Guareschi stories into a loose chronicle. The Italian and French versions differ. The French cut is longer, extending the attempted suicide, the brawl, the football match and Signora Cristina's funeral, and adding a short exchange with a statue of Our Lady. The US version adds an English narration by Orson Welles.
advisories:
Fist fights and comic brawling, including by the priest.

Two young lovers attempt suicide by drowning (longer in the French version).

Political insults and threats played for comedy.

Suitable for families with older children.

title: The Return of Don Camillo
decision: PUBLISH: Roberto Chiesi's Cinema Ritrovato programme note and the Cinematografo record document the exiled priest's grief at the silence of the crucifix, his return and the Po flood as the film's core, and identify the French version as the fuller one (Italian censors cut scenes, including the crucifix carried through the snow). Contemporary and later criticism (Zannino 1953; Bertarelli 2001) is recorded; comic pranks and a joke 'sale' of a soul are disclosed.
summary: Duvivier's sadder sequel sends Don Camillo into mountain exile, brings him home to his feud with Peppone, and ends with the Po in flood.
synopsis: Exiled to Montenara, a poor village in the mountains, Don Camillo finds a half-ruined church, an empty rectory and parishioners who ignore him. He misses his town, his people and the crucifix that used to talk to him. Back home, Peppone needs him: a stubborn landowner refuses to allow flood defences on his land, and only the priest can move him. The mayor asks the bishop to bring Don Camillo back. The feud resumes at once with a boxing match, a race between the town-hall clock and the church bells, a forged party letter and a castor-oil toast. Don Camillo also visits Peppone's unhappy son at boarding school. Then the Po bursts its banks. The villagers are evacuated to the main embankment while Don Camillo stays alone in his church.
inclusion: Roberto Chiesi calls this the more melancholy and bitter of the first two films, and its exile scenes the best in either. Duvivier lets the fog, the cold rectory and the silent crucifix register without milking them. Fernandel is again excellent, and Gino Cervi's Peppone is more vulnerable. The comic middle section is looser. Contemporary critic F. Zannino found the conflicts superficial and resolved as soon as they appear, while Massimo Bertarelli later praised its warmth and called it tender and very funny. Both are right. Use the French version where possible. Italian censors cut several scenes, including the most beautiful religious sequence.
themes: The heart of the film is a priest's loneliness without his Lord. In exile the crucifix of the mountain church is silent. In the French version Don Camillo carries his old crucifix up to the rectory, stumbles under its weight in falling snow, and rejoices when it speaks to him again. The flood shows the priest as shepherd: he stays in his church when everyone else leaves. Duvivier wanted the priest to drown and wake in a paradise like his own town. Guareschi and the producer refused, so the film keeps only a dream of heaven, from which he wakes to Peppone's face. The comic subplot in which an old man buys a young militant's "soul" is a joke, not a theology.
history: The film continues Guareschi's Don Camillo stories. The Po flooded the Polesine in November 1951, and Guareschi later wrote it into his village's world. The production used newsreel and location images of the flood at Brescello. A mostly French co-production, the film premiered in Paris on 5 June 1953 and was released in Italy that September. The mountain scenes were filmed at Rocca di Cambio.
liberties: Guareschi objected strongly to Duvivier's changes, and the ending is a compromise between them. The French and Italian versions differ substantially: besides the crucifix scene, the Italian cut softens a harsh episode with a draft-dodger that shows Don Camillo's petty side and trims a scene with Peppone's son. Running times range from about 100 minutes (Italian) to 115 (French).
advisories:

A flood with danger to life; a dream of death.

A comic subplot about selling one's soul.

Suitable for families with older children.

title: The Miracle of the Bells
decision: GREY: The ending is now established in outline: the statues turn because the crowd's weight shifts their pillars over a weak, mine-undermined foundation; Father Paul knows this; the press agent begs him not to tell the people. Sources then divide. The AFI Catalog says Bill persuades him to say divine intervention played some part; a detailed fan account says he refuses to lie and preaches instead on the miracle of Olga's goodness. Either way the film's message is that the people's faith matters more than whether the miracle is real, which sits badly with Trent's rule that no new miracle be acknowledged without the bishop. The parish's Catholic life (Latin Mass, Angelus, St Michael) is genuine. Not HOLD: the plot is known and the question can be stated. The exact wording of Father Paul's announcement would settle it: a claimed miracle points to REJECT, a sermon on Providence to PUBLISH.
summary: A press agent brings a dead actress home to a mining town, pays every church to ring its bells, and sets off a 'miracle' the priest knows is not one.
synopsis: Bill Dunnigan, a press agent, escorts the body of Olga Treskovna to Coaltown, the mining town where she grew up poor. Olga, a struggling actress, had been cast as Joan of Arc and finished the film knowing she was dying of tuberculosis caught from the coal dust of her childhood. The producer now refuses to release it. Bill asks Father Paul of the poor Polish parish of St Michael's to bury her, then pays every church in town, with cheques he cannot cover, to ring its bells for three days. Crowds and reporters arrive. At the funeral the statues of St Michael and Our Lady turn on their pillars to face her coffin. Father Paul finds the natural cause; Bill begs him not to take the miracle from the people. The story spreads, and the studio releases the film.
inclusion: There is real Catholic texture here. James Day, in the National Catholic Register, notes that Father Paul says Mass in Latin, explains the Angelus to Bill, and keeps his parish devoted to St Michael, and he calls the film a near masterpiece. Frank Sinatra, cast only after the producer had sought the Church's approval, plays the priest, and Day praises his sincerity; Fred MacMurray plays the press agent and Alida Valli plays Olga. Michael De Sapio grants that the film is often dismissed as saccharine but argues it is a sombre post-war document with noir touches. Most critics disagreed. Time and James Agee mocked its piety, the Golden Turkey Awards later ridiculed Sinatra, and it lost about $640,000.
themes: The devotion to St Michael, the Latin Mass and the life of a poor parish are specific and sincere. The problem is the climax. Father Paul, to his credit, finds the natural cause at once; Russell Janney's novel stresses the Church's caution about the miraculous. But the film, at Bill's urging, lets the parish go on believing, and, as Moria Reviews objected, its closing message seems to be that renewed faith matters more than whether the event was supernatural. Pre-conciliar discipline (Trent, Session XXV) forbids acknowledging new miracles without the bishop's judgement and orders superstition removed. Whether Father Paul affirms divine intervention or only preaches on Olga's goodness decides how serious this is. His remark that St Michael freed St Peter from prison goes beyond Acts 12, which says 'an angel of the Lord'.
history: Jesse L. Lasky produced the film for RKO from Russell Janney's 1946 bestseller, with a script by Ben Hecht and Quentin Reynolds. It opened in New York on 16 March 1948 and nationally on 27 March. It was poorly reviewed and lost about $640,000.
liberties: Fiction. The film condenses Janney's long novel, drops many subplots, and makes Olga's film a life of Joan of Arc rather than an unnamed religious picture. A Pennsylvania man sued RKO, claiming he was caricatured as the undertaker Nick Orloff.
advisories:
An actress dies of tuberculosis; long deathbed and funeral scenes.

No sexual content of note.

Suitable for older children and up.

The ending turns on a priest letting his parish believe that a natural event was a miracle.

grey.question: During the funeral two statues turn to face the coffin. The priest quickly finds the cause: the crowd's weight has shifted their pillars. The press agent begs him not to tell the people, and the film sides with the agent, ending on the message that faith matters more than whether the miracle was real. Accounts differ on what Father Paul then says. In one he credits divine intervention with a part; in the other he preaches only on the dead girl's goodness. The first would be a priest knowingly endorsing a false miracle; the second, a pious evasion. The wording of that sermon settles it.

title: The Keys of the Kingdom
decision: GREY: The Legion of Decency passed the film for general audiences with a doctrinal reservation (AFI Catalog), and the film's dialogue shows what it most likely meant: Chisholm's question whether God values creed, his reported remarks that not all atheists are godless and that Confucians have more humour than Christians, and an atheist's death without reconciliation. These lean towards indifferentism but are not endorsed outright, and the rector answers the creed question orthodoxly, so it is a weighable reservation rather than a REJECT. The Legion's own review text, naming the statements, would settle it.
summary: Gregory Peck plays a Scottish priest whose fifty years, most of them as a missionary in China, are read from his diary in Fox's handsome adaptation of Cronin's bestseller.
synopsis: In 1938 a monsignor arrives at a Scottish parish to retire its elderly priest, Francis Chisholm, whose unorthodox preaching has drawn complaints, and reads his journal overnight. Francis's parents died after an anti-Catholic mob attacked his father; the girl he loved bore a child out of wedlock and died; at seminary he was rebuked for questioning what he was taught. Sent to China, he finds his mission church destroyed by flood, turns away converts who come only for rice, cures a mandarin's son but refuses the father's offer to convert out of gratitude, and rebuilds with the land the mandarin gives. An aristocratic nun, Mother Maria Veronica, despises him until his humility wins her over. Civil war reaches the mission, and his unbelieving friend Dr Willie Tulloch is killed. Methodist missionaries arrive and are welcomed. Chisholm goes home, and the monsignor lets him stay.
inclusion: Peck carries the film across half a century of one man's life, and the role brought him an Oscar nomination for best actor; Bosley Crowther praised his quiet force. The film drew four nominations in all, among them Arthur C. Miller's black-and-white photography and the art direction of its Chinese village. The portrait of a poor, stubborn missionary who will not buy converts with rice or favours is attractive, and Steven Greydanus calls the film an edifying celebration of Christian virtue in an imperfect hero. It is also long and vague in its piety. James Agee came to find its sincerity and ethics bland, Crowther thought it a surface shadow of Cronin's novel, and the Church that sent Chisholm barely appears. It is worth seeing for Peck and for its picture of missionary patience, with the doctrinal question below kept in mind.
themes: The film admires Chisholm's charity, humility and refusal to coerce belief, and Mother Maria Veronica's change of heart carries the middle of the film. The Church itself is thin. Chisholm is never shown saying Mass or administering a sacrament; the nearest is a joke about confession. Cronin's novel was openly sceptical of the Church's unique claim, and the film tones this down without removing it. Chisholm asks whether God sets an exclusive value on creed, an accident of birth; his reported sermons say not all atheists are godless and that the Confucian has the better sense of humour. He tells the mandarin that the Methodist newcomers serve the same true God, and at Willie's deathbed he prays the De profundis but does not press him to believe. Taken together, these lean towards the indifferentism Pius XI condemned in Mortalium animos.
history: A. J. Cronin, himself a Catholic, wrote the novel, and by 1941 the Production Code office was warning prospective buyers about its unflattering priests and an episode in which a priest endorses a false claim of stigmata. Catholic reviewers attacked the book, and religious figures opposed a film. Fox's version opened in New York on 29 December 1944 and went into general release in January 1945. Chisholm is fictional.
liberties: Fiction, from Cronin's novel. The script was shaped with Breen's office and two Jesuit advisers, Albert O'Hara and Wilfrid Parsons, to meet the Code's objections to the novel's worldly priests and false-stigmata episode. The novel's line comparing Christ and Confucius became a remark about Christians and Confucians. The Chinese village was made orderly and clean after the Chinese consul objected.
advisories:

An anti-Catholic mob attacks the boy's father, and both parents drown.

An illegitimate birth and the young mother's death are referred to.

Long (about 137 minutes) and slow in places; suitable for older children and up.

The Legion of Decency noted statements by the priest open to a meaning contrary to Catholic doctrine.

grey.question: The Legion of Decency passed this film for all audiences but flagged statements by the priest open to a meaning "not in accordance with Catholic doctrine". The dialogue shows the likely candidates. As a student Chisholm asks whether God values creed, which he calls an accident of birth. His sermons are quoted as saying not all atheists are godless and that Confucians have more humour than Christians. He lets his unbelieving friend die unpersuaded. None of this is endorsed outright, and his rector rebukes the creed question, but the drift is towards indifferentism. The Legion's own review text, naming the passages, would settle it.

title: God Needs Men
decision: GREY: Séquences (1958) and the Fiches du Cinéma synopsis on Unifrance establish that the lay sacristan hears confessions, gives absolution to a dying man and prepares to say Mass before a priest arrives, and that the lawful curé is drawn as harsh and backed by gendarmes. The film stops short of a simulated Mass, ends with Thomas submitting and the islanders going to Mass to ask pardon, and won the OCIC prize at Venice in 1950, so it is not a REJECT; but the sympathy it gives to lay usurpation of sacraments against legitimate authority is a real question. A Centrale Catholique cote or a scene-level account of the absolution and the ending would settle it.
summary: On a priestless Breton island, a fisherman-sacristan is pushed by his parish into the priest's role, and the film watches him go too far.
synopsis: Île de Sein, off Brittany, in the mid-19th century. The islanders fish and loot wrecks, and their discouraged rector leaves. They will not do without the sacraments, so they turn to the sacristan, Thomas Gourvennec (Pierre Fresnay), a fisherman who can barely write. He agrees to lead prayers and preach on Sundays, insisting that he is not a priest. The pressure grows. He hears confessions, among them that of the young Joseph Le Berre (Daniel Gélin), who admits to a crime, and he gets ready to say Mass with hosts he has made. A priest from the mainland arrives under gendarme escort before he can. Joseph kills himself, and the islanders turn against the curé over the suicide's funeral. Thomas, who has already absolved the dying man, leads the islanders out in their boats to give the body to the sea, then leads them to Mass to ask forgiveness.
inclusion: Few films put the question so bluntly: what is a priest for, and what happens to people who lose one? Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost adapted Henri Queffélec's novel, and Delannoy stages it with care. Robert Lefebvre's photography gives strong high-angle views of the island and of Thomas hemmed in by his parishioners, and the choral music is used heavily. Fresnay dominates as a decent, unlettered man frightened by what is being asked of him. The International Catholic Film Office (OCIC) gave it its prize at Venice in 1950, and the Canadian Catholic film review Séquences called it frankly religious. It also has real faults. Séquences found the acting theatrical, Fresnay's gestures included, and the island's poverty too polished and picturesque; Fr Beirnaert of the Jesuit review Études, quoted there, missed the novel's sea and wind. It is worth seeing for its subject and for Fresnay's committed central performance.
themes: The islanders' faith is crude but real: they want sacraments, not ideas, and they fear damnation. Thomas knows he is not a priest and says so, yet he hears confessions, absolves a dying man and handles hosts he has baked, and the film treats him with great sympathy. The curé who comes with gendarmes is shown as cold and authoritarian; he scornfully throws away the hosts Thomas made, although Séquences notes that he does try to make concessions. Séquences noted that the film sets a 'democratic' lay leader against an odious cleric, which is why Protestants and anticlericals liked it as much as Catholics did. Against that, Thomas finally submits to the curé, and the story still rests on the need for an ordained priest.
history: Queffélec based his novel, Un recteur de l'île de Sein, loosely on events on Sein in 1641. When two Jesuit missionaries landed, they found that a fisherman, François Le Su, had acted as catechist and preacher since the rector's death. They sent him to study on the mainland; he was ordained and returned as the island's priest. Queffélec's sacristan oversteps his lay powers, but the novel still ends with him entering the seminary.
liberties: The film moves the story from the 17th century to the mid-19th century and drops the ending of both the history and the novel, in which the sacristan becomes a priest. It enlarges the two confession scenes and creates an open conflict between Thomas and an authoritarian curé, which is not in the novel. Bretons objected that the real Church had welcomed the fisherman rather than opposing him.
advisories:
A suicide, and the crime confessed by Joseph, are central to the plot.

The islanders loot shipwrecks; there are scenes of anger and confrontation with gendarmes.

No sexual content of note. Suitable for older children with an adult; the story's questions are for adults.

A layman hears confessions, pronounces absolution and prepares to say Mass, and the film is more sympathetic to him than to the lawful priest; no layman can validly absolve or consecrate.

grey.question: A fisherman acting as sacristan hears confessions, absolves a dying man and prepares to say Mass with hosts he has made, and the film is plainly on his side. The lawful priest who stops him arrives with gendarmes and is drawn as cold and authoritarian. The International Catholic Film Office gave it a prize, and Thomas does submit at the end, but in 1958 the Catholic review Séquences already called the ending equivocal. Whether the film defends the priesthood or quietly undermines it is the question; a Centrale Catholique rating or a close account of the final scenes would settle it.

title: The Unfrocked One
decision: GREY: The film's thesis is plainly orthodox: holy orders leave an indelible mark, so the apostate's mock consecration is valid and therefore sacrilegious, the young priest consumes the wine to stop its profanation, and the ending gives the dying priest's absolution and the apostate's contrition. The sacrilege is shown as horror, not approved, so REJECT does not apply. It is grey because a valid-in-the-fiction consecration is staged in a cabaret for shock, and because no contemporary Catholic review (Centrale Catholique cote, Radio-Cinéma, La Croix) has been found; present treatment evidence is a ciné-club note, a traditionalist recommendation, a hostile blog and viewer reviews. Finding the 1954 Centrale Catholique cote would settle it.
summary: Pierre Fresnay plays an apostate priest who mocks the Church, and Pierre Trabaud the young convert who becomes a priest to win him back, in Joannon's blunt, provocative drama.
synopsis: In a German officers' camp in 1945, Maurice Morand reveals that he is a priest when he gives the last rites to the dying chaplain. Morand has left the Church and despises it, but the young Gérard Lacassagne is moved and decides to become a priest himself, against his family and his fiancée. After the war Morand, back at the Sorbonne, publishes an attack on religion, while Gérard, in the seminary, keeps trying to bring him back. In a cabaret Morand mockingly says the words of consecration over white wine; since he is still a priest, Gérard takes it for the Blood of Christ and drinks it rather than leave it to be profaned. After his ordination Gérard visits Morand once more. They quarrel and Morand strikes him, reopening an old wound. Dying, Gérard absolves him, and Morand is left in tears and prayer.
inclusion: Fresnay, who had played St Vincent de Paul in Monsieur Vincent and a lay 'rector' in Dieu a besoin des hommes, gives the film its force; even the hostile blogger Narkissos admires his conviction, though some viewers find him overemphatic. The opening, with a sick chaplain collapsing at Mass and Morand forced to reveal himself, is the passage even detractors praise. The ciné-club de Montereau calls the film incisive and violent, the dialogue often brilliant, and praises Trabaud and Nicole Stéphane; it won a Bronze Bear at Berlin in 1954. It is a thesis film in the old French Catholic manner, built on the sacramental character of the priesthood, and it argues its case with melodrama: its detractors find the later scenes close to grand guignol, and Narkissos, comparing it with Bresson and Melville, dismisses it. A traditionalist reviewer, by contrast, praises its classical theology and calls the craft exceptional.
themes: Everything rests on the doctrine that ordination imprints an indelible character. Because Morand is still a priest, his cabaret consecration is real, and his blasphemy is a sacrilege rather than a joke; Gérard treats the wine as the Blood of Christ and consumes it to stop its profanation. The film also shows the last rites and the slow growth of a vocation against family opposition. The ending turns on sacramental absolution given by a dying priest to the man who has killed him. Its detractors' complaint, that it relies on shock where Bresson worked by restraint, has force.
history: Joannon wrote the film with Denys de La Patellière, with dialogue by Roland Laudenbach, for Gaumont and the Société Française de Cinématographie. It was shot in late 1953 at La Celle-Saint-Cloud and Joinville, released in France on 26 February 1954 and awarded a Bronze Bear at the Berlin festival that year.
advisories:
A sacrilege against the Eucharist is shown on screen: an apostate priest mockingly consecrates wine in a cabaret, and a seminarian drinks it to prevent its profanation.

A newly ordained priest is fatally struck by the man he is trying to save; a death in a wartime prison camp.

Adult themes of apostasy and self-hatred. Older teenagers and adults.

French with subtitles.

grey.question: The film's theology is traditional: an ordained man stays a priest, so his mock consecration in a cabaret is real and sacrilegious, and the young priest drinks the wine rather than leave it to profanation. The sacrilege is shown as horror and the ending turns on absolution and contrition. The question is one of taste and reverence: whether staging a valid consecration for shock, with the drunkenness and vomiting viewers describe, serves the argument or cheapens the Sacrament. A 1954 Catholic film-office rating has not been found and would settle how it was judged at the time.

title: Jesus of Nazareth
decision: REJECT: Editor ruling under the Founder's position (2026-10-11). Zeffirelli shaped the film by Nostra Aetate, and that conciliar reading is built into the drama: the invented scribe Zerah engineers the arrest and Judas becomes a well-meaning dupe, shifting the Gospel account of responsibility. This is the post-conciliar outlook applied to the Gospel itself, not a reservation a viewer can set aside.
summary: Zeffirelli's six-hour Gospel life, from the Annunciation to the empty tomb, with Robert Powell's grave Christ and an invented scribe who engineers the arrest.
synopsis: In occupied Judea, Mary is betrothed to Joseph and receives the angel's message. The Nativity, the Magi, Herod's massacre and the Holy Family's return to Nazareth take up much of the first part. John the Baptist preaches at the Jordan and Jesus begins His ministry, calling Peter and Matthew, healing the sick, raising Jairus's daughter and Lazarus, and teaching in parables and the Sermon on the Mount. Zerah, a scribe of the Sanhedrin, watches the new rabbi with growing alarm and draws Judas into a plan to bring Jesus before the council. After the Last Supper Jesus is arrested in Gethsemane, tried before Caiaphas and Pilate, scourged and crucified. The tomb is found empty, and the risen Christ appears to His disciples.
inclusion: This is still the screen life of Christ most people picture. Powell plays Him grave and hieratic, with a fixed, piercing gaze; Steven Greydanus finds the Shakespearean diction stiff, but the performance has outlasted its rivals. The first ninety minutes are the strongest. Greydanus calls them the best screen telling of the Christmas story to date, and he ranks the Annunciation, built almost entirely on Olivia Hussey's reactions to an unseen presence, among the best ever filmed. Zeffirelli gives the miracles naturalistic touches, such as a paralysed man's limbs slowly unlocking. Rod Steiger's troubled Pilate and Peter Ustinov's witty, frightened Herod are memorable. The film is also slow to start, uneven in the middle, and its post-Resurrection ending is hasty and muted. Only the complete version, about six hours, is worth seeking; the 270-minute abridgement cuts too much.
themes: Christ is presented as the Son of God who works real miracles, forgives sins, dies and rises. The Last Supper is reverently staged, Mary is shown with tenderness and restraint, and the Passion is grave rather than sensational. The reservations concern who is responsible for the Cross. Zeffirelli cited Nostra Aetate, the Council's 1965 declaration on non-Christian religions, as a guiding influence, and the film moves the plot against Jesus onto Zerah, an invented scribe, while rewriting Judas. The Gospels show a thief who sells his Master (John 12:6; Matthew 26:15). Ian McShane's Judas is a well-meaning zealot who wants Jesus to prove Himself before the council, and the silver is an afterthought. Greydanus calls this the film's most troubling departure from the Gospel story.
history: Lew Grade's ITC and the Italian broadcaster RAI produced the film after, by Grade's account, Paul VI suggested a life of Jesus. Anthony Burgess, Suso Cecchi d'Amico and Zeffirelli wrote it, consulting experts of several religions, and it was shot in Morocco and Tunisia over 186 days. RAI broadcast it in five weekly episodes from 27 March 1977; ITV and NBC showed it in two parts on Palm Sunday and Easter Sunday, 3 and 10 April 1977. Paul VI praised it publicly.
liberties: Zerah is invented and drives the plot against Jesus; Judas's motive is rewritten so that greed largely disappears. The Magi's visit to Herod, the Temptation in the desert, Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb and Simon of Cyrene are omitted. Mary Magdalene is played as a repentant prostitute, following the traditional Western identification. Peter is called Simon Peter from the start. The post-Resurrection appearances are brief and hurried.
advisories:
The scourging and crucifixion are shown with some blood but without the extended brutality of later Passion films.

The Massacre of the Innocents and an exorcism may frighten young children.

title: Teresa de Jesús
decision: PUBLISH: Gil de Muro's Carmelite survey, Alonso Franch's production study and the decine21 review give accessible, specific evidence of fidelity to Teresa's life and writings and of how the series stages prayer, the Inquisition and opposition to the reform; RTVE and the Universidad de Navarra fix identity. RTVE's 'modernity' framing and the medical aside in Alonso Franch are disclosed; neither is shown to be the series' own account of Teresa's mysticism.
summary: Josefina Molina's eight-hour TVE series, carried by Concha Velasco, follows Teresa of Ávila from the Encarnación to her death through illness, prayer, reform and opposition.
synopsis: The series picks Teresa up at twenty-three, a nun in the large, sociable Carmelite convent of the Encarnación in Ávila. Years of sickness and half-hearted prayer give way to a deeper conversion. Against the hostility of the town council and of many in her own order she founds San José, a small, poor, enclosed house, and then takes to the roads to found more. Her autobiography attracts the attention of the Inquisition; the friars opposed to the reform imprison John of the Cross. Each episode takes its title from one of her books. The eighth, 'Hija de la Iglesia', covers her last hours and her death as, in her own words, a daughter of the Church.
inclusion: This is the most ambitious attempt Spanish film or television has made at Teresa. Carmen Martín Gaite wrote the dialogue, the Teresian scholar Víctor García de la Concha advised on the scripts, and the Encarnación was rebuilt in the studio down to the colour of the habits and the refectory bowls. It was shot on 35mm, like a cinema feature. Concha Velasco spent days studying Discalced Carmelite life before filming; her Teresa is shrewd, funny, stubborn and often ill, and both the Carmelite writer Eduardo Gil de Muro and decine21 call it the performance of her career. The length is the point: the series has time for what most saints' films skip, from convent politics, money and letters to long dry stretches of prayer and the slow cost of a vocation.
themes: Mental prayer is the centre: Teresa's struggle to pray, her visions and raptures, and a reform built so that nuns can pray in poverty and enclosure. Molina, an agnostic, set out to show a woman walking towards holiness rather than the finished saint, and the ecstasies are played physically; Velasco arches and cries out. Alonso Franch writes that Molina filmed them without violating their mystery, and the series does not offer a medical explanation. RTVE's catalogue blurb sells Teresa as a pioneer of 'liberation of the spirit' and European modernity, a framing the series' own ending, on her dying profession of loyalty to the Church, does not bear out. Alonso Franch's article also repeats, as an aside, a modern claim that she was neurotic and epileptic; that is his remark, not the drama's thesis.
history: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada (1515–1582) entered the Encarnación in 1535 and founded San José in 1562, the first of her reformed Carmels. The Inquisition held her autobiography for years but never condemned it. She was canonised in 1622 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970. The series was filmed in 1983, premiered in Ávila and broadcast on TVE in 1984.
liberties: Dialogue is newly written to sound natural rather than quoted from her books, and events years apart are brought together in single scenes. The physical staging of rapture and levitation is an interpretation. Eight hours still leave out a good deal of her life, and Gil de Muro records that the Teresian scholar Tomás Álvarez had reservations he does not spell out. Shorter versions exist: a feature-length condensation and a four-episode cut.
advisories:
Prolonged illness, convulsive ecstatic states, a death-bed scene and the imprisonment of John of the Cross.

Slow and dialogue-heavy over about eight hours; best for teenagers and adults.

title: Clare and Francis
decision: PUBLISH: Greydanus's review and the reported reaction of the Assisi friars document a reverent, Church-loyal portrait with no invented romance; the producer's catalogue confirms Clare's vows are shown. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Here the inventions are dramatic connective tissue, and the friars' objections concern depth and craftsmanship, not distortion of either vocation.
summary: A two-part Rai drama that tells the conversions of Francis and Clare side by side; its Clare is convincing, its young Francis less so.
synopsis: Assisi, 1198: the merchant families storm the towers of the nobility. Francesco, the cloth merchant Bernardone's son, is throwing stones; Chiara, a girl of the noble Offreduccio household, is trapped inside her besieged home. Years later the two meet again across a family table. Francesco renounces his father's wealth, rebuilds a ruined chapel with his own hands and attracts companions to a life of poverty. Chiara watches, and on the night of Palm Sunday she slips out of her house. In the little church Francesco has restored she lays aside her shoes and fine clothes, he cuts her hair, and she vows poverty, chastity and obedience. The rest of the drama follows the two communities, and the two friends, as they grow.
inclusion: Most films about Francis treat Clare as a footnote; this one gives her equal weight, and Mary Petruolo plays her as calm and self-possessed from the start. Steven Greydanus judged it a 'pick' and found the converted Francis 'joyful in humility' and devoted to the Church, though he thought the drama much less successful with Francis's worldly youth. It is a conventional Lux Vide production of the kind Rai made often in the 2000s, and some Assisi friars complained about its sets and images. Its best quality is restraint about the relationship at its centre. Father Vincenzo Coli of the Sacro Convento praised it for avoiding the cliché of the 'two little sweethearts', a romance for which there is no historical evidence.
themes: The vows are shown explicitly and treated as the climax: Clare's flight, tonsure and profession are staged as a consecration rather than an elopement. Poverty is a choice for Christ, not a social programme, and Francis's submission to the Church is part of his character. The friendship between the two saints is presented as love of each other in Christ. Some friars at Assisi, quoted in La Repubblica, felt that Francis's theological and human depth was thinned for television, a fair criticism of a drama that is stronger on gesture than on prayer.
history: Clare (1194–1253) left her family on Palm Sunday night 1212 and was received by Francis at the Porziuncola. She led the Poor Ladies at San Damiano for over forty years and outlived Francis by twenty-seven. Her rule was the first written by a woman to receive papal approval.
liberties: The early meetings between the two, their families' dinner and much of the dialogue are invented. The siege that opens the film draws on Assisi's civil conflict of 1198–1200 but is shaped for drama. Greydanus thought the portrait of Francis before his conversion weak and unconvincing. The film calls the church of Clare's profession simply one Francis restored; tradition places it at the Porziuncola.
advisories:
Mild violence in the street fighting that opens the film.

A few unpleasant images of leprosy.

Two long episodes (about 200 minutes); younger viewers may need it in parts. The US DVD offers Italian or an English dub.

title: Saint Rita
decision: GREY: identity secure (FilmTV, Wikipedia, Ignatius); Rita was canonised in 1900, so neither hard rule applies, and nothing reported suggests post-conciliar framing. The only independent assessment is Greydanus's one-paragraph 'Pick' (NCR, 2007), which praises it but gives no account of its treatment beyond calling the arranged marriage a liberty (it is in fact traditional). Settles with a detailed review or a documented viewing of the Ignatius DVD covering Paolo's conversion and murder, Rita's prayer about her sons, her admission to the convent, the thorn wound and the presentation of her obedience in marriage.

grey.question: The only independent assessment is Steven Greydanus's one-paragraph recommendation of the DVD. It praises the film but says little about how it treats Rita's faith, and the one liberty it names, her arranged marriage, is in fact the traditional account. As a modern Italian television production it cannot be assumed sound. A detailed review or documented viewing covering Paolo's conversion and murder, Rita's prayer about her sons, her admission to the convent and the wound of the thorn would settle it.

summary: Lux Vide's two-part Italian television life of Rita of Cascia: unwilling bride, peacemaking wife and widow, and finally Augustinian nun, amid the blood feuds of fourteenth-century Umbria.
synopsis: Rita Lotti, the only child of elderly parents in the hills above Cascia, wants to become a nun, but her parents arrange her marriage to Paolo Mancini, a hot-tempered young man from a family caught up in local feuds. Through patience and prayer she draws him away from violence, and they raise two sons. The feud does not end with his change of heart. After she loses her husband and her sons, Rita seeks admission to the Augustinian convent in Cascia, where she must first make peace between the families before she can begin her life as a religious.
inclusion: It is the fullest screen life of Rita of Cascia, one of the most popular saints of Italian devotion. It was made in 2004 by Lux Vide, a company that specialised in television lives of saints, and broadcast on Canale 5 in two parts. Vittoria Belvedere plays Rita from girlhood to old age, opposite Martin Crewes as her husband Paolo, and Mgr Marco Frisina, the Roman priest-composer, wrote the score. Steven Greydanus gave the Ignatius Press DVD a short 'Pick' in the National Catholic Register, calling it engaging and edifying, with a crisp screenplay, solid performances and good production values, and comparing its feud plot to The Godfather. He recommended the Italian soundtrack with subtitles over the English dub.
themes: The film's subject is forgiveness in a culture of vendetta: a wife who draws her husband away from violence, a mother who wants her sons to forgive rather than avenge their father, and a widow who enters religious life only after reconciling the feuding families. Marriage, motherhood and the convent appear as stages of one vocation, which is the traditional shape of Rita's life. What has not been checked is the framing, for instance whether her obedience in marriage is shown as a virtue or as an injustice, and how the miraculous elements are handled; Greydanus raises no doctrinal problem.
history: Rita (c. 1381–1457; the 1912 Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1386–1456) married at twelve in obedience to her parents, lived eighteen years as a wife and mother, saw her husband murdered and prayed that her sons would not avenge him; both died reconciled to God. Refused at first by the Augustinians of Cascia, she was admitted after persistent pleading. She was canonised in 1900.
liberties: Greydanus says the film takes licence with the few known facts and singles out the arranged marriage against her wish for the convent; that marriage is in fact the traditional account given by the Catholic Encyclopedia. Other inventions of incident and dialogue have not been documented.
advisories:
Restrained menace and violence, including killings in a feud and a possible threat of rape.

Suitable for older children and up with parents; not rated.
