title: Padre Pio: Miracle Man
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Padre Pio, canonised 2002).
summary: Sergio Castellitto plays Padre Pio as gruff, funny and suffering in Carlei's Mediaset biopic, framed by an invented night-long interrogation by a sceptical envoy from Rome.
synopsis: Shortly after midnight on 22 September 1968 a prelate from Rome arrives at San Giovanni Rotondo, where crowds already wait for the morning Mass. Sent to expose the old friar's stigmata and miracles as a fraud, he questions the dying Padre Pio, and Pio answers by telling his life. We see Francesco Forgione as a peasant boy in Pietrelcina, tormented by the devil and drawn to God; his entry into the Capuchins; his illnesses; the stigmata; the crowds; and the long investigations by Church authorities, who for years restrict him to saying Mass in private. In the end the hostile cross-examination turns into the visitor's own confession, and Pio dies the next night.
inclusion: Castellitto is the reason to watch. He ages Pio from thirty to eighty and catches the dialect, the temper and the dry humour as well as the piety, and decine21 counts it among his best work. Steven Greydanus thought it the most consistently edifying of the Italian saints' miniseries he reviewed: vivid, unsentimental about the saint's irascibility, and serious about the priesthood. It is a hagiography in television form: the flashbacks march through the life in order, and Italian viewers' complaints were that it is a pious biography rather than a probing one. But the drama keeps the confessional and the Mass at the centre of Pio's life, and it is honest that a saint can be hard to like and still be obeying God.
themes: Pio's priesthood is shown through what he spent his life doing: saying Mass and hearing confessions, often sternly. Diabolical attacks are treated as real, as Pio himself described them. The Church's scrutiny of him, from the Holy Office's verdict that his phenomena were not proven supernatural to the restrictions on his ministry, is part of the story, and Pio submits to it; one scene even has him rounding on a local mayor who attacked the bishop. The frame turns on confession: the man sent to judge him ends on his knees. Mediaset's publicity, which spoke of a friar who rejected authority, does not describe the film or the man.
history: Pio (1887–1968) received the stigmata in 1918. The Holy Office sent Mgr Raffaele Rossi to investigate in 1921, declared in 1923 that the supernatural character of the phenomena was not established, and in 1931 confined him to private Mass; Pius XI lifted the ban in 1933. In 1960 John XXIII approved an apostolic visitation by Mgr Carlo Maccari, after which Pio's Masses and concelebration were limited; Paul VI removed those limits. He was canonised in 2002.
liberties: No Roman visitor interrogated Pio on the night before his death. The frame is a composite of real investigators such as Rossi (1921) and Maccari (1960), compressed into one fictional prelate. Dialogue and many incidents are invented or arranged for effect. Phillip Campbell notes that the film shows Pio slapping the mayor of San Giovanni Rotondo, where sources record him grabbing the man by the collar. The film is based on Renzo Allegri's popular biography rather than on the archival scholarship.
advisories:
Frightening scenes of diabolical attack, including the devil as a black dog, and some disturbing images of suffering.

References to misconduct by priests and one brief apparent instance (Greydanus).

Pio's temper includes physical blows. Teenagers and adults; not for young children.

Runtimes vary: about 206 minutes on Italian television, with shorter DVD cuts. The Ignatius DVD offers Italian, Spanish or an English dub.

title: Saint Philip Neri: I Prefer Heaven
decision: PUBLISH: Edoardo Aldo Cerrato of the Oratorian Confederation's procura, the best-qualified critic available, judges the portrait of Philip's priesthood, confession and obedience 'sostanzialmente positiva' while listing the historical errors, which are disclosed here. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Unlike Bakhita and Moscati, the inventions here alter chronology and the Oratory's social make-up, not Philip's own vocational choices or his obedience.
summary: Gigi Proietti makes a warm, mischievous Philip Neri in Campiotti's two-part Rai drama, which is generous with invention but true to the saint's spirit.
synopsis: Filippo, already a priest, arrives in sixteenth-century Rome meaning to join Ignatius of Loyola's missionaries bound for the Indies. Instead he finds his mission in the streets around him: gangs of half-starved boys, families in debt, young men drifting. He gathers the boys, feeds them, teaches them to pray and plays with them, and his house becomes the Oratory. Opposition comes from the powerful and from Church authority, which at one point suspects him, and he bears it without breaking with the Church. In the second part the Oratory opens to adults, and young men formed there, among them a fictionalised Cesare Baronio, become priests of a new congregation.
inclusion: Gigi Proietti, a great Roman comic actor, was a natural Philip: shrewd, playful, quick to deflate pride, and plainly a man of prayer. Cerrato praised both him and the sets, and the drama mixes comedy with child poverty and illness. Its spiritual instincts are good. Cerrato, who saw it before broadcast at the producer's invitation, singled out a priest who goes to confession as well as hears it, who stays humbly faithful to the Church under trial, and who joins work and contemplation without setting them against each other. Several of the saint's own short prayers are woven into the dialogue. As history it is unreliable; as a picture of what a joyful priest looks like, it works.
themes: Confession is central. Philip hears the confessions of the boys and of Rome, and the film also shows him going to confession himself. Obedience under pressure is the other thread: when Church authority doubts him, he submits rather than rebels. His humour serves holiness. The recurring line 'State buoni, se potete' ('Be good, if you can') is invented, as Cerrato notes, but it fits the saint's gentle realism. The Oratory's prayer, music and charity are shown as means of bringing young people to the sacraments, not as social work alone.
history: Philip Neri (1515–1595) came to Rome as a young layman, lived there for years as a lay catechist and hermit in the city, and was ordained only in 1551. The Oratory grew from informal gatherings for prayer and spiritual conversation open to men of every class; the Congregation of the Oratory was approved in 1575. He was canonised in 1622.
liberties: Large. Philip arrives as a middle-aged priest, not the young layman he was; his meeting with Persiano Rosa is rearranged; the Oratory becomes chiefly a refuge for street boys rather than a gathering of young men and adults of all classes; Baronio is heavily fictionalised; and many episodes are invented outright. Cerrato lists these 'incongruenze storiche' while defending the film's spirit.
advisories:
Child poverty, hunger, illness and death, including the deaths of children.

Some menace from street gangs and from powerful enemies; no graphic violence is described in the sources.

Suitable for families with older children; the history needs correcting with a biography.

Italian with English or Spanish subtitles on the Ignatius DVD.

title: Saint John Bosco: Mission to Love
decision: PUBLISH: A detailed Salesian review (interested but specific and critical) documents catechesis, Dominic Savio, Bosco's own words on holiness and his obedience to the Pope in the conflict with his archbishop, and lists the compressions and renamed characters disclosed here. Rai Teche and RaiPlay fix identity. Invented-material threshold applied to the Lux Vide/Rai saint dramas: invented scenes, composite characters, compressed chronology and renamed antagonists are acceptable when they dramatise the documented character and vocation; a record goes to HOLD when an invention changes the saint's own choices about vocation, chastity or obedience in a way the historical record contradicts (e.g. a romance for the saint, an unauthorised absence from the convent). Here inventions are composites and telescoping that do not alter Bosco's vocation or obedience.
summary: Flavio Insinna plays Don Bosco in a brisk, compressed Rai/Lux Vide life of the Turin priest who built schools and a religious family for abandoned boys.
synopsis: A Piedmontese farm boy who lost his father young, Giovanni Bosco follows his mentor into the seminary and arrives in Turin as a young priest. The city is full of hungry, exploited and violent boys, some in prison. He gathers them on Sundays, feeds them, teaches them catechism and a trade, and is chased from site to site by suspicious neighbours, officials and clergy. A wealthy noblewoman, the Marchesa Barolo, helps and then drops him. His mother Margherita comes to cook for the boys. Dominic Savio arrives. A liberal official, played by Charles Dance, schemes against him, and his friendship with the archbishop turns to conflict, which Bosco ends by submitting at the Pope's request. The Salesian congregation is founded to carry the work on.
inclusion: Flavio Insinna, later a popular television host, plays Bosco, with Lina Sastri as Mamma Margherita and Charles Dance as the liberal official who opposes him. The film does what the best Bosco lives do: it shows a priest whose kindness to delinquent boys always aims at their souls. It quotes Bosco's own sayings on holiness, gives time to the catechism lessons, and introduces Dominic Savio, the pupil he raised to sanctity. The Salesian reviewer FrMike judges that it presents Don Bosco's mission and personality well, while poking at details: the repeated 'Father Bosco' of the dub, an Oratory placed miles out in the country, and needless name changes. He also found the Italian-origin lines well dubbed into English for the US DVD.
themes: The Preventive System is shown as religion, reason and kindness, with the sacraments and catechism at its heart, not as a secular method. Bosco's priesthood is active and pastoral, and his holiness is ordinary hard work and trust in Providence. The best scene, by the Salesian reviewer's account, is his conflict with the archbishop: the film shows an early friendship, the archbishop's zeal for training priests, his view of Bosco as proud, and Bosco's eventual humbling of himself in obedience to the Pope to end the dispute. Anticlerical politics of the Risorgimento form the background.
history: John Bosco (1815–1888) opened his Oratory at Valdocco in 1846, founded the Salesians in 1859 and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. His long dispute with Archbishop Lorenzo Gastaldi of Turin in the 1870s–80s was settled under Leo XIII. Dominic Savio died in 1857 aged fourteen. Bosco was canonised in 1934.
liberties: Events from 1844 to 1882 are telescoped, so Mamma Margherita (d. 1856) and Joseph Cafasso (d. 1860) are present at a finale set decades after their deaths. Opponents are renamed: the Salesian reviewer notes that the vicar Cavour becomes the 'Prefect Clementi', who later absorbs Urbano Rattazzi, and that in the version he saw Archbishop Gastaldi becomes 'Cardinal Fassati'. The Oratory is placed in open country rather than on Turin's edge.
advisories:
Neglected and abused children, prison scenes, illness and death.

Scuffles and street violence of a mild, television kind.

Good for families with children over ten, with an adult on hand to correct the compressed history.

Shot partly in English with British supporting actors; Italian and English tracks exist, and the English-subtitled Italian version condenses the dialogue.

title: Blessed Duns Scotus: Defender of the Immaculate Conception
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (John Duns Scotus, cult confirmed 1993).
summary: A low-budget Italian drama in which the Franciscan theologian Duns Scotus teaches, prays and argues for Mary's Immaculate Conception: earnest, talky and unusually serious about ideas.
synopsis: In Paris in 1303 the friar John Duns Scotus refuses to sign King Philip IV's appeal against Pope Boniface VIII and is expelled from the university. The film moves between his teaching, his memories of a Scottish boyhood spent wanting to join the Franciscans, and the formation of three novices, one of whom falls for a pious orphan girl and must decide whether he has a vocation. Scotus tells a brilliant student that he studies too much and prays too little, and grounds his own theology in adoration before the Eucharist. The climax is an open-air disputation with Dominican masters over whether Mary was conceived without original sin.
inclusion: Films about theologians are rare because argument is hard to film; this one makes a real attempt. Adriano Braidotti plays Scotus with quiet conviction and makes dry scholastic reasoning sound like something worth living by. The film's point is that thinking about God is a form of prayer and needs prayer: study grows from contemplation of the Eucharist, and the doctrine defended is understood as an act of love for Our Lady. The blog critic Mercuriade called it a successful experiment that avoids the syrup of most saints' films. Its faults are plain. The budget is small, the debates rely on exposition, the novices' subplot is formulaic, and the devotional tableaux are sugary.
themes: The Immaculate Conception is presented as Scotus argued it: Christ, the perfect Redeemer, preserved his Mother from original sin by a more perfect redemption, in view of his merits. That is substantially what Pius IX defined in Ineffabilis Deus in 1854. Before then the question was open. St Bernard opposed the feast, and St Thomas Aquinas and St Bonaventure did not accept the doctrine in the form Scotus later defended, and in 1483 Sixtus IV forbade either side to call the other heretical. The film is a Franciscan partisan of a side that the Church later vindicated; viewers should not take its Dominicans as villains. Loyalty to the Pope and devotion to the Eucharist frame the argument.
history: John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Scottish Franciscan, taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne. Contemporary sources on his life are thin. He was among the friars expelled from Paris in 1303 for siding with Boniface VIII against Philip IV, and his Sentences commentary laid out the argument from preservative redemption. His cult was confirmed, amounting to beatification, by John Paul II in 1993.
liberties: The novices, their romance and much of the dialogue are invented. The climactic public disputation with the Dominicans comes from later Franciscan tradition about a Paris debate and is not documented in contemporary sources; the arguments are Scotus's, the event is staged. Scenes of his boyhood vocation are imaginative.
advisories:
A brief, sudden image of Christ's scourging (about 16 minutes in).

A chaste romantic subplot about discernment.

Dense philosophical dialogue; best for older teenagers and adults.

Available in English as Blessed Duns Scotus: Defender of the Immaculate Conception (Ignatius Press DVD, Italian or English audio).

title: Into Great Silence
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church, presented as normal or exemplary: the Grande Chartreuse as it lives today, after the Carthusians' post-conciliar liturgical revision.
summary: Philip Gröning's near-wordless documentary about the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse: almost three hours of prayer, work and seasons, with no narration at all.
synopsis: Gröning asked the Carthusians for permission to film in 1984; they answered sixteen years later. He then lived at the Grande Chartreuse, the order's mother house in the French Alps, for about six months, shooting alone with available light. The film follows the cycle of the year and of the day: night Office in the dark church, solitary meals passed through hatches, wood-chopping, tailoring, a barber's chair, snow. Two postulants are received as novices and tonsured. On the weekly walk the monks talk and laugh. Late in the film an old, blind monk speaks about death, God's Providence and the loss of faith in the world outside.
inclusion: This is cinema used for something it rarely attempts: making time felt. There is no commentary, no interview to explain things, and no music except the monks' chant. Scripture verses return as intertitles, and the repetitions build up the rhythm of a life given entirely to prayer. Gröning's images, many of them grainy from the low light, have a painterly patience, and the film rewards a viewer who stops waiting for events. The monks' weekly walk, full of talk and laughter, comes as a welcome surprise. At 164 minutes it is long and some find it stupefying; it is best watched in one sitting in a dark room, or not at all.
themes: The content is unmistakably Catholic. The monks chant a patristic text on the Holy Spirit that is, as Greydanus puts it, a small catechesis in Trinitarian doctrine. The intertitles quote the Gospels and the prophets on giving up everything to follow Christ. The reception of novices and the blind monk's reflections show vocation as an answer to God, not a lifestyle. The Carthusians kept their own ancient rite, and much of what is seen and heard, from Latin chant to the night Office, would be recognisable to monks of earlier centuries, but this is a community filmed in the early 2000s, not a reconstruction of older practice.
history: St Bruno founded the Carthusians in 1084 in the Chartreuse massif. The Grande Chartreuse is the order's mother house and admits no visitors; the monks live as hermits in community, meeting for the Office, Sunday meal and a weekly walk.
liberties: A documentary still shapes what it shows. Gröning shot more than 120 hours and arranges his material by season rather than strict chronology. Nothing is explained, so the Carthusian rule, the order's history and the meaning of particular customs stay off screen.
advisories:
Nothing problematic in content, according to Greydanus.

Very slow, almost silent and 164 minutes long; most children will not sit through it.

The little speech there is is French, with Latin chant; subtitled.

title: No Greater Love
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's Catholic content is the post-conciliar Church, presented as normal or exemplary: a present-day Carmel filmed in 2009.
summary: Michael Whyte spent a year filming the enclosed Carmelite nuns of Notting Hill; the result is quieter than Into Great Silence and more personal, because the sisters talk.
synopsis: Behind a wall in St Charles Square, Notting Hill, a community of Discalced Carmelite nuns lives an enclosed life of prayer and work. Whyte, who lived across the square for years without knowing it was still occupied, took about ten years to gain permission and then filmed alone over a year. The film runs two lines side by side, a single day and a whole year, centred on Holy Week. A nun rattles a clapper down a dark corridor to wake her sisters; they sing the Office, garden, and bake altar breads by the million for the churches of Westminster. A young sister makes her profession. An old sister dies and is buried. Between these events the nuns talk about their vocations, about prayer, and about long years when God seemed absent.
inclusion: The interviews make the film. The sisters are clever, funny and candid, quote Gerard Manley Hopkins and St John of the Cross, and talk about the habit and gardening as easily as about the dark night of the soul. Whyte's camera has a Vermeer-like feel for light at a window, and the editing sets the old nun's death against the community's Easter in a way that gives the whole film its shape. Greydanus called that juxtaposition its most inspired stroke. It is less austere and less ambitious than Gröning's Carthusian film, and more accessible: a good introduction to what contemplative life is for.
themes: The Resurrection is the film's spine: Holy Week, including the Mandatum in which the prioress washes her sisters' feet, leads to Easter, and a sister's death is placed inside that faith. The nuns pray for people who do not pray for themselves. Their accounts of spiritual darkness are the heart of the interviews: one went two years without any sense of God's presence, the elderly prioress around eighteen. Laughing, the prioress admits she sometimes thinks the atheists could be right, and adds that if she is wrong nobody will be there to tell her, and if she is right someone will meet her. It is the dark night described by John of the Cross, recounted by someone still living through it, not a profession of doubt.
history: The Monastery of the Most Holy Trinity is a house of Discalced Carmelite nuns on St Charles Square in North Kensington, still enclosed. Whyte notes that enclosure customs have relaxed in recent decades: the nuns no longer veil their faces before men, though workmen are still escorted.
liberties: A year of footage is cut into a day-and-year structure, and the interviews are personal testimony chosen by the director. Liturgical music and practice are those of an English community in the 2000s.
advisories:
A close-up of a dead sister in her coffin, and her funeral.

Frank talk about spiritual desolation and doubt, including the prioress's remark about atheism; best for teenagers and adults who can take it in context.

Gentle pace; little or no other content of concern is mentioned by reviewers.

synopsis: The title comes from Kolbe's childhood vision, in which Our Lady offered him two crowns, one white for purity and one red for martyrdom, and he chose both. Michał Kondrat follows him from his boyhood in Zduńska Wola through the Franciscans, the founding of the Militia of the Immaculata, the vast friary-publishing house of Niepokalanów, and the mission to Japan, to Auschwitz, where in 1941 he offered to take the place of a condemned prisoner. Franciscans and historians speak to camera, and Kondrat addresses the viewer himself. Staged scenes with Adam Woronowicz as Kolbe and Cezary Pazura as Brother Zeno fill in episodes, and the Auschwitz survivor Kazimierz Piechowski, who knew Kolbe, gives testimony.
inclusion: The value here is information and witness, not drama. The film gathers material that is hard to find elsewhere in one place, especially on the Japanese mission and Niepokalanów, and Piechowski's testimony is moving. Woronowicz's Kolbe is, in Przewodnik Katolicki's words, full of patience and peace. As cinema it is weak: Filmweb's Jakub Popielecki gave it two stars out of ten and called it a hagiographic primer, and even the friendly Przewodnik Katolicki review found it lacking in dynamism and too reluctant to show human weakness. Best used as a well-researched introduction for parishes and schools.
themes: Marian consecration runs through every chapter: Kolbe's movement, his presses and his missions are all offered to the Immaculata. The film presents his zeal for the Pope and the Church, his patience and generosity at Auschwitz, and his teaching that holiness means submitting one's will to God's. A healing with Lourdes water is presented as a miracle. His death is shown as the end of a lifetime's consistent self-offering rather than a single heroic gesture.
history: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941), a Conventual Franciscan, founded the Militia of the Immaculata in 1917 and Niepokalanów in 1927, and worked in Nagasaki from 1930 to 1936. Arrested in 1941 and sent to Auschwitz, he volunteered to die in place of Franciszek Gajowniczek and was killed by lethal injection in the starvation bunker on 14 August 1941. John Paul II canonised him as a martyr in 1982.
liberties: Dialogue and gestures in the staged scenes are invented. Reviewers note the interview-and-reconstruction pattern becomes repetitive and the portrait is idealised. The film's world premiere was an event screening alongside the 2017 Cannes festival, not a festival selection.
advisories:
Concentration-camp imprisonment and Kolbe's death; the sources do not describe how graphically the bunker is shown.

No other content of concern is reported.

Suitable for older children and up; slow and explanatory.

title: Silence
decision: REJECT: Too grave to leave to the reader (Founder standard, 2026-10-11), not a scope ruling. At the climax a voice from the fumie, presented as Christ's, tells the priest to trample His image, and the film's added final image (his wife placing a hidden crucifix in his hands at his Buddhist cremation) presents his public apostasy as compatible with a fidelity kept in secret. Catholic critics who admire the film (Greydanus, Mirus, Fr Martin) and those who condemn it (Miller) agree on these facts; they disagree only about the voice's source, which Scorsese leaves open. A film whose climax puts permission for apostasy in Christ's mouth and whose ending honours a hidden faith contradicts the duty to confess the faith under persecution (Mt 10:33; Summa II-II q.3 a.2). That is the question the brief asked to be judged, and the answer is yes.

title: Conclave
decision: REJECT: a fictional papal-election thriller whose resolution argues for change in Catholic teaching, as secular and Catholic critics agree. Stephanie Zacharek (TIME) reads its point as that the Church 'must change' its views on women and LGBTQ people; Kayleigh Hearn (Looper) calls it a film about tradition versus progress in which 'progress prevails'; Nina Starner (SlashFilm) reads the ending as challenging the Church's patriarchy, quoting the director that it is 'not a takedown of the church' but that 'not everyone needs to agree with the movie'. Brad Miner (The Catholic Thing) objects that the plot ends with the cardinals knowingly electing a pope who, by the film's own account, is a woman. title: Brother Sun, Sister Moon
decision: REJECT: Editor ruling under the Founder's position (2026-10-11). The film recasts St Francis as a 1970s counter-cultural figure, makes the bishop and papal court the antagonists, and stages vernacular worship with the priest facing the people at San Damiano as the purified Church: the post-conciliar reform presented as the ideal (hard rule 2 in substance).
summary: Zeffirelli's lyrical, flower-power life of the young Francis of Assisi, from his return from war to his audience with Innocent III, with songs by Donovan.
synopsis: Francesco Bernardone, the spoiled son of a rich Assisi cloth merchant, comes home sick from the war with Perugia. During a long fever he turns from his old life to the fields, birds and flowers. In his father's dye-works he sees the workers' misery, frees them and throws his father's cloth to the poor. Pietro drags him before the bishop, where Francesco strips off his clothes, renounces his inheritance and leaves the town. At the ruined chapel of San Damiano a voice tells him to rebuild the church, and he begs for stones. Friends join him, among them Bernardo, back from the Crusade, and Clare, who nurses lepers. Their chapel is burned and one brother dies. Francesco walks to Rome, abandons the speech prepared for him and rebukes the papal court with the Sermon on the Mount. Innocent III calls him back, kisses his feet and approves the brotherhood.
inclusion: The film's strongest case is visual. Ennio Guarnieri's photography of Umbrian poppy fields and the grey rubble of San Damiano won the Nastro d'Argento, the art direction was nominated for an Oscar, and the closing audience, shot among the gold mosaics of Monreale standing in for Rome, is real spectacle. Alec Guinness gives Innocent III weight in a few minutes. The film also takes Francis's poverty seriously: Ron Reed in Christianity Today points out that the words viewers find naive are mostly Christ's own. The weaknesses are as well known. Graham Faulkner is wide-eyed and fey, Donovan's songs date it badly, and Roger Ebert and Vincent Canby found it sugary and simple-minded. It stops in 1210, so there are no stigmata, no sickness and no Rule.
themes: Francis's conversion comes through nature, the crucifix and the Gospel: he quotes Christ on God and money, rebuilds San Damiano and embraces poverty, chastity and obedience. Clare's vocation is treated delicately. But the film frames all this in the terms of 1972. ACEC Toscana's critic contrasts a cathedral Mass, where the rich stand frozen while the bishop celebrates with his back to them, with San Damiano, where the poor sing in the vernacular and the priest faces them across the altar, and reads it as a probable allusion to the Council's liturgical reform. The papal court is a gilded trap. The Pope's best-known line, as Reed quotes it, is 'In our obsession with original sin we too often forget original innocence', which sits badly with Trent's decree on original sin.
history: Francis Bernardone (c.1181–1226) was held prisoner for a year after a skirmish with Perugia, renounced his inheritance before the bishop of Assisi, and rebuilt San Damiano after hearing a voice there. Bishop Guido commended him in Rome, where Innocent III gave verbal approval to his way of life and permission to preach. Clare joined him in Lent 1212. Honorius III approved the Rule in 1223; Francis received the stigmata in 1224, died in 1226 and was canonised by Gregory IX in 1228.
liberties: Bishop Guido, who supported Francis, is made an opponent. The father's dye-works, the freeing of the workers, the burning of San Damiano and a brother's death are invented or reworked. Paolo, the worldly friend, is a composite. The Pope's public foot-kissing and his confession of the Church's wealth are invented. The film ends in 1210, omitting the Rule, the stigmata and Francis's death. The Italian and international cuts differ in order, dialogue and songs.
advisories:
Francis strips off his clothes in front of the bishop and walks out of the town naked: brief, non-sexual nudity. Rated PG in the United States.

Fevered flashbacks of war; a chapel is burned and one of the brothers dies.

Suitable for older children and up.

Two versions exist: the international English-language cut (about 121–122 minutes, songs by Donovan) and a longer Italian cut (about 135 minutes) with a different order of scenes and songs by Claudio Baglioni. The English-language reviews cited here are of the international version.

The film's picture of the Church is shaped by the late 1960s: the hierarchy appears mainly as wealth and power, and one line sets 'original innocence' against original sin.

title: Thérèse
decision: GREY: Greydanus (B+, +3/−2) documents real reverence and real problems: cryptic sexual allusions, dream imagery that blends martyrdom with rape-fantasy imagery, an invented nun's unhealthy fixation on Thérèse, and an accidental desecration of a host. Canby confirms the sexual feelings belong to other nuns, not to Thérèse, and no critic consulted says the film itself sexualises her love of Christ; that rules out REJECT on present evidence. Not PUBLISH because the dream sequence concerns a canonised saint (1925) and has not been described scene by scene. A viewing log of the dream, the Lucie subplot and the host scene would settle it either way.
summary: Cavalier's austere portrait of Thérèse Martin, from her girlhood longing for Carmel to her death at twenty-four, told in spare vignettes against a bare backdrop.
synopsis: Thérèse Martin, the youngest daughter of a devout Normandy family, wants to follow two of her sisters into the Carmel at Lisieux, though she is only fifteen. She presses her case as far as Pope Leo XIII. Admitted, she lives the enclosed life of work, silence and prayer among sisters who are sometimes petty, sometimes eccentric, and one of whom, Lucie, becomes fixated on her. Thérèse speaks of her vocation as a love affair with Jesus and prays for sinners, among them the condemned murderer Pranzini. At Christmas the nuns celebrate the birthday of the Child they call their husband. After her father's death, the hardships of the convent wear her down; she suffers physically, is shaken by doubt, and dies of tuberculosis.
inclusion: On artistic grounds it is among the most honoured saint films: it won the Jury Prize at Cannes and five Césars, including best film. Catherine Mouchet plays Thérèse as a determined teenager whose love for Christ is concrete and urgent, and the scholar Mary Bryant called the film the most effective and challenging screen version of her story in its decade. Cavalier strips everything away: sets and props are pared to a minimum against a neutral backdrop. Vincent Canby noted that there are no heavenly choirs and no visions bathed in light, and that the beauty of the images is not ornament. Greydanus compares the restraint to Bresson, as Marina Warner did. The film follows Thérèse's own conviction that love, not suffering for its own sake, is the point of sacrifice. Its weakness is that it observes her without explaining her: Greydanus calls it a reverie rather than a meditation, leaving her a riddle.
themes: The film is built on Story of a Soul: Thérèse's vocation, her small sacrifices, her prayer for Pranzini, the daily life of the Carmel and her last illness. Her love for Jesus is presented as the centre of her life and in the romantic language she herself used. The film passes no judgment on her, and some critics, Andrew Sarris among them, have read it through Freud. Greydanus answers that psychoanalysis cannot account for her selflessness. The trouble lies around her rather than in her: an invented sister's unhealthy attachment, other nuns' sexual feelings, a dream sequence that mixes martyrdom with sexual violence, and an accidental desecration of a host.
history: Thérèse Martin (1873–1897) entered the Lisieux Carmel at fifteen, after asking Leo XIII in person for permission, and died of tuberculosis at twenty-four. Pius XI beatified her in 1923 and canonised her in 1925. Her spiritual memoir, Story of a Soul, made her and her 'little way' known worldwide after her death.
liberties: Sister Lucie is a fictional character. The film works in elliptical vignettes and omits large parts of the life, including much of the family background. The dream imagery is Cavalier's invention.
advisories:
Several sexual allusions and a disturbing dream sequence that mixes martyrdom with sexual violence imagery; a nun's obsessive attachment to Thérèse.

An accidental desecration of a consecrated host.

Illness and death from tuberculosis. Adults and older teenagers.

title: The Mission
decision: GREY: The Catholic substance is well documented (Greydanus, A−): Mendoza's penance, the Guaraní missions as Christian communities, Gabriel's death carrying the Blessed Sacrament. The reservation is real and can be stated plainly: the film's moral climax honours two Jesuits who defy their superiors under threat of excommunication, one of them breaking his vows to fight, and the historical record runs the other way (the Society's General ordered surrender; the Guaraní fought under their own leaders, per Whigham and Herzog). Not PUBLISH because the film treats disobedience as the nobler course without arguing it; not HOLD because the facts are now established. It would move to PUBLISH only if the Founder rules that Gabriel's non-violent refusal is an acceptable case of conscience and the history is disclosed, which this record does.
summary: Bolt and Joffé's epic of the Jesuit missions of Paraguay, destroyed after a 1750 treaty, with Jeremy Irons as a peaceful priest and Robert De Niro as a penitent slaver.
synopsis: In the 1750s Father Gabriel climbs the cliffs beside the Iguazú Falls, above which the Guaraní have sent a missionary to his death, and wins their trust by playing the oboe. Rodrigo Mendoza, a mercenary who captures Guaraní for slavers, kills his brother in a fit of anger. Gabriel sets him a penance: to haul his armour up the falls. He reaches the Guaraní he once hunted, is received among them and becomes a Jesuit. Then the Treaty of Madrid hands the territory to Portugal. A papal envoy, Cardinal Altamirano, tours the missions and must decide their fate, knowing that defending them could bring the Society of Jesus down in Europe; he orders them abandoned. Gabriel and Mendoza refuse to leave. Mendoza breaks his vows and trains the Guaraní to fight; Gabriel leads a procession with the Blessed Sacrament. Colonial troops destroy the mission and both priests are killed.
inclusion: The craft is not in doubt. Chris Menges's photography of the falls and the forest won an Oscar, Ennio Morricone's score is widely praised, and the film won the Palme d'Or. Its finest passages are thoroughly Catholic: Mendoza dragging his armour up the cliff as penance is a strong image of contrition, and the closing procession of the Blessed Sacrament through gunfire, the monstrance taken up by a Guaraní when Gabriel falls, is the film's most striking scene. The drama is weaker than the images. Greydanus finds the structure diffuse and Altamirano, the narrator, underwritten, and the film never quite settles whose story it is. Roger Ebert was harsher: every moment is watchable, he wrote, but the moments never add up to a story, and the final battle dissolves into chaos.
themes: Penance and forgiveness drive the first half, and the missions are shown as an attempt at a Christian society in which the Guaraní can live in peace. The second half turns on obedience. Gabriel defies his superiors but refuses violence and dies carrying the monstrance. Mendoza breaks his vows and takes up the sword. The film prefers Gabriel, but it treats both men's disobedience as nobler than the Church's compliance, and it closes on the envoy admitting that men like him made the world as it is. Greydanus argues that grave danger to souls could justify Gabriel's refusal, and that a priest may not take up arms, but notes the film never makes either argument itself.
history: The 1750 Treaty of Madrid transferred seven Jesuit missions east of the Uruguay River from Spain to Portugal. The Jesuits petitioned the king against it, but their General, Ignazio Visconti, ordered compliance and sent Fr Lope Luis Altamirano to enforce it. The Guaraní refused to move against the orders of both governor and missionaries, and fought under their own leaders, Sepé Tiaraju and Nicolás Ñeenguirú. They were crushed at Caaybaté in 1756. Madrid and Lisbon blamed Jesuit intrigue. The treaty was annulled in 1761.
liberties: The real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, not a cardinal sent by the Pope. The film turns the official record on obedience round: the Society's General ordered compliance. Some individual Jesuits were accused of helping the rebels, but the Guaraní fought under their own leaders, whom the film leaves out, and historians now credit them with organising their own resistance. Gabriel and Mendoza are invented.
advisories:
Bloody battle violence and killings, including the shooting of priests and villagers in a procession.

Non-sexual ethnographic nudity among the Guaraní.

A man kills his brother in a fit of anger. Rated PG in the United States but better for teenagers and adults.

The film presents disobedience to religious superiors, and a Jesuit's armed resistance, as admirable, and it inverts the Society's official obedience.

grey.question: The Mission ends by honouring two Jesuits who defy their superiors and a threat of excommunication; one breaks his vows and leads an armed defence, while the Church's envoy stands for cynical compliance. The film never argues that this disobedience was justified, it simply assumes it. It also turns history round: the real Altamirano was a Jesuit sent by his own General, the Society ordered the missions surrendered, and the Guaraní fought under their own leaders. Viewers who can hold Gabriel's martyrdom apart from the film's view of obedience will find much to admire.

title: The Exorcist
decision: REJECT for scope as a recommendation, in every edition: the film's force depends on extended obscene and sacrilegious material — a child possessed by a demon masturbating with a crucifix, the desecration of a church, and sustained sexual obscenity and blasphemy — which its own Jesuit adviser Fr John Nicola protested and the U.S. Catholic Conference's film office publicly judged unsuitable for a wide audience (A-IV, adults with reservations). Chambers (History of the Human Sciences, 2021) and America's 1974 symposium document a divided Catholic reception, including private readings of the film as favourable to faith. That defence is real, but no edition can be recommended without a substantial reservation on reverence and moral content. This is not a claim that the film is condemned or that its picture of priesthood and the rite is false.
summary: Friedkin's horror film about two Jesuits who attempt to exorcise a possessed twelve-year-old girl in Georgetown.

title: Au revoir les enfants
decision: REJECT on scope only, and narrowly. The film is excellent and its priest is a genuine hero, but its subject is a boy's friendship with a hidden Jewish classmate, his unwitting betrayal and his loss of innocence; Catholic life is the setting, not the subject. Catholic critics who admire it (Mary Joseph in The Catholic Weekly; Criteria at CatholicCulture.org) describe Mass, prayer, a confession and a sermon as texture around a coming-of-age and Holocaust story, with the headmaster's sacrifice as its climax. Under the Founder's Catholic-centred bar, which excludes On the Waterfront despite its central priest, consistency requires exclusion. This is not a judgment against the film; if the Founder treats the priest's witness as central, it can move straight to PUBLISH on the existing evidence.
summary: Louis Malle's memory of the winter of 1944 at a Carmelite boarding school, where a rich boy befriends a new pupil who turns out to be a Jew hidden by the headmaster.
synopsis: Julien Quentin, eleven, returns after Christmas to a Carmelite school near Fontainebleau. The headmaster, Père Jean, brings in three new boys, among them Jean Bonnet, clever and aloof. Julien resents him, then discovers that his real name is Kippelstein and that the monks are hiding him. They become friends over books and the piano. A kitchen hand is sacked for black-market dealing. In January 1944 the Gestapo arrive, tipped off by him. Julien's glance gives Bonnet away, and the boys watch the priest led off with the three Jewish pupils.
inclusion: This is Malle's finest film: restrained, precisely observed, and devastating in its last minutes. The school's routines, cold dormitories, Mass and the Our Father said for a classmate are rendered without sentiment or satire. Père Jean, based on the Carmelite Père Jacques de Jésus, is a portrait of quiet priestly courage. The film won the Golden Lion at Venice and the César for best film. Its centre, though, is the friendship of two boys and the guilt of the survivor.
themes: The Catholic material is real and respectful: the boys pray, serve Mass, confess; Père Jean preaches to wealthy parents about the poor of a starving country and hides Jewish children at the cost of his life. Mary Joseph notes the film's feel for the sacramental life. The faith is the atmosphere of the school rather than the question the film asks.
history: Malle attended the Petit Collège d'Avon, run by Discalced Carmelites. On 15 January 1944 the Gestapo arrested its headmaster, Père Jacques de Jésus (Lucien Bunel), and three Jewish pupils. The boys died at Auschwitz; Père Jacques died in June 1945 shortly after the liberation of Mauthausen. Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations; his cause for beatification opened in 1990.
liberties: Names are changed, and the friendship and its details are Malle's reconstruction of a childhood memory.
advisories:
Schoolboy talk about sex and a boy reading erotic stories; some bad language.

The raid and its aftermath are quietly devastating rather than violent. Teenagers and adults.

title: Fátima, Terra de Fé!
decision: GREY: Identity, outline and production context are established by the Cinemateca Portuguesa and Público's Cinecartaz. The Cinemateca's programme note and the Diário de Notícias comment on its craft and its place in the Estado Novo's official cinema, but no source assesses how it treats the apparitions or the faith. grey.question: The film is well identified: Jorge Brum do Canto's 1943 feature, preserved and screened by the Cinemateca Portuguesa. What has not been assessed is how it treats Fátima. Its story of a sceptical doctor converted by his son's cure is fiction, set beside a staged account of the 1917 apparitions, and the only critical comments, from the Cinemateca and the Portuguese press, concern its craft and its official character under the Salazar regime. A contemporary Catholic review or a recorded viewing would settle it.

summary: Jorge Brum do Canto's wartime Portuguese drama of a sceptical doctor converted by his son's cure, set beside a staged account of the Fátima apparitions.
synopsis: A doctor without faith has become estranged from his family over religion and devotes himself to his patients. When his son is badly injured in an accident, his medicine proves insufficient, and the boy's recovery, attributed to the intervention of Our Lady of Fátima, brings the father to belief. The film sets this invented story against the shrine and includes an episode that reconstructs the 1917 apparitions to the shepherd children. The father's struggle between science and faith is the dramatic spine. The sources found do not describe how the cure is staged, how the family is reconciled or how closely the apparition episode follows the historical accounts.
inclusion: The Cinemateca Portuguesa calls this the classic Portuguese sound film on Fátima. It was an ambitious studio picture, shot at Tóbis Portuguesa as the first production of Filmes Portugueses, the new company of the cinematographer César de Sá. Brum do Canto was one of the leading directors of the period, and the Diário de Notícias presents the film as an example of the Estado Novo's official production. He himself dismissed it as commissioned work with little of himself in it, except the apparition episode and the doctor's religious dilemma. The Cinemateca nonetheless singles out passages of documentary interest and some well-directed sequences. It is a document of how Portugal presented Fátima to itself in wartime, a quarter-century after the apparitions.
themes: The film turns on a healing and the conversion it brings: a man of science confronted with a cure his medicine could not achieve. That pattern reflects Fátima's place as a shrine of pilgrimage and prayer for the sick, and the film adds a staged account of the apparitions themselves. The healing is fiction and should not be mistaken for one of the documented events of Fátima. How the film presents the Lady's message, prayer, penance and the Rosary, has not been described by any source.
history: Three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, reported six apparitions of Our Lady at the Cova da Iria, near Fátima, between May and October 1917, ending with the solar phenomenon seen by a large crowd on 13 October. The Bishop of Leiria declared the apparitions worthy of belief in 1930. By 1942 Fátima was a national shrine, and Pius XII consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary that October.
liberties: The doctor, his family and the cure are invented for the film. The 1917 apparitions appear as a reconstructed episode within the fiction; how closely it follows Lúcia's accounts is not known.
advisories:
A child is seriously injured in an accident.

No source records violence or sexual content. The Cinemateca screened it with an M/12 classification.

summary: A 19-minute Portuguese record of the coronation of the Fátima statue by Pius XII's legate in May 1946, made by the Spanish director Eduardo García Maroto.
synopsis: The film records the ceremonies of 13 May 1946, when Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella, sent by Pius XII as papal legate, crowned the statue of Our Lady of Fátima at the Cova da Iria. According to the Cinemateca Portuguesa, it also shows the pilgrimage and the route and region around the shrine. The crown, made in Lisbon, was the gift of Portuguese women in thanksgiving that the country had been kept out of the Second World War. The archive's note does not describe the film's narration, music or structure, and no other account of its contents has been found.
inclusion: Its value is as a record. The 1946 coronation was a papal act that gave a shrine not yet thirty years old Rome's public recognition. García Maroto, a Spanish director who made the Luso-Spanish co-production A Mantilha de Beatriz the same year, filmed it. The Cinemateca Portuguesa preserved it and screened it in 2017, before Brum do Canto's Fátima, Terra de Fé!, in a season of seven films about Fátima, and the Diário de Notícias presented the pair as a contrast between the regime's official fiction and the record of the event. Nothing is known about its quality as filmmaking. It is chiefly for viewers interested in the history of the shrine.
themes: The film's Catholic content is a liturgical and devotional event: the solemn crowning of an image of Our Lady by a papal legate, an honour granted by the Pope to images with a long and fervent cult. The coronation followed Pius XII's 1942 consecration of the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary and showed Fátima as a shrine with Rome's explicit approval. How the film frames the event, whether chiefly as devotion, as national celebration, or both, is not described in any source.
history: Pius XII authorised the canonical coronation of the Fátima statue, carved by José Ferreira Thedim and enthroned in the Chapel of the Apparitions in 1920. His legate, Cardinal Benedetto Aloisi Masella, crowned it on 13 May 1946 before a large crowd of pilgrims. The crown, of gold set with pearls and precious stones and made without charge by Lisbon craftsmen, had been offered by the women of Portugal in 1942 in thanksgiving for the country's neutrality in the war.

title: Faustina
decision: REJECT: Scope (Founder ruling, 2026-10-11). The film's subject is recognised as saint or blessed only through a canonisation or beatification made after the Second Vatican Council (Faustina Kowalska, beatified 1993, canonised 2000; her Divine Mercy writings were also placed under restriction by the Holy Office in 1959).
summary: A spare Polish television-produced portrait of Sister Faustina Kowalska, the peasant nun whose visions of Christ became the Divine Mercy devotion, told by an elderly sister looking back.
synopsis: An old nun, Sister Feliksa, remembers the young Faustina, a barely educated peasant girl who joined the Congregation of Our Lady of Mercy and worked in its kitchens and gardens. Faustina reports that Christ appears to her and asks for an image of His mercy to be painted. Her superiors and sisters doubt her; some mock her. Her confessor, Fr Michał Sopoćko, takes her seriously and has the picture made. Sick with tuberculosis, she keeps a diary of her visions. Feliksa's memories are coloured by regret for how the community treated her.
inclusion: Dorota Segda's performance as a sickly but joyful mystic is the film's strength. Wojciech Kilar wrote the score. The film's interest lies in its picture of an ordinary convent, its kitchens, rivalries and suspicion of a sister claiming visions. Frank Swietek found it reverent but too fragmentary and elliptical, with an unnecessarily intricate flashback structure.
themes: The film concerns religious life, obedience under suspicion, and the claim of private revelation. It treats Faustina's visions of Christ sympathetically. The devotion she promoted was placed under a Holy Office prohibition in 1959, and the film's handling of that history has not been documented.
history: Helena Kowalska (1905–1938) entered the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in 1925 as Sister Maria Faustina. Her confessor in Vilnius, Fr Michał Sopoćko, had the Divine Mercy image painted in 1934. She died of tuberculosis in Kraków in 1938. On 6 March 1959 the Holy Office prohibited the spread of images and writings promoting the devotion in the forms she proposed; the prohibition was rescinded in 1978. She was canonised in 2000.
liberties: Sister Feliksa's narration is a framing device; how far the film dramatises or composites the convent's treatment of Faustina has not been established.
advisories:
Illness and death from tuberculosis; scenes of a sister being mocked by her community.

No known violence or sexual content, but no source confirms this in detail.

Polish with subtitles.

The film presents private revelations that the Holy Office restricted in 1959.

title: The Bells of Nagasaki
decision: GREY: identity is secure (Shochiku, NFAJ: 94 min, 22–23 September 1950, script by Shindō, Mitsuhata and Hashida from Nagai's books) and the outline and censorship history are documented (Seid/PFA, Shibata). Treatment of the faith is described only in a paragraph each by Shibata and Seid, who disagree on whether the conversion is shown; Nipponica judges it a good Ofuna-style work but says nothing of faith. Not HOLD because identity and content are established. Settles with a scene-level account (viewing or the 1950 Kinema Junpō review; Tadao Satō) of the conversion, Midori's faith and death, the treatment of the bomb as providence, and the ending.

grey.question: The film's identity is secure, but no critic has described in any detail how it presents Takashi Nagai's Catholic faith. The two scholarly accounts give a paragraph each and disagree on whether his conversion happens on screen. Nagai's own reading of the bomb as a burnt offering to God is disputed, and it is not known whether the film adopts it. A scene-level account of the conversion, his wife Midori's faith and death, and the ending, from a viewing or from the 1950 Japanese reviews, would settle it.

summary: Shochiku's occupation-era melodrama of Takashi Nagai, the Catholic radiologist of Nagasaki, and the first Japanese feature to approach the atomic bombing, made under heavy American censorship.
synopsis: Takashi Nagai, a medical student in Nagasaki, turns to radiology at a time when older doctors scorn the field. He is supported by his wife Midori. His early X-ray work exposes him to radiation, and he learns that he is dying before the war ends. Through the years of war he balances his research against duty to his wife and children, and he is drawn towards the Catholic faith of the city's Urakami Christians. In the last third of the film the atomic bomb falls on Nagasaki; the explosion is seen only as a cloud over the mountains. Afterwards the dying Nagai and the survivors set about rebuilding the city, and the bell of the ruined cathedral rings again.
inclusion: This is the first Japanese feature to approach the atomic bombing, made under Occupation censorship that rejected the first two script outlines and required a hopeful ending of survivors rebuilding their city. It adapts the books of Takashi Nagai, the Catholic radiologist of Urakami, from a script co-written by Kaneto Shindō, with music by Yūji Koseki, whose theme song became hugely popular. The Nipponica encyclopedia counts it among the good films that showed the best side of Hideo Ōba's Ofuna studio style; Steve Seid of the Pacific Film Archive calls it a somewhat sentimental melodrama. Its interest for a Catholic viewer is that a major Japanese studio built a 1950 film round a Catholic convert's faith and death. How fully it shows that faith is the open question.
themes: According to the archive notes and Yuko Shibata's study, the film shows Nagai drawn to the Catholic faith of his wife Midori and of the Urakami Christians, and accepting his own death from radiation with resignation; Shibata says he treats the bombing as a test given by God. The closing bell is the Angelus bell of Urakami Cathedral. Nagai himself taught that the bomb was a burnt offering accepted by God, a reading later criticised by some survivors. Whether the film adopts that theology, and whether it shows his baptism or only his attraction to the faith, has not been established.
history: Takashi Nagai was a radiologist at Nagasaki Medical College who was baptised a Catholic at 26, influenced by his wife Midori's faith. His X-ray work had already given him a fatal dose of radiation when the bomb of 9 August 1945 devastated Urakami, the Catholic district, and killed Midori. His book The Bells of Nagasaki was cleared by the Occupation censors only on condition that it appeared with an account of Japanese atrocities in Manila; it was published in 1949, and the film followed the next year.
liberties: Shibata calls the film a "somehow fictionalized" version of Nagai's story. The Occupation censors forced the omission of many scenes from Shindō's script and required the rebuilding finale. The bombing is shown only as a distant cloud over the mountains. Sources disagree on whether Nagai's conversion is shown within the film.
advisories:
Terminal illness from radiation, and a wife's death in the bombing; the explosion itself is seen only at a distance.

Wartime hardship.

No English-subtitled home-video edition has been found; the Pacific Film Archive holds a restricted subtitled print.

title: All That Remains
decision: PUBLISH: Respinti's review and the distributor and festival records document a Catholic conversion and family story, the bombing of Nagasaki, Nagai's illness and writing, and an imagined closing reunion; Higgins's account of five years' work and survivor interviews supports the seriousness of the research. Nagai is a Servant of God, not a canonised saint.
summary: A British low-budget hybrid of drama, CGI and archive footage about Takashi Nagai, the Nagasaki radiologist and convert who lost his wife to the atomic bomb.
synopsis: Takashi Nagai is a brilliant, sceptical young doctor in Nagasaki who lodges with a family of Catholics descended from Japan's hidden Christians. Their faith and their daughter Midori draw him, slowly, into the Church, and they marry. He throws himself into pioneering radiology, neglecting his family and his health, and is diagnosed with leukaemia. On 9 August 1945 the atomic bomb falls on Urakami, the Catholic heart of the city. Midori is killed. Nagai, injured and dying, works among the survivors, cares for his two children and, increasingly bedridden, writes the books that made him famous. The film ends with an imagined reunion with Midori at the cathedral, as on their wedding day.
inclusion: Nagai's story is important and little known outside Japan, and the Higgins brothers treat it with care: Dominic Higgins spent about five years on the project and interviewed survivors. The mix of live action, CGI and archive footage is a resourceful answer to a small budget, and Respinti found the archive images of the bombing chilling. Marco Respinti called it a film about the saint who beat the bomb. Its real strength is that faith is not decoration here. Conversion, Christian marriage and a doctor's charity are the story, and the film shows Nagai reading the catastrophe in the light of Providence and the Cross, as he did in his writings.
themes: The film is a conversion story first: an atheist scientist is drawn to Christ through the witness of a Catholic family and community with centuries of hidden fidelity behind them. Marriage is shown as a vocation, and its loss as a real grief. Nagai's response to the bomb, serving the wounded, raising his children and praying, is presented as Christian hope rather than stoicism. The closing reunion is a poetic image of hope in the resurrection. It is not a vision, and nothing in the sources suggests the film claims it is.
history: Takashi Nagai (1908–1951) was baptised in 1934 and married Midori Moriyama, whose family had kept the faith in secret through the persecutions. Already diagnosed with radiation-induced leukaemia, he survived the bombing of 9 August 1945, which killed Midori. He spent his last years in a tiny hut, writing; his books include The Bells of Nagasaki. His cause for beatification was opened in 2021.
liberties: Dialogue is invented and the narrative selects heavily from Nagai's life. The final reunion is imagined. CGI reconstructions stand in for prewar and bombed Nagasaki. The film is a family story and does not attempt a full account of the war or of the decision to use the bomb.
advisories:
Archive images of the atomic bombing and its victims, described by one reviewer as chilling; mass death and severe injury.

Bereavement, terminal illness and children who have lost their mother.

Best for teenagers and adults.

title: Don Bosco
decision: GREY: identity and production history are secure (ANICA visa, Torino Film Festival restoration, Enciclopedia del Cinema in Piemonte). The only independent critical text read is Cinema Illustrazione (1935), which judges craft, not faith. Pre-conciliar Catholic approval (Segnalazioni cinematografiche; L'Osservatore Romano and Rivista del Cinematografo) is known only at second hand, via Salesian ANS and an unpublished essay quoted by Prono. Salesians wrote the treatment, negotiated the script and later owned the negative. Settles with the 1935 Segnalazioni/Rivista del Cinematografo texts or a documented viewing of the 2021 restoration (dreams, Generala episode, Church–State material).

grey.question: The film's identity and production history are well documented, but no independent critic has described how it treats the faith. Approval from the Catholic film press of 1935 survives only at second hand, in Salesian accounts and an unpublished essay. The Salesians supplied the story, negotiated the script and later owned the film. A reading of the 1935 Catholic reviews, or a documented viewing of the restored version that covers Bosco's dreams, the reshot Generala episode and the Church–State material, would settle it.

summary: Lux's first production, made the year after John Bosco's canonisation: a Turin-shot life of the saint with one professional actor, Gian Paolo Rosmino, and real Salesians around him.
synopsis: A Monferrato farm boy who has lost his father clashes with his older half-brother Antonio and finds a mentor in the old priest Don Calosso, who teaches him Latin. After Calosso's death Giovanni leaves home to study at Chieri, where the death of his friend Luigi Comollo marks him. Ordained, he goes to Turin, where townspeople distrust his rowdy Sunday gatherings of poor boys. Help comes, surprisingly, from anticlerical authorities, who suggest a society whose members keep their civil rights. The Oratory becomes schools and workshops, the Salesians and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians follow, and missionaries leave for Patagonia. The film ends with his death in 1888 and a coda of his canonisation in St Peter's.
inclusion: It is the first sound feature about Don Bosco and the first production of Riccardo Gualino's Lux, later one of the major Italian studios. It was shot in a snowbound Turin, at Chieri and in the Monferrato, with Gian Paolo Rosmino as Bosco and non-professionals around him, real Salesians among them. Giorgio Federico Ghedini wrote the score. Alessandrini, by his own account not a practising Catholic, said he kept to Bosco's memoirs and the historians and invented only linking scenes. Contemporary opinion was mixed. Cinema Illustrazione's critic praised Rosmino and the death scene but found the film disjointed, often superficial and close to an informational documentary. It failed in first-run cinemas and found its audience in parish halls. The 2021 restoration makes it viewable again.
themes: Salesian accounts and archive synopses agree on the shape: a vocation that grows into institutions, from a priest's Sunday gatherings of poor boys to schools, workshops, two religious congregations and missions in Patagonia. The Salesian historian Fr Rufillo Uguccioni wrote the first treatment, and the order's delegate negotiated the script throughout. The ending turns to the canonisation in St Peter's. How the film presents Bosco's prophetic dreams, his confessional ministry and the anticlerical state, which in this telling helps him found his society, has not been described by an independent critic.
history: John Bosco was canonised by Pius XI on Easter Sunday, 1 April 1934, five years after the Lateran Pacts. The Salesian historian Pietro Stella has written that the Rome and Turin celebrations read easily as a seal on the Church–State agreement under Fascism. The film was made in this climate. Its producer, Gualino, was an industrialist the regime had sent into internal exile on Lipari. The film historian Alberto Farassino notes that he saw advantages in obliging both the Salesians and the regime, and that he later ceded the negative to the Salesians.
liberties: The first version, released in April 1935, included an episode at the Generala reformatory that the Salesians considered invented. After their protests the scene was reshot, with a caption stressing Bosco's role, and a second version reached cinemas in September 1935. A third version became the standard print. The 2021 restoration reconstructs the second version. Bosco's real outing with Generala inmates in 1855 suggests the scene dramatised an actual episode, but this is unresolved.
advisories:
Poverty, the death of a friend and a deathbed scene.

An early sound film with period acting and recording; patience required.

No age classification found.

title: La mies es mucha
decision: PUBLISH: Ernesto Fayé's detailed 1949 review in Cristiandad, read in full, documents a restrained, humorous and devout missionary drama with named religious advisers and judges the one doubtful Christmas Mass gag innocent; RTVE fixes the plot and audience guidance. The director's role as the Franco regime's official filmmaker and the film's place in national-Catholic cinema are disclosed; neither source shows the film carrying political propaganda.
summary: Sáenz de Heredia's missionary drama sends a young Spanish priest to a plague-stricken Indian village, and balances sacrifice with gentle comedy.
synopsis: Father Santiago, a young Spanish missionary, arrives at Kattinga in India to replace the ailing Father Daniel, who dies soon after. He finds the villagers in the grip of Sandem, a trader and moneylender whose loans end in forced labour in a mine. To free them, Santiago signs for the debts of the whole village. When the note falls due, Sandem demands payment. At the same moment people sick with plague begin arriving, and Santiago gives himself to their care. The comedy of a newcomer learning the mission's ways, including a Midnight Mass where the wrong gramophone record plays, gives way to the cost of staying with his flock.
inclusion: Unlike much Spanish religious cinema of the 1940s, it trusts the facts more than the rhetoric. The 1949 Cristiandad critic praised its 'gran contención': no showy technique, no melodramatic tricks, and humour that makes it a pleasure rather than a seminary lecture. Fernando Fernán Gómez is in the cast. A Vincentian missionary who had served at Cuttack advised on the village, which was reconstructed in Spain, and the Augustinian Félix García advised on religious matters. The story of a priest who pledges himself for his people's debts and then serves them through an epidemic is a clean, strong one. The Indian characters are seen through a 1940s Spanish lens, with all its limits.
themes: The title is Christ's own: the harvest is plentiful and the labourers few. The film's Catholic case is missionary charity in its literal form. The priest takes on his people's debt, then risks and ultimately gives his life in the plague. The Midnight Mass gag, in which an unexpected record replaces the carols, worried some contemporaries. Cristiandad's critic, who was alert to irreverence elsewhere, judged it innocent and typically Spanish, with no offence to the Mass itself. Evangelisation is presented as service to the poor against exploitation, not conquest.
history: Shot in 1948 and premiered in Madrid in March 1949, the film grew from a screenplay by Vicente Escrivá and José Rodulfo Boeta that won the first prize in a competition of Spain's Consejo Superior de Misiones. José Luis Sáenz de Heredia, José Antonio Primo de Rivera's first cousin, was the regime's official filmmaker: he directed Raza (1941) from Franco's own story and later the documentary Franco, ese hombre. La mies es mucha belongs to the national-Catholic cinema of the 1940s, and its critics praised it partly as a credit to Spanish missions.
liberties: An original story, not a biography. The Indian setting is reconstructed with Spanish locations and actors in some roles, and the picture of Indian society is simplified. Recorded runtimes vary widely between versions.
advisories:
Plague, illness and the death of priests and villagers.

Forced labour and debt bondage.

RTVE rated its broadcast not recommended for under-12s.

A comic mix-up during Midnight Mass may bother some viewers; contemporary Catholic critics judged it harmless.

title: Le Sorcier du ciel
decision: GREY: identity is secure (CNC visa 8067, Unifrance, Cinematografo). A brief pre-conciliar Catholic critical judgment now exists: Séquences no. 16 (January 1959) cites the film as an example of the artifice Pius XII warned against, the director having gone astray by chasing the sensational side of the saint, notably the devil. Kind 'reservations' rather than 'unverified' because the concern is now stated by an independent source. Not REJECT: Vianney was canonised in 1925. Settles with the Centrale Catholique cote, a 1949 Radio-Cinéma or La Croix review, or a documented viewing of the devil scenes.

grey.question: The question is one of emphasis. Le Sorcier du ciel gives the Devil a speaking part and stages the Curé d'Ars's night-time struggles with him as set-pieces. Writing in 1959, the Quebec film review Séquences cited it as an example of the artifice Pius XII warned against: the director went astray chasing the sensational side of the saint's life, and spiritual combat sits badly in a presbytery bedroom. No fuller review has been found. A contemporary French Catholic review or rating, or a documented viewing, would show whether the saint or the spectacle dominates.

summary: A French life of the Curé d'Ars, with Georges Rollin as Vianney facing a hostile village and a Devil who argues with him at night.
synopsis: In 1818 the young priest Jean-Marie Vianney is sent to Ars, a village of unbelievers and anticlericals, and is met with jeers from the blacksmith Sanson and the innkeeper Mairey, whose wedding is being celebrated. Poor and worn by work and fasting, he preaches boldly, while the Devil works against him and the two of them argue at night. Falsely accused of plotting against the government, he is about to be arrested when he cures Mairey's crippled son, and the father returns to the faith. His fame grows, and he confesses day and night and reads souls. He tries to flee the celebrity but is brought back. At the end only Sanson resists, until the old curé's death.
inclusion: The subject is the patron of parish priests, and the film builds its story round what made him famous: preaching, penance, the long hours in the confessional and a village won back to the faith. Georges Rollin plays Vianney, Marie Daëms plays his helper Catherine Lassagne, and René Jolivet wrote the script. Unifrance records a selection at Venice in 1949. It is one of the few films to take the saint's reported struggles with the devil literally and put them on screen, which is exactly what its critics questioned. Made two years before Bresson's Diary of a Country Priest, it is a useful point of comparison for anyone interested in how French cinema of the period filmed the priesthood.
themes: The film presents the conversion of a parish through a priest's suffering and prayer: preaching against the tavern and the dance, the confessional as the place where souls are won, and the devil's attacks as a sign that the work is succeeding. The cure of the innkeeper's son and the last holdout's conversion at Vianney's death make grace visible. The Devil is a speaking character who argues with the priest at night. In 1959 Séquences judged that Blistène had gone astray in pursuing the surprising side of the saint's life, and that spiritual combat is poorly contained in the closed, material space of a presbytery room.
history: Jean-Baptiste-Marie Vianney became parish priest of Ars in 1818, when his bishop warned him there was little love of God in the parish. He made the church his home and disciplined himself with vigils and fasts. In his last years he spent sixteen hours or more a day in the confessional and was credited with reading souls and healing the sick, especially children. He longed to flee into solitude but never abandoned his post. He died at Ars on 4 August 1859, was beatified in 1905 and canonised in 1925.
liberties: Unifrance's synopsis says the film presents his life "en forme un peu romancée". The named village antagonists and the false political accusation have not been checked against the historical record. The departure and return compress his recorded longing to leave Ars into a single episode. The Devil appears as a speaking character, a dramatic device Séquences considered misjudged.
advisories:
Night scenes in which the Devil harasses and argues with the priest; these may frighten children.

Village hostility and mockery of a priest; a crippled child; a deathbed.

General-audience classification in France (CNC).

title: Caterina da Siena
decision: PUBLISH: The contemporary judgment of the Centro Cattolico Cinematografico (preserved in the Italian bishops' film-commission archive) approves the film for all audiences as made with elevated intentions, finds Catherine's mysticism well conveyed and asks parish halls to cut one bedroom scene; ANICA and Film Atlas establish identity and the 1947 censorship certificate. Intermezzo's hostile review and Gianluca della Maggiore's account cover craft and reception. The weak craft and the parish-hall cut are disclosed; neither is a doctrinal problem. Distinct from Palella's later Io, Caterina (1956).
summary: Oreste Palella's modest postwar life of St Catherine of Siena, from her childhood vision to her death in Rome, approved by Italy's Catholic film office.
synopsis: In Siena, the young Caterina Benincasa has a vision of Christ and gives herself to prayer and penance. Her forceful mother, Lapa, wants her married; Caterina answers that she is already the bride of Jesus, and her father and her confessor take her side. She joins the Mantellate, the Dominican women of penance, while still living at home, and the order approves her teaching. After a stay in Florence she returns to nurse the victims of plague in Siena. In 1376 she persuades Pope Gregory XI to bring the papacy back from Avignon to Rome, and miracles are attributed to her. She dies in Rome on 29 April 1380, her last words recorded as 'Blood, blood, blood.'
inclusion: This is an early screen life of Catherine of Siena, made in the poverty of postwar Italy by Oreste Palella, a minor director who returned to the saint in Io, Caterina (1956). Regana De Liguoro plays Catherine, with Rina De Liguoro as her mother. The script by Fernando Leonardi and Palella draws on Catherine's life and letters. The contemporary verdicts are mixed. Italy's Catholic Film Centre found passages of good workmanship and judged Catherine's mysticism well conveyed, but thought the whole rather fragmentary and her political work poorly drawn; it praised the score. The magazine Intermezzo was harsher, saying such a subject needed more preparation and less limited means. The historian Gianluca della Maggiore records that it won over neither critics nor audiences. It is a period piece rather than a lost classic, and copies are hard to find.
themes: Catherine's mystical life is the centre of the film: the childhood vision, her refusal of marriage because she is already given to Christ, penance, and her life as a Dominican tertiary living in the world. Her nursing of the plague-stricken shows prayer turning into charity. Her mission to Gregory XI presents loyalty to the Pope as part of the same holiness, though the Catholic Film Centre thought this public side the weakest part of the film. Its moral verdict was that the film had been conceived and made with elevated intentions and could be shown to everyone in public cinemas.
history: Caterina Benincasa (1347–1380), the daughter of a Sienese dyer, joined the Dominican Mantellate as a laywoman and became known for her prayer, her penances, her care for the sick and her letters to popes and princes. She urged Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome, which he did in 1377. Her Dialogue and nearly four hundred letters survive. She was canonised by Pius II in 1461 and named a patron of Italy by Pius XII in 1939.
advisories:
Plague scenes and a deathbed.

The Catholic Film Centre passed it for all audiences in public cinemas, but asked parish halls to cut a first-half sequence showing the character Monna Gioiosa in her bedroom or dressing room.

Cheaply made and, by contemporary accounts, fragmentary; copies are scarce.

title: The Dark Night
alternateTitles: The Dark Night of the Soul
decision: REJECT: problem too grave. Saura described his subject as John's inner process and a 'secular mysticism' rather than religion. Mariona Visa Barbosa's scene-by-scene study (2009) records that the film has St John of the Cross tell his jailer that he sinned when he met a nun, Ana de Jesús, at a convent; shows that nun succumbing to lust and possessed; casts the same actress as the Virgin Mary; and stages the soul's union with the Bridegroom as John and the Virgin kissing on the mouth and embracing. The Cinémathèque française confirms Julie Delpy plays both the Virgin and a temptress. An invented sin tied to a lustful nun for a canonised Doctor of the Church, and an erotic treatment of Our Lady, presented approvingly as mystical union, cannot be listed even with reservations. The hard rule on post-1965 canonisations does not apply (John was canonised in 1726).
