title: Golgotha
decision: PUBLISH: Identity from Unifrance and AlloCiné; substantive treatment from James Travers's detailed review and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register essay, which together establish Scripture-based dialogue for Christ, a reverent Passion and a depicted Resurrection. The portrayal of the Temple authorities is disputed in secondary comment and is flagged rather than treated as resolved by silence.
summary: The first sound film of the Passion: Duvivier's dark, crowded Holy Week, with Jean Gabin's Pilate and Harry Baur's Herod, and a crucifixion staged as a cosmic storm.
synopsis: Christ enters Jerusalem to the crowd's acclaim. The high priests, fearing his popularity, plot with Judas and press the Roman authorities. At the Last Supper Christ foretells his betrayal. He is arrested, taken before Caiaphas, Herod and Pilate, mocked and scourged. Pilate, warned by his wife Claudia, tries to release him, but the crowd chooses Barabbas. Christ carries the cross to Golgotha and is crucified as a storm breaks over the city. The film continues past his death and burial to the Risen Christ.
inclusion: Duvivier keeps Christ at a distance for the first half, seen from behind or across a crowd, and lets us read him through the people around him: Our Lady, Peter, Judas, Caiaphas, Herod, Pilate. K. V. Turley, writing for the National Catholic Register, finds the method illuminating and the film well judged at about ninety minutes. Robert Le Vigan speaks only words from the Gospels and plays them quietly. The supporting cast is the strength: Harry Baur's massive Herod, Gabin's tired, almost decent Pilate, Edwige Feuillère as his wife. Jules Kruger's photography and Ferdinand Earle's Jerusalem give it real scale for a French production, and James Travers rightly singles out the crucifixion sequence. The script is thin and the characters stay at arm's length; some viewers will find it stiff.
themes: The Passion is played straight from the Gospels, without invented speeches for Christ. Travers stresses the film's emphasis on Christ's humanity and suffering; that is a matter of emphasis, not denial, since the film shows the Risen Christ with the wounds of the nails, and Turley calls it a cinematic icon for praying through Holy Week. Our Lady's presence is reverent. The Last Supper is staged after Leonardo. The film locates guilt in a small group of conspirators and in Pilate's weakness, though some later viewers find the Temple authorities visually stereotyped.
liberties: Pilate is made more sympathetic than the Gospels require, and Claudia Procula's role is enlarged. Herod's scene is built up for Harry Baur. Some reports say the film ends with the Ascension, others with the Resurrection; the ending was not verified.
advisories:
Scourging, mockery and crucifixion, shown without modern graphic detail but with real force.

Some viewers consider the costuming and casting of the Jewish authorities stereotyped in the manner of 1930s European films.

Suitable for older children and up; the crucifixion storm is frightening.

title: Miracle of Saint Thérèse
decision: PUBLISH: Unifrance confirms identity (FAF / Films Fernand Rivers, released 29 August 1952); Steven Greydanus's Decent Films review (A+, +4, nothing objectionable) gives detailed evidence of a reverent biography that presents the Little Way, Carmelite life and her death faithfully. Main checks against Thérèse's own Story of a Soul show no material distortion; minor chronological points are noted.
summary: A plain, reverent French biography of St Thérèse of Lisieux, from her childhood at Les Buissonnets to her death in Carmel, framed by her cause for canonisation.
synopsis: Framed by documentary-style scenes of her canonisation cause, the film tells Thérèse Martin's life. A pious child in a devout family, she hears her father read about Joan of Arc and wants to be a saint. Gravely ill as a girl, she is cured when a statue of Our Lady seems to smile at her. She follows two sisters into the Carmel of Lisieux, overcoming the objections of the convent's ecclesiastical superior. Inside, a prioress rebukes her ambition to be a saint as presumptuous; she answers with Christ's call to be perfect. As novice mistress she teaches her 'little way' of spiritual childhood. She dies young of tuberculosis after a painful illness.
inclusion: Greydanus gives it his highest grade and calls it an excellent, reverent biopic, and the reasons are clear from his account: it takes Thérèse's spirituality seriously instead of turning her into a sugary icon. Her 'little way' is shown in friction with the more severe piety around her, and the film is willing to show a young nun quietly correcting her elders. France Descaut is a sincere Thérèse, Jean Debucourt plays her father, Suzanne Flon is among the nuns, and the black-and-white photography and convent sets are convincing. The canonisation-process frame is stiff, and the titles in both languages promise something it is not. The only English home release is dubbed.
themes: The film is about sanctity in small things. Thérèse wants to be a saint, is told that this is presumption, and replies that Christ commanded it. Her 'little way' is love expressed in ordinary duties and acceptance of suffering; as novice mistress she spares a novice a harsh penance that harms body and work. Greydanus draws out her childhood devotion to Joan of Arc and her love for the missions. The Marian cure and a snowfall are shown as signs of grace without exaggeration, and her death of tuberculosis is treated as a consuming of love rather than a defeat.
history: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in 1873. In May 1883, aged ten, she was cured of a grave illness when the statue of Our Lady seemed to smile at her. On 20 November 1887 she asked Leo XIII to let her enter Carmel at fifteen; he replied that she would if it was God's will. She entered on 9 April 1888 and died in 1897. She was canonised in 1925.
liberties: Greydanus's account places her cure at about eight; she was ten. The film's snowfall at her entry to Carmel may shift a later event. Convent dialogue is invented. Some English-language summaries wrongly say her father opposed her vocation; in the film, as in history, the opposition came from the convent's superior.
advisories:
A long final illness and death from tuberculosis.

Greydanus finds nothing objectionable and rates it for children and up. The English DVD is dubbed, without the French track.

title: Teresa de Jesús
decision: PUBLISH (judgment call): Fernando Sanz Ferreruela's archival study (Artigrama, 2023) establishes identity (Agrupa Films; shot September to December 1961; Madrid premiere 14 May 1962; Interés Nacional, 8 June 1962) and shows that the Carmelite objections often attached to this title were made against an earlier, banned script; the filmed script was passed by a Carmelite adviser appointed by the Order and by the Bishop of Madrid in July 1961. Tracie Amend's scene-by-scene study guide supplies substantive treatment. The invented courtship and forced entry are a real distortion and are disclosed.
summary: Aurora Bautista plays St Teresa of Ávila from courted girl to dying foundress in Juan de Orduña's long-delayed, Carmelite-approved Spanish biography.
synopsis: In Ávila the young Teresa is courted by her cousin Pedro and by Álvaro. When the two men duel in the garden, her father sends her to the convent of the Encarnación the next morning. Years later, as a nun, she fasts and scourges herself until she collapses, and her prioress calls it pride. Learned men fear her prayer is the devil's work and her confessor burns her books, until St Francis Borgia tells her to obey God and found a reformed house. With Doña Guiomar's help she opens a poor convent despite a hostile town. She travels Castile founding more houses, drives the Princess of Eboli out of Pastrana and answers the Inquisition in Seville. She dies asking her daughters' pardon.
inclusion: Aurora Bautista, Orduña's star from Locura de amor, carries the film, and the verdicts on her divide: Fernando Méndez-Leite counted it among her best performances, while Eduardo Gil de Muro thought casting her a mistake. Sanz Ferreruela, who reconstructed the production from the censorship file, calls the finished script a hagiography full of commonplaces, and he regrets the bolder script the censors banned. The conventional choices are mostly sound ones, though. The film follows Teresa's own account of long trial by suspicious confessors, Borgia's discernment, the poverty of St Joseph's, the road with her coachman, Pastrana and Seville. Its picture of a mystic who is tested by the Church, not set against it, is the right one.
themes: The film is about testing a vocation. Teresa's early penances are sincere but excessive. The prioress who calls them pride is not a villain, and Teresa confesses pride more than once. Her prayer is treated as genuine, yet the learned men's fear that it may be diabolical is given full weight, and she herself panics that the devil has taken Christ's form. The reform is about poverty and enclosure, set against an Encarnación whose parlour has become a salon for well-dressed visitors. At the trial she answers that she was led by God and denies calling herself a saint. Her death is quiet and penitent.
history: Teresa de Ahumada (1515–1582) was sent by her father to the Augustinian nuns of Ávila to be educated. In November 1535 she entered the Carmelite Incarnation, leaving home without his consent; he then yielded. After years of illness, St Francis Borgia and St Peter of Alcántara guided her through her mystical experiences. She founded St Joseph's at Ávila on 24 August 1562, and later houses included Pastrana and Seville. Jerónimo Gracián's appointment as apostolic visitor was followed by four years of persecution of the reform. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582 and was canonised in 1622.
liberties: The opening is invented, and it reverses the history. There were no rival suitors and no duel, and her father did not order her into the convent the next morning: he sent her to the Augustinians for schooling, and she entered Carmel against his wishes. Álvaro's later visits and roses are also fiction. The Encarnación's laxity is sharpened for drama; a Carmelite historian asked in 1957 that the script not show the Order as persecuting innocence. One detailed summary has her travelling to Ávila to die, but she died at Alba de Tormes.
advisories:
Self-flagellation and fasting to the point of collapse, shown as excess and rebuked.

An opening arrest of a fraudulent stigmatic, with a bloody knife; a sword duel; a torch-bearing mob; Inquisition interrogations; a deathbed scene.

Suitable for teens and older; younger viewers may find the penances disturbing.

title: The Gospel According to St. Matthew
decision: PUBLISH: Identity and awards confirmed by the Italian Cultural Institute (Venice Special Jury Prize; OCIC prize); Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review (A+, +4) shows near-verbatim fidelity to Matthew, matter-of-fact miracles and a contemplative rather than political Christ. Pasolini's Marxism and unbelief are a documented context, but the critical evidence shows the text of the Gospel is not reinterpreted; the film shows the Resurrection.
summary: An atheist Marxist poet filmed St Matthew's Gospel almost word for word, with peasants for actors and southern Italy for Palestine, and made the most austere of Jesus films.
synopsis: The film follows Matthew's Gospel in order. Joseph learns that Mary is with child and is reassured by an angel; Christ is born, the Magi come, the Holy Family flees and Herod kills the infants. John baptises in the Jordan. Jesus, young and severe, calls fishermen, preaches, heals, walks on water, and confronts the scribes and Pharisees. The Sermon on the Mount comes as a barrage of close-ups. He enters Jerusalem, drives the traders from the Temple, eats the Passover with the Twelve, is betrayed, denied by Peter, tried and crucified, watched by his aged mother. On the third day the tomb is empty and he sends his disciples to all nations.
inclusion: Pasolini took no liberties with the words: the dialogue is Matthew's, cut and sometimes reordered, but not rewritten. He cast non-professionals, including a Spanish student as Christ and his own mother as the older Mary, and shot in central and southern Italy, including the cave dwellings of Matera. The result looks like no other Bible film: weathered faces, bare landscapes, abrupt cuts, and long stretches where the images carry the narrative that Matthew's own voice would supply. Greydanus gives it his highest artistic grade and calls it one of the most contemplative Jesus films made. It is demanding: long silent passages assume you know the text, and the Passion is notably restrained. But few films let the Gospel speak so directly.
themes: The film's faith is the Gospel's own. Miracles happen without fuss: an angel simply stands there, Christ walks on the water, the loaves multiply. Enrique Irazoqui's Christ is urgent, stern and human without being diminished. Pasolini called himself an unbeliever with a nostalgia for belief, and critics have long read the film as a Marxist allegory of the poor; Greydanus answers that the text is not bent to politics. Our Lady is played in youth by a silent teenager and at the Cross by Pasolini's own mother. The Resurrection and the command to baptise all nations close the film.
history: Pasolini had been convicted in 1963 of insulting the state religion for his short film La ricotta. The Gospel premiered at Venice on 4 September 1964 and won the Special Jury Prize and the prize of the Office Catholique International du Cinéma. Pasolini dedicated it to the memory of John XXIII, who had died the year before.
liberties: Matthew's genealogy and the Transfiguration are omitted; some episodes are reordered or compressed. The Pharisees' tall hats are borrowed from Renaissance painting. Settings are southern Italian, not Palestinian, and the music is anachronistic by design.
advisories:
Massacre of the Innocents and the Crucifixion are shown, but with little blood.

No sexual content. Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up; its pace and silence suit older children and adults better.

title: The King of Kings
decision: PUBLISH: AFI Catalog identity; Steven Greydanus's detailed Decent Films review, Charles Musser's Criterion essay and K. V. Turley's National Catholic Register piece establish a reverent Gospel film with a Eucharistic Last Supper, a reverent Our Lady and a careful handling of guilt for the Crucifixion. The invented Magdalene prologue, Protestant-default intertitles and one unscriptural intertitle are disclosed rather than disqualifying.
summary: DeMille's silent life of Christ opens as a lurid Hollywood spectacle, then settles into a surprisingly reverent Gospel film, with H. B. Warner's quiet Christ and a Resurrection in colour.
synopsis: Mary Magdalene, a rich courtesan, is told that her lover Judas has gone off after a carpenter from Nazareth. She drives out in a chariot drawn by zebras to win him back, meets Jesus, and is freed of seven devils. The film then follows Christ through healings, the call of the disciples, conflict with the Temple authorities and the Roman occupiers, and into Holy Week: the Last Supper, Gethsemane, Judas's betrayal, the trial before Pilate, the way of the cross and the Crucifixion, cut against Judas's suicide, with an earthquake that splits the Temple. The Resurrection follows, in colour.
inclusion: Greydanus calls it flawed but powerful, and that is fair. The first reel is pure DeMille: a half-dressed Magdalene, an orgy, zebras. Then the tone changes. H. B. Warner, past fifty and rather old for the part, gives Christ dignity and gentleness; his scenes with children, including one where he mends a child's doll, are the warmest in the film. DeMille's craft is formidable: the crowds, the lighting, the cutting between the Crucifixion and Judas's death, the storm that follows. Musser, in his Criterion essay, finds Warner's divinity rendered by lighting rather than acting and some of the halo effects kitsch, and he has a point. But for a silent epic it holds attention, and its seriousness about the Passion is unmistakable.
themes: The Last Supper is handled with reverence: Peter holds the chalice to his heart, while Judas crumbles the host and lets it fall, a clear sign that the film treats the Eucharist as sacred. Our Lady appears with dignity throughout. The intertitles are mostly from the King James Bible and the sensibility, as Greydanus says, is Protestant by default, but nothing in it attacks Catholic belief. Turley objects to one intertitle in which Mary urges her Son to go back to Nazareth, which is unscriptural. On the Crucifixion, the film places guilt on Caiaphas as a Roman appointee and has him plead that he alone is guilty, a deliberate attempt to avoid blaming the Jewish people.
liberties: The opening, with Mary Magdalene as a courtesan and Judas's lover, is invented. Events are rearranged thematically: episodes about taxes are merged and crowd scenes moved. Caiaphas's final prayer is DeMille's invention. The 1927 roadshow version (about 155 minutes) and the 1928 general release (about 112) differ; the longer cut adds an exorcism and other material but also puts the opening in colour, which weakens the colour Resurrection.
advisories:
The opening shows a decadent party and a scantily dressed Magdalene; it is brief.

The scourging and Crucifixion are restrained by modern standards; Judas's suicide is cut against the Crucifixion; earthquake and storm.

Silent with intertitles. Greydanus rates it suitable for children and up, with these caveats.

title: The Nun's Story
decision: PUBLISH (adults and older teens): The AFI Catalog and Greydanus's Decent Films review show a serious, largely respectful account of pre-conciliar religious formation whose heroine leaves by lawful dispensation after judging herself unable to keep obedience, not a film that attacks the vows. Zinnemann deliberately withholds a verdict on her departure (AFI: no end-title music for that reason); Greydanus calls it neither anti-religious nor anti-Catholic. The film's ambiguity about whether the Rule or the nun is at fault is recorded plainly in the text and advisories.
summary: Audrey Hepburn plays a Belgian surgeon's daughter who becomes a nursing sister, serves in the Congo, and after years of struggle with obedience asks to be released from her vows.
synopsis: In the 1920s Gabrielle Van der Mal enters a nursing order in Bruges, hoping to serve in the Congo. As Sister Luke she learns the Rule: silence, custody of the eyes, obedience to the bell. Her superiors test her pride; one even urges her to fail an exam as an act of humility. She is sent to an asylum, then at last to the Congo, where she works beside a brilliant, irreligious surgeon and falls ill with tuberculosis. Recalled to Belgium, she faces the German occupation. Ordered to show charity to the enemy, she secretly helps the Resistance, and when her father is killed she finds herself full of hatred. Concluding that she can no longer be a true nun, she asks for release, signs the papers, changes into a dress and walks out of the convent.
inclusion: No Hollywood film before or since has shown the formation of a religious so carefully. The first hour, which the New York Times likened to a documentary, explains the vows through the words of superiors, and the rituals of the novitiate are filmed with patience. Hepburn is superb, entirely inward; Edith Evans is formidable as a superior, and Peter Finch plays the atheist surgeon who tells her she is a 'worldly nun' and that her real illness is the struggle to conform. Franz Planer's photography of Bruges and the Congo is beautiful. The film is long and its second half loses some of the first half's concentration. It is not a happy story. But it treats the religious life as a real and serious calling, and its sisters include warm and holy women as well as harsh ones.
themes: The film is about obedience. Sister Luke's struggle is not with faith in God but with the surrender of her will: leaving a dying patient at the sound of the bell, accepting humiliation, forgiving the men who killed her father. The Rule is presented in its own terms, and the superiors explain why the sacrifice of liberty matters. Greydanus notes that the bad advice to fail an exam is later corrected by another superior. The Congo scenes include a priest serving lepers in penance for his sins, and a sister murdered by a man in thrall to a witch doctor, whose fellow nuns' forgiveness draws villagers to the Christmas Eve service. Where the film is open to question is its refusal to judge the outcome: it never settles whether the fault lies with the Rule, the community or Sister Luke herself, and some viewers will read her departure as liberation. Read faithfully, it is the story of a vocation honestly found wanting, not of a vocation exposed as false.
history: Kathryn Hulme's 1956 novel was based on Marie-Louise Habets, a Belgian nursing sister who left her order during the Second World War; Hulme met her among refugees in 1945. The film was shot in Rome, Belgium and the Belgian Congo, including a leper settlement, and a real Congo missionary played Father André.
liberties: Names and some events are fictionalised from Habets's life by way of Hulme's novel. The Resistance episodes and the doctor's role are shaped for drama. The order is not named in the film.
advisories:
A violent attack in a mental asylum and a murder in the Congo; wartime bombing; scenes in a leper colony.

No sexual content, but unspoken attraction between the nun and the surgeon.

The heroine leaves religious life at the end, and the film does not say whether she was right. Greydanus rates it for adults; it suits mature teens with discussion.
